knowledge_statements.title: Simple Undirected Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite simple undirected graphs, excluding loops and parallel edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite simple undirected graph is an ordered pair \(G=(V,E)\), where \(V\) is a finite set and \(E\subseteq \binom{V}{2}=\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in V,\ u\ne v\}\). Each edge is therefore an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Because \(E\) is a set of pairs, at most one edge has any prescribed pair of endpoints, and because every member of \(E\) has cardinality two, no edge is a loop.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple undirected graph has finitely many vertices and unordered edges joining distinct vertex pairs, with neither loops nor parallel edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\subseteq \binom{V}{2}\).

notation.meaning: set of two-element subsets of V

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Undirected graphs p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simple undirected graphs and their basic traversal objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines loopless simple undirected graphs, degrees, walks, paths, cycles, and connectedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simple undirected graph is a pair \(G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal E)\), where every edge is an unordered pair \(\{i,j\}\subseteq\mathcal N\) with \(i\ne j\); thus \(\{i,j\}=\{j,i\}\), and self-edges are excluded. The degree of a node is the number of incident edges, and the degree of the graph is the maximum node degree. A walk is a finite sequence \(i_1,\ldots,i_t\) satisfying \(\{i_k,i_{k+1}\}\in\mathcal E\) for every \(k<t\). It is a path when no node repeats, and it is a cycle when \(i_1,\ldots,i_{t-1}\) are distinct, \(i_t=i_1\), and \(t-1\ge 3\). The graph is connected exactly when every two distinct nodes are joined by a path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple undirected graph has distinct-node unordered edges and no self-edges. Node degree counts incident edges, and graph degree is the maximum node degree. A walk follows adjacent nodes; a path has no repeated nodes; a cycle returns to its initial node after at least three distinct nodes; and the graph is connected when every distinct node pair has a path between them.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is connected}\iff \forall i,j\in\mathcal N,\ i\ne j\Rightarrow\exists\text{ an }i\text{--}j\text{ path}.

children.top_down_role: Undirected structures permitting self-incidence.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e\text{ is a loop at }v\iff \partial(e)=\{v,v\}\), and \(\partial\) is injective.

notation.meaning: finite set of distinguishable edge objects

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite undirected graphs permitting loops but excluding parallel edges.

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Undirected graphs p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite looped undirected graph is a triple \(G=(V,E,\partial)\), where \(V\) and \(E\) are finite sets and \(\partial:E\to\{M:M\text{ is a two-element multiset over }V\}\) is an injective map assigning an unordered endpoint multiset to every edge. An edge \(e\in E\) is a loop at \(v\in V\) exactly when \(\partial(e)=\{v,v\}\). Loops are permitted, while injectivity of \(\partial\) excludes distinct edges with the same endpoint multiset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite looped undirected graph assigns each edge an unordered pair of endpoints that may coincide, while excluding parallel edges with the same endpoint multiset.
knowledge_statements.title: Looped Undirected Graphs

children.title: Parallel-Edge Multigraphs
children.top_down_role: Undirected structures permitting multiple edges between a vertex pair.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Edge Multigraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite loopless undirected multigraphs allowing repeated endpoint pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite loopless undirected multigraph is a triple \(G=(V,E,\partial)\), where \(V\) and \(E\) are finite sets and \(\partial:E\to\binom{V}{2}\) maps each edge object to its unordered pair of distinct endpoints. Two distinct edges \(e,f\in E\) are parallel when \(\partial(e)=\partial(f)\). Thus parallel edges are permitted precisely because \(\partial\) need not be injective; loops are excluded because every endpoint set belongs to \(\binom{V}{2}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A loopless undirected multigraph uses distinct edge objects and may map several of them to the same pair of distinct endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e\parallel f\iff e\ne f\text{ and }\partial(e)=\partial(f)\).

notation.meaning: edges e and f are parallel

children.title: Directed Graphs
children.top_down_role: Graphical structures whose edges carry orientations.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite directed graphs represented by distinguishable arcs and endpoint maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite directed graph is a quadruple \(D=(V,A,t,h)\), where \(V\) is a finite vertex set, \(A\) is a finite set of arc objects, and \(t,h:A\to V\) assign each arc its tail and head. An arc \(a\) is directed from \(t(a)\) to \(h(a)\). A loop satisfies \(t(a)=h(a)\), and distinct arcs \(a,b\) are parallel when \((t(a),h(a))=(t(b),h(b))\). Simplicity may be imposed by forbidding loops and requiring the ordered-endpoint map to be injective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed graph assigns every arc an ordered tail and head; additional restrictions determine whether loops or parallel arcs are allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\text{ is the arc }t(a)\to h(a)\).

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Directed graphs p. 28

children.title: Mixed Graphs
children.top_down_role: Graphical structures containing both arcs and undirected edges.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite graphs containing both undirected edges and directed arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite mixed graph is a tuple \(M=(V,E,A,\partial,t,h)\), where \(V\) is finite, \(E\) and \(A\) are disjoint finite sets of undirected edges and directed arcs, \(\partial:E\to\binom{V}{2}\) assigns an unordered endpoint pair to each edge, and \(t,h:A\to V\) assign a tail and head to each arc. Hence adjacency contributed by \(e\in E\) is symmetric, whereas an arc \(a\in A\) has the ordered incidence \(t(a)\to h(a)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed graph combines undirected edges with directed arcs on one vertex set, preserving unordered and ordered incidence respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\cap A=\varnothing\), with incidence maps \(\partial:E\to\binom{V}{2}\) and \((t,h):A\to V\times V\).

notation.meaning: edge endpoint, arc tail, and arc head maps

children.title: Orientation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Relationships between undirected ground graphs and their directed orientations.

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orientations of loopless undirected multigraphs, including constrained orientation families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,\partial)\) be a finite loopless undirected multigraph. An orientation is a pair of maps \(t,h:E\to V\) such that \(\{t(e),h(e)\}=\partial(e)\) for every \(e\in E\); it replaces each undirected edge independently by one of its two possible directions. An orientation regime is any specified family \(\mathcal O\) of such orientations, possibly defined by degree, reachability, connectivity, or prescribed-direction constraints. The unconstrained regime consists of all \(2^{|E|}\) orientations of the distinguishable edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orientation chooses one direction for each loopless undirected edge; an orientation regime is a family of choices satisfying stated constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O\subseteq\{(t,h):\{t(e),h(e)\}=\partial(e)\text{ for every }e\in E\}\).

notation.meaning: chosen tail and head of edge e

children.title: Hypergraphs
children.top_down_role: Higher-arity edge systems over a common vertex ground set.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypergraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite simple hypergraphs with arbitrary nonempty edge cardinalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite hypergraph is an ordered pair \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\), where \(V\) is a finite vertex set and \(\mathcal E\subseteq 2^V\setminus\{\varnothing\}\) is a family of nonempty subsets called hyperedges. A vertex \(v\) is incident with a hyperedge \(F\) exactly when \(v\in F\). Hyperedges may have arbitrary cardinality; imposing \(|F|=r\) for every \(F\in\mathcal E\) gives an \(r\)-uniform hypergraph. Treating \(\mathcal E\) as a set excludes repeated hyperedges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite hypergraph consists of vertices and a family of nonempty vertex subsets, called hyperedges, whose sizes need not equal two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal E\subseteq 2^V\setminus\{\varnothing\}\).

children.title: Clutters
children.top_down_role: Inclusion-minimal set families used in covering and blocking structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Clutters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite antichain hypergraphs under set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A clutter is a finite hypergraph \(C=(V,\mathcal E)\) whose hyperedge family is an antichain under inclusion: for all distinct \(F,F'\in\mathcal E\), neither \(F\subseteq F'\) nor \(F'\subseteq F\). Equivalently, \(F\subseteq F'\) for members \(F,F'\in\mathcal E\) implies \(F=F'\). Thus every edge of a clutter is inclusion-minimal within its edge family, and no edge properly contains another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clutter is a finite hypergraph in which no hyperedge properly contains another hyperedge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall F,F'\in\mathcal E,\ F\subseteq F'\Rightarrow F=F'\).

notation.meaning: clutter with vertex set V and edge family E

children.title: General Set Systems
children.top_down_role: Families of subsets without uniformity or minimality restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: General Set Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite ground sets equipped with unrestricted families of subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite set system is an ordered pair \((V,\mathcal F)\), where \(V\) is a finite ground set and \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^V\) is an arbitrary family of subsets. Unless extra conditions are stated, \(\mathcal F\) may be empty, may contain \(\varnothing\) or \(V\), and need not be uniform, intersecting, inclusion-closed, or an antichain. Its incidence relation is \(I=\{(v,F)\in V\times\mathcal F:v\in F\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite set system is a finite ground set together with an otherwise unrestricted family of its subsets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^V\) and \(I=\{(v,F):v\in F\}\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\in E_v\iff v\in F\), and \(M(H^*)=M(H)^{\mathsf T}\).

notation.meaning: incidence dual of H, represented with an indexed dual-edge family
dual edge indexed by the original vertex v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dualization of finite incidence systems by transposing membership incidence while retaining indexed dual edges.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Elements of graphs and hypergraphs p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) be a finite set system. Its incidence dual is the incidence system \(H^*=(\mathcal E,(E_v)_{v\in V})\), whose vertex set is \(\mathcal E\) and whose dual edge indexed by \(v\in V\) is \(E_v=\{F\in\mathcal E:v\in F\}\). Thus \(F\in E_v\) if and only if \(v\in F\). If the incidence matrix \(M(H)\) has rows indexed by \(V\) and columns indexed by \(\mathcal E\), then \(M(H^*)=M(H)^{\mathsf T}\). When distinct vertices have identical incidences, their equal sets \(E_v\) remain distinct members of the indexed dual-edge family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The incidence dual exchanges the two indexed sides of the membership relation, transposes the incidence matrix, and retains distinct dual-edge indices even when their incident sets coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Incidence Duals

children.title: Walk Systems
children.top_down_role: Traversal structures permitting repeated vertices or edges.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,\partial)\) is a finite loopless undirected multigraph with \(\partial:E\to\binom{V}{2}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W\in\mathcal W\Rightarrow \partial(e_i)=\{v_{i-1},v_i\}\text{ for }1\le i\le k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Families of finite walks in a finite loopless undirected multigraph.

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Undirected graphs p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,\partial)\) be a finite loopless undirected multigraph with \(\partial:E\to\binom{V}{2}\). A walk of length \(k\ge 0\) is an alternating sequence \(W=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) such that \(\partial(e_i)=\{v_{i-1},v_i\}\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,k\). Vertices and edges may repeat. A walk system is any specified family \(\mathcal W\) of such walks in \(G\), possibly restricted by endpoints, length, or other stated predicates. The walk is closed exactly when \(v_0=v_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A walk system in a finite loopless undirected multigraph is a family of alternating vertex-edge sequences in which each intervening edge joins its neighboring vertices; vertices and edges may repeat.
knowledge_statements.title: Walk Systems

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1 Undirected graphs p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Walks, paths, trails, and directed walks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The composite extract supports these traversal definitions at Walk Systems; connectivity, Eulerian, Hamiltonian, tree, and branching material is not assigned here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a graph or digraph, a walk is a finite alternating sequence $W=v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k$ with $k\ge0$, where each edge or arc $e_i$ has endnodes $v_{i-1}$ and $v_i$. Its origin and terminus are $v_0$ and $v_k$, its internal nodes are $v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}$, and its length is $k$. In a digraph, the walk is directed when $e_i=(v_{i-1},v_i)$ for every $i$. A path is a walk whose nodes are all distinct, whereas a trail is a walk whose edges or arcs are all distinct. A directed path is a path that is also a directed walk.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A walk alternates vertices with incident edges or arcs and may have length zero. A directed walk follows every arc from the preceding vertex to the succeeding vertex. A path has no repeated vertices, a trail has no repeated edges or arcs, and a directed path is both a path and a directed walk.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W\text{ is a path}\iff v_0,\ldots,v_k\text{ are distinct},\quad W\text{ is a trail}\iff e_1,\ldots,e_k\text{ are distinct},\quad W\text{ is directed}\iff e_i=(v_{i-1},v_i)\ \forall i.

children.top_down_role: Simple terminal-to-terminal traversal structures.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,\partial)\) is a finite loopless undirected multigraph with \(\partial:E\to\binom{V}{2}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\in\mathcal P\Rightarrow v_i\ne v_j\text{ whenever }0\le i<j\le k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,\partial)\) be a finite loopless undirected multigraph with \(\partial:E\to\binom{V}{2}\). A path of length \(k\ge 0\) is a walk \(P=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) satisfying \(\partial(e_i)=\{v_{i-1},v_i\}\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,k\), with the vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_k\) pairwise distinct. Consequently, its edges are also distinct. A path system is any specified family \(\mathcal P\) of paths in \(G\), possibly restricted by prescribed endpoint pairs or other stated predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path system in a finite loopless undirected multigraph is a family of walks with no repeated vertices, possibly restricted by endpoints or other explicit conditions.

children.title: Trail Systems
children.top_down_role: Traversal structures without repeated edges.

knowledge_statements.title: Trail Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite undirected-graph definition, allowing open and closed trails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A trail of length \(m\ge 0\) is an alternating sequence \(T=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_m,v_m)\) such that each edge \(e_i\) has endpoints \(v_{i-1}\) and \(v_i\), and the edges \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\) are pairwise distinct. Vertices may repeat. The trail is closed when \(v_0=v_m\), and open otherwise. A trail system is an indexed family \(\mathcal T=(T_j)_{j\in J}\) of trails in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trail is a walk with no repeated edge; vertices may repeat. A trail system is an indexed family of such trails in one finite graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T=(T_j)_{j\in J}\) is a trail system exactly when every \(T_j\) is a trail in \(G\).

notation.meaning: A trail represented by its alternating vertex-edge sequence.

children.title: Cycle Systems
children.top_down_role: Closed traversal structures across directed and undirected settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple cycles in finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A cycle is a closed trail \(C=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_m,v_m)\) with \(m\ge 3\), \(v_m=v_0\), and pairwise distinct vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_{m-1}\). Thus its edges are also pairwise distinct. A cycle system is an indexed family \(\mathcal C=(C_j)_{j\in J}\) of cycles of \(G\); no disjointness between different members is implied unless imposed separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cycle is a closed trail of length at least three with no repeated vertex except the common start and end. A cycle system is an indexed family of cycles.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph without loops.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C=(C_j)_{j\in J}\) is a cycle system exactly when every \(C_j\) is a cycle of \(G\).

children.top_down_role: Vertex-disjoint, edge-disjoint, and internally disjoint traversal families.

knowledge_statements.title: Traversal Disjointness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise disjointness conventions for finite families of graph traversals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For traversals \(T_1,\ldots,T_k\) in a graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(E(T_i)\) and \(V(T_i)\) denote their used edges and vertices. The family is edge-disjoint when \(E(T_i)\cap E(T_j)=\varnothing\) for all \(i
e j\), and vertex-disjoint when \(V(T_i)\cap V(T_j)=\varnothing\) for all \(i
e j\). Given a permitted terminal set \(R\subseteq V\), it is internally vertex-disjoint relative to \(R\) when \((V(T_i)\setminus R)\cap(V(T_j)\setminus R)=\varnothing\) for all \(i
e j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Traversals may be pairwise edge-disjoint, vertex-disjoint, or internally vertex-disjoint after permitted common terminals are removed.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq V\) is the set of vertices allowed to be shared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed pairwise intersection predicates define the edge-, vertex-, and relative internal-vertex-disjointness regimes.

notation.meaning: Vertices permitted to occur in multiple traversals.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Internally Disjoint Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General path-disjointness terminology independent of a particular routing model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(\mathcal P\) of paths is internally disjoint if no two distinct paths in \(\mathcal P\) have an edge or an internal vertex in common. Their endpoints may coincide. When the endpoint set is fixed, such paths are also sometimes called vertex-disjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Paths are internally disjoint when no two share an edge or an internal vertex; they may share endpoints. With fixed endpoints, they are also sometimes called vertex-disjoint.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal P\text{ is a set of paths}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P\text{ is internally disjoint}\iff\forall P\ne Q\in\mathcal P:\ E(P)\cap E(Q)=\varnothing\text{ and }\operatorname{int}V(P)\cap\operatorname{int}V(Q)=\varnothing

children.title: Graph Cuts
children.top_down_role: Edge boundaries induced by vertex partitions in undirected graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected edge cuts and their capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. For \(S\subseteq V\), the edge cut induced by \(S\) is \(\delta_G(S)=\{uv\in E: u\in S,\ v\in V\setminus S\}\). It is proper when \(\varnothing\ne S\ne V\). If \(c:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\) assigns edge capacities, the cut capacity is \(c(\delta_G(S))=\sum_{e\in\delta_G(S)}c(e)\). The sets \(S\) and \(V\setminus S\) induce the same undirected cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph cut consists of edges with one endpoint in a vertex set and the other outside it; its capacity is the sum of their capacities.
assumptions_latex: \(c:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\) when cut capacities are considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_G(S)=\delta_G(V\setminus S)\), with capacity \(\sum_{e\in\delta_G(S)}c(e)\).

notation.meaning: The undirected edge boundary of vertex set \(S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Undirected cuts, separating edge sets, and bridges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The empty edge set is always a cut. It is representable by a nonempty proper shore, and hence is a nontrivial cut, exactly when the graph is disconnected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $G=(V,E)$ and $U\subseteq V$, let $\delta_G(U)$ be the set of edges joining $U$ to $V\setminus U$, and let $d_G(U)=|\delta_G(U)|$. A cut is an edge set $F=\delta_G(U)$; it is nontrivial when $\varnothing
eq U
eq V$. For all $T,U\subseteq V$, $\delta(T)	riangle\delta(U)=\delta(T	riangle U)$, so the cuts are closed under symmetric difference. If $s\in U$ and $t
otin U$, then $\delta(U)$ is an $s$-$t$ cut; it is an $S$-$T$ cut when $S\subseteq U$ and $T\subseteq V\setminus U$. An edge set is $s$-$t$ disconnecting when it meets every $s$-$t$ path. Every $s$-$t$ cut is $s$-$t$ disconnecting, and every inclusionwise minimal $s$-$t$ disconnecting edge set is an $s$-$t$ cut. An edge $e$ is a bridge iff $\{e\}$ is a cut, and $G$ is bridgeless iff it has no bridge. For $U,W\subseteq V$, $E[U,W]$ is the family of edges having one end in $U$ and the other in $W$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut is the edge boundary of a vertex subset. Cuts include the empty set and are closed under symmetric difference. Every terminal cut separates its terminals, while every inclusion-minimal terminal-separating edge set is a terminal cut. A bridge is an edge whose singleton is a cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta(T)\triangle\delta(U)=\delta(T\triangle U),\qquad \delta(U)\text{ an }s\text{-}t\text{ cut}\Rightarrow\delta(U)\text{ meets every }s\text{-}t\text{ path},\qquad F\text{ inclusionwise minimal }s\text{-}t\text{ disconnecting}\Rightarrow F\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ cut}.

knowledge_statements.title: Cocycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary cut-space definition for finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), identify an edge set with its incidence vector in \(\mathbb F_2^E\). The cocycle space is \(\mathcal B^*(G)=\{\delta_G(S):S\subseteq V\}\), where addition is symmetric difference. Equivalently, \(F\subseteq E\) is a cocycle precisely when every cycle of \(G\) meets \(F\) in an even number of edges. A nonempty inclusion-minimal cocycle is a bond. Distinct vertex sets may represent the same cocycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cocycles are graph cuts viewed as vectors over the binary field; equivalently, they meet every cycle evenly. Minimal nonempty cocycles are bonds.
assumptions_latex: Edge-set addition is symmetric difference, equivalently addition in \(\mathbb F_2^E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\in\mathcal B^*(G)\) if and only if \(|F\cap E(C)|\equiv 0\pmod 2\) for every cycle \(C\) of \(G\).

notation.meaning: The binary cocycle or cut space of the graph.
The cut induced by vertex set \(S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separating sets, cocycles, cutsets, and source–sink cutsets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-separation definitions, with arc orientations ignored when the input is a digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(N,A) be a graph, or a digraph viewed without arc orientations. A set C\subseteq A is a separating set if (N,A\setminus C) has more connected components than G; an inclusion-minimal separating set is a cocycle. For every cocycle C, there is a partition N=S\mathbin{\dot\cup}T such that C consists exactly of the arcs with one endpoint in S and the other in T, and G-C contains no s\text{--}t path for s\in S and t\in T. A separating set consisting of all arcs crossing such a partition is a cutset. A cutset need not be a cocycle because it need not be minimal. It is an (s,t)-cutset when s\in S and t\in T.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ignoring arc orientations in a digraph, a separating set is an arc set whose deletion increases the number of connected components, and a cocycle is an inclusion-minimal separating set. Every cocycle is exactly the crossing set of some vertex bipartition, and its deletion leaves no path between opposite sides. A separating crossing set is a cutset, which need not be minimal; it is an (s,t)-cutset when s and t are on the designated opposite sides.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is a graph, or a digraph whose arc orientations are ignored.}
N=S\mathbin{\dot\cup}T\text{ when a partition-induced crossing set is considered.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is a cocycle precisely when it is an inclusion-minimal separating set; every cocycle equals the crossing set of some bipartition, whereas a cutset need not be minimal.}

knowledge_statements.title: Bisets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Biset notation and the associated undirected edge boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A biset on a finite ground set \(V\) is an ordered pair \(\mathbb X=(X_O,X_I)\) with \(X_I\subseteq X_O\subseteq V\). The sets \(X_I\), \(X_O\), and \(X_O\setminus X_I\) are its inner part, outer part, and boundary. Its co-biset is \(\overline{\mathbb X}=(V\setminus X_I,V\setminus X_O)\). In an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), the biset cut is \(\delta_G(\mathbb X)=\{uv\in E:u\in X_I,\ v\in V\setminus X_O\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A biset consists of nested inner and outer vertex sets. Its graph boundary contains edges from the inner set to vertices outside the outer set.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is undirected when the biset cut is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_G(\mathbb X)=E_G(X_I,V\setminus X_O)\), and \(X_O\setminus X_I\) is the biset boundary.

notation.meaning: A biset with outer part listed first and inner part second.
Edges from the inner part to outside the outer part.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Cut Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entering and leaving cuts in finite directed graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph and \(S\subseteq V\). The leaving cut and entering cut of \(S\) are \(\delta_D^+(S)=\{uv\in A:u\in S,\ v\in V\setminus S\}\) and \(\delta_D^-(S)=\{uv\in A:u\in V\setminus S,\ v\in S\}\), respectively. They satisfy \(\delta_D^+(S)=\delta_D^-(V\setminus S)\). For arc capacities \(c:A\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), their capacities are obtained by summing \(c(a)\) over their arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed cut separates arcs leaving a vertex set from arcs entering it. Complementation exchanges the two orientations.
assumptions_latex: \(c:A\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) when directed-cut capacities are considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_D^+(S)=\delta_D^-(V\setminus S)\) and \(\delta_D^-(S)=\delta_D^+(V\setminus S)\).

children.title: Connected Components

knowledge_statements.title: Connected Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical vertex partition of a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. Define \(u\sim v\) when a path in \(G\) joins \(u\) to \(v\), including the length-zero path when \(u=v\). This is an equivalence relation on \(V\). Its equivalence classes are the connected components of \(G\); equivalently, each component is an inclusion-maximal vertex set \(C\subseteq V\) for which the induced subgraph \(G[C]\) is connected. The components form a unique partition of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertices belong to the same connected component exactly when a path joins them. The components uniquely partition the graph's vertex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V=C_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_k\), where each \(G[C_i]\) is connected and no edge joins distinct classes.

notation.meaning: The subgraph induced by vertex set \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Connected graphs and connected components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Components are nonempty and maximal with respect to the subgraph relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph $G=(V,E)$ is connected iff every pair $u,v\in V$ is joined by a path. A connected component is a maximal connected nonempty subgraph. Every component is induced, and every vertex and every edge belongs to exactly one component. Equivalently, the vertex sets of the components are the equivalence classes of $u\sim v$ iff a path joins $u$ and $v$. A component is odd or even according as its number of vertices is odd or even.

Its connected components are the maximal nonempty connected subgraphs; they are induced, partition the vertices and edges, and coincide with the equivalence classes of path reachability. Component parity is determined by its number of vertices.

knowledge_statements.title: Biconnected Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximal two-vertex-connected subgraphs; bridges and isolated vertices are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A biconnected block is an inclusion-maximal vertex set \(B\subseteq V\), with \(|B|\ge3\), such that \(G[B]\) is connected and remains connected after deletion of any one vertex of \(B\). Equivalently, every two distinct vertices of \(B\) are joined in \(G[B]\) by two internally vertex-disjoint paths. Distinct biconnected blocks may intersect only at articulation vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A biconnected block is a maximal induced subgraph of at least three vertices that stays connected after any single vertex is removed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(v\in B\), the graph \(G[B\setminus\{v\}]\) is connected, and no proper superset of \(B\) has this property.

notation.meaning: The vertex set of a biconnected block.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical mutual-reachability partition of a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph. Define \(u\sim_D v\) when both a directed path from \(u\) to \(v\) and a directed path from \(v\) to \(u\) exist. This is an equivalence relation on \(V\). Its equivalence classes are the strongly connected components of \(D\), equivalently the inclusion-maximal vertex sets inducing strongly connected subgraphs. Contracting each strong component to one vertex produces an acyclic directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two vertices share a strong component exactly when each is reachable from the other. These components partition the vertices, and their contraction is acyclic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equivalence classes of \(\sim_D\) uniquely partition \(V\), and the component-contraction digraph is acyclic.

knowledge_statements.title: Separator-Based Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition induced by deleting a vertex separator from an undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected finite undirected graph and let \(S\subsetneq V\) be a vertex separator, so \(G-S\) has connected-component vertex sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\) with \(k\ge2\). Then \(V=S\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_k\), no edge joins \(C_i\) to \(C_j\) for \(i\ne j\), and \(G\) is represented by the pieces \(G[S\cup C_i]\), whose pairwise vertex intersections are exactly \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting a vertex separator yields components with no edges between them; adjoining the separator to each component gives overlapping decomposition pieces.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subsetneq V\) and \(G-S\) has at least two connected components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=\bigcup_{i=1}^kG[S\cup C_i]\), with \((S\cup C_i)\cap(S\cup C_j)=S\) for \(i\ne j\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(u,v\in V\) be distinct. Define the local edge-connectivity \(\lambda_G(u,v)\) as the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint \(u\)-\(v\) paths. If \(u\) and \(v\) are nonadjacent, define the local vertex-connectivity \(\kappa_G(u,v)\) as the maximum number of pairwise internally vertex-disjoint \(u\)-\(v\) paths. Then \(\lambda_G(u,v)\) equals the minimum cardinality of a set \(F\subseteq E\) such that \(u\) and \(v\) are disconnected in \(G-F\). When \(u\) and \(v\) are nonadjacent, \(\kappa_G(u,v)\) equals the minimum cardinality of a set \(S\subseteq V\setminus\{u,v\}\) such that \(u\) and \(v\) are disconnected in \(G-S\).

If the vertices are nonadjacent, the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint paths equals the minimum number of other vertices whose deletion separates them.

children.title: Global Connectivity
children.top_down_role: Whole-structure resistance to vertex or edge separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected global edge-connectivity, expressed uniformly over all nontrivial cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected multigraph with \(|V|\ge 2\). For \(S\subset V\), let \(\delta_G(S)\) be the set of edges having exactly one endpoint in \(S\). The global edge-connectivity of \(G\) is
\[
\lambda(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}|\delta_G(S)|.
\]
For an integer \(k\ge 1\), the graph is globally \(k\)-edge-connected precisely when \(\lambda(G)\ge k\), equivalently when deleting any set of fewer than \(k\) edges leaves \(G\) connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global edge-connectivity is the smallest size of a nontrivial edge cut; it is at least k exactly when fewer than k edge deletions cannot disconnect the graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is globally \(k\)-edge-connected if and only if \(\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}|\delta_G(S)|\ge k\).

notation.meaning: Edge boundary of the vertex set S in G.

children.title: Rooted Connectivity

knowledge_statements.title: Rooted Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected rooted edge-connectivity from one distinguished vertex to every other vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected multigraph, let \(r\in V\), and let \(k\ge 1\). The rooted graph \((G,r)\) is rooted \(k\)-edge-connected if
\[
|\delta_G(S)|\ge k\qquad\text{for every }\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(v\in V\setminus\{r\}\), there exist at least \(k\) pairwise edge-disjoint paths joining \(r\) to \(v\). Thus every vertex remains reachable from the root after deletion of fewer than \(k\) edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rooted graph is k-edge-connected when every cut separating the root from any vertex has at least k edges, equivalently when k edge-disjoint root-to-vertex paths exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((G,r)\) is rooted \(k\)-edge-connected if and only if every \(r\)-to-\(v\) edge cut has size at least \(k\).

notation.meaning: Edges with exactly one endpoint in S.

children.title: Directed Connectivity Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Connectivity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard weak, unilateral, and strong connectivity classes for finite directed graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph. It is weakly connected when the undirected graph obtained by forgetting arc orientations is connected. It is unilaterally connected when, for every distinct \(u,v\in V\), either a directed \(u\)-to-\(v\) path or a directed \(v\)-to-\(u\) path exists. It is strongly connected when both such directed paths exist for every ordered pair. Consequently,
\[
\text{strong connectivity}\Longrightarrow\text{unilateral connectivity}\Longrightarrow\text{weak connectivity}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed graphs admit nested weak, unilateral, and strong connectivity regimes according to whether reachability exists after ignoring orientation, in one direction, or in both directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every strongly connected digraph is unilaterally connected, and every unilaterally connected digraph is weakly connected.

notation.meaning: Directed graph with vertex set V and arc set A.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite undirected bipartite graphs and their odd-cycle characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) is bipartite if there are disjoint sets \(X,Y\subseteq V\) such that \(V=X\mathbin{\dot\cup}Y\) and every edge has one endpoint in \(X\) and the other in \(Y\). Equivalently, there is a map \(c:V\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(uv\in E\). A finite undirected graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no cycle of odd length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is bipartite when its vertices split into two classes and every edge crosses between them; equivalently, the graph has no odd cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is bipartite if and only if \(G\) contains no odd cycle.

notation.meaning: Disjoint union of the two vertex classes.
A proper two-coloring of the vertices.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartite and complete bipartite graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bipartite graphs, records their even-circuit characterization, and defines complete bipartite graphs, stars, and claws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph $G=(V,E)$, the following are equivalent: $\chi(G)\le 2$; there is a partition $V=U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W$ such that every edge has one endpoint in $U$ and the other in $W$; and every circuit of $G$ has even length. The sets $U$ and $W$ are called colour classes and need not be unique. A complete bipartite graph is a simple graph whose vertex set has such a partition and whose edges are exactly the pairs $\{u,w\}$ with $u\in U$ and $w\in W$. If $|U|=m$ and $|W|=n$, it is denoted $K_{m,n}$. The graphs $K_{1,n}$ are stars and, when $n\ge 3$, are also called claws.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is bipartite exactly when its vertices can be partitioned into two color classes so that every edge joins the classes; equivalently, every circuit has even length. The complete bipartite graph with class sizes m and n is denoted K_m,n. The graphs K_1,n are stars and, for n at least 3, are also called claws.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is bipartite}\iff \chi(G)\le 2\iff \text{every circuit of }G\text{ has even length}

knowledge_statements.title: Eulerian Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connected finite undirected multigraphs characterized by Euler tours and even degrees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite undirected multigraph \(G=(V,E)\) with at least one edge is Eulerian if it has a closed trail containing every edge exactly once. Such a trail is an Euler tour. The graph \(G\) is Eulerian if and only if all vertices incident with edges belong to one connected component and
\[
\deg_G(v)\equiv 0\pmod 2
\]
for every \(v\in V\). Loops contribute two to the degree, so the characterization also applies to multigraphs with loops.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An Eulerian graph has a closed trail using every edge once; this occurs exactly when its nonisolated part is connected and every vertex has even degree.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected multigraph with at least one edge.
Each loop contributes two to its incident vertex's degree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has an Euler tour if and only if its nonisolated vertices are connected and every vertex has even degree.

notation.meaning: Degree of v in G, counting each loop twice.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An orientation \(D=(V,A)\) of an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) is Eulerian if \(\deg_A^{\mathrm{in}}(v)=\deg_A^{\mathrm{out}}(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). The graph \(G\) has an Eulerian orientation if and only if \(\deg_G(v)\) is even for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orientation is Eulerian when every vertex has equal indegree and outdegree. An undirected graph has an Eulerian orientation exactly when every vertex has even degree; connectivity is not required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is Eulerian}\iff \forall v\in V,\ \deg_A^{\mathrm{in}}(v)=\deg_A^{\mathrm{out}}(v),\qquad G\text{ has an Eulerian orientation}\iff \forall v\in V,\ \deg_G(v)\text{ is even.}

knowledge_statements.title: Parity Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut and cycle parity laws linking Eulerian and bipartite graph structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. For every \(S\subseteq V\) and every subgraph \(H\) in which all vertex degrees are even,
\[
|E(H)\cap\delta_G(S)|\equiv 0\pmod 2.
\]
Thus every Eulerian subgraph crosses every cut an even number of times. Dually, a vertex two-coloring exists exactly when every cycle has even length. These two tests expose the cut-side and cycle-side parity constraints underlying Eulerian and bipartite graph regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eulerian subgraphs meet every cut evenly, while bipartite graphs have only even cycles; these are the fundamental cut-side and cycle-side parity tests.
assumptions_latex: Every vertex of \(H\) has even degree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|E(H)\cap\delta_G(S)|\) is even for every \(S\subseteq V\), and \(G\) is bipartite exactly when all its cycles are even.

notation.meaning: Cut consisting of edges with exactly one endpoint in S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Planar embeddings, planar graphs, and faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric representation of a graph in the plane without crossings and the face decomposition induced by a fixed embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A planar embedding of a graph \(G\) consists of an injective map \(\psi:V(G)\to\mathbb{R}^2\) and, for every edge \(e=\{x,y\}\), a polygonal arc \(J_e\) with endpoints \(\psi(x)\) and \(\psi(y)\), such that \[\bigl(J_e\setminus\{\psi(x),\psi(y)\}\bigr)\cap\left(\{\psi(v):v\in V(G)\}\cup\bigcup_{e'\in E(G)\setminus\{e\}}J_{e'}\right)=\varnothing.\] A graph is planar if it has a planar embedding. For a fixed planar embedding \(\Phi=(\psi,(J_e)_{e\in E(G)})\), its faces are the open connected regions of \[\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\left(\{\psi(v):v\in V(G)\}\cup\bigcup_{e\in E(G)}J_e\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A planar embedding maps distinct vertices to distinct points and represents edges by polygonal arcs whose interiors meet no embedded vertex or other edge arc. A graph is planar if such an embedding exists. The faces of a fixed embedding are the open connected regions left after removing its vertices and edge arcs from the plane.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is planar}\iff G\text{ has a planar embedding, and the faces of }\Phi\text{ are the open connected regions of its complement.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Planar Embeddings, Plane Graphs, and Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines planar embeddings, planar and plane graphs, and the faces determined by a plane graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A planar embedding of a graph \(G\) represents distinct vertices by distinct points of \(\mathbb R^2\) and each edge by a simple curve joining its ends and meeting no other vertex, with every intersection of two edge-curves being an end of both edges. A graph is planar if it has a planar embedding, and a plane graph is a graph together with a chosen planar embedding. The faces of a plane graph are the equivalence classes of points outside its vertices and edges under connection by a simple curve lying entirely outside the graph. Every plane graph has exactly one unbounded face, called the infinite face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A planar embedding draws a graph in the plane without edge crossings except at common endpoints. A planar graph admits such an embedding, while a plane graph includes a chosen embedding. Its faces are the curve-connected regions outside the drawing, exactly one of which is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is planar}\iff G\text{ has a planar embedding},\qquad \text{every plane graph has exactly one unbounded face}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Planar embeddings, faces, and Euler's formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Plane-embedding terminology, face incidence, and the Euler relation for connected plane graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An embedding of a graph \(G\) in a topological space \(S\) is a continuous injection of \(|G|\) into \(S\). The graph \(G\) is planar if it embeds in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). For a fixed plane embedding, the components of \(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus |G|\) are the faces of \(G\). A vertex or edge is incident with a face when it is contained in the face boundary, and two faces are adjacent when they are incident with a common edge. There is a unique unbounded face, whose boundary is the outer boundary of \(G\). If \(G=(V,E)\) is connected and \(\mathcal F\) is its face collection, then \(|V|+|\mathcal F|=|E|+2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A planar graph admits an embedding in the plane. A fixed plane embedding determines its faces, incidences, adjacencies, and unique unbounded face. Every connected plane graph satisfies Euler's vertex-edge-face formula.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ has a fixed embedding in }\mathbb{R}^2\text{ for the face terminology}
G=(V,E)\text{ is connected for Euler's formula}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |V|+|\mathcal F|=|E|+2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence and uniqueness of planar embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions using facial boundary walks, with a conditional facial-edge-set characterization and sphere terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G be a connected planar graph, and let G_1 and G_2 be planar embeddings of G. The embeddings G_1 and G_2 are equivalent if every walk obtained by traversing the boundary of a face of G_1 can also be obtained by traversing the boundary of a face of G_2. If G is 2-connected and loopless, then G_1 and G_2 are equivalent if and only if every edge set bounding a face of G_1 also bounds a face of G_2. The graph G is uniquely embeddable in the plane if every two planar embeddings of G are equivalent; it is also called uniquely embeddable on the sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two planar embeddings of a connected planar graph are equivalent when every facial boundary walk of the first is also a facial boundary walk of the second. For a 2-connected loopless graph, this is equivalent to preservation of every facial edge set. The graph is uniquely embeddable when every two planar embeddings are equivalent; the same terminology is used for the sphere.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a connected planar graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}G_1\sim G_2&\iff\text{ every facial boundary walk of }G_1\text{ is facial in }G_2,\\ G\text{ 2-connected and loopless}&\Longrightarrow\bigl(G_1\sim G_2\iff\text{ every facial edge set of }G_1\text{ is facial in }G_2\bigr),\\ G\text{ uniquely embeddable}&\iff\text{ every two planar embeddings of }G\text{ are equivalent.}\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex levels and k-outerplanar graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines embedding-dependent outer-face levels and records the stated recognition bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a planar embedding of G. The level-1 vertices are the vertices on its exterior face. For i\ge 2, the level-i vertices are the vertices on the exterior face of the inherited embedding after deleting all level-1 through level-(i-1) vertices and their incident edges. The graph G is k-outerplanar if it has a planar embedding in which every vertex has level at most k. Whether G is k-outerplanar can be determined in time polynomial in k and n=|V(G)|.

A graph is k-outerplanar when some embedding places every vertex within the first k levels. The extract also states that this property can be recognized in time polynomial in k and the number of vertices.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is }k\text{-outerplanar}\iff\exists\text{ a planar embedding of }G\text{ in which every vertex has level at most }k

knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotation-system representation of cellular embeddings of connected graphs in the oriented sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a finite connected graph with dart set \(D\). Let \(\alpha\) be the fixed-point-free involution reversing each dart, and let \(\sigma\) be a permutation whose cycles give the cyclic order of darts incident with each vertex. The pair \((\sigma,\alpha)\) is a combinatorial embedding. Its facial boundary walks are the cycles of \(\sigma\alpha\). It represents a cellular embedding in the oriented sphere precisely when
\[
|V(G)|-|E(G)|+c(\sigma\alpha)=2,
\]
where \(c(\sigma\alpha)\) is the number of facial cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rotation system records the cyclic edge order at each vertex. Face tracing and Euler's formula determine when it represents a cellular embedding in the oriented sphere.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) contains the two oppositely oriented darts of every edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\sigma,\alpha)\) represents an oriented spherical embedding if and only if \(|V(G)|-|E(G)|+c(\sigma\alpha)=2\).

notation.meaning: Involution pairing the two darts of each edge.

knowledge_statements.title: Topological Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crossing-free topological realizations of finite graphs in a surface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph and let \(\Sigma\) be a surface. A topological embedding \(\varphi\) assigns distinct points of \(\Sigma\) to the vertices and assigns to each edge \(uv\in E\) a simple arc with endpoints \(\varphi(u)\) and \(\varphi(v)\). The interior of every edge arc must avoid all vertex images, and interiors of distinct edge arcs must be disjoint. The connected components of
\[
\Sigma\setminus\varphi(G)
\]
are the faces; the embedding is cellular when every face is homeomorphic to an open disk.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A topological embedding maps vertices to distinct surface points and edges to noncrossing arcs. Its complementary regions are faces, and it is cellular when every face is a disk.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi\) is a graph embedding exactly when edge arcs intersect only at images of their common endpoints.

notation.meaning: Topological realization of G in the surface.

knowledge_statements.title: Embedding Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orientation-preserving equivalence for labeled connected graph embeddings in the sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) be embeddings of the same finite connected labeled graph \(G\) in the oriented sphere. They are orientation-preservingly equivalent if an orientation-preserving homeomorphism \(h\) of the sphere satisfies \(h\circ\varphi_1=\varphi_2\) on every vertex and edge of \(G\). This holds if and only if \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) induce the same cyclic order of incident darts at every vertex. Allowing an orientation-reversing homeomorphism simultaneously reverses all cyclic orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two oriented spherical embeddings of a labeled connected graph are equivalent exactly when their cyclic orders agree at every vertex; mirror equivalence reverses all orders simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite connected labeled graph.
\(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) embed \(G\) in the oriented sphere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) are orientation-preservingly equivalent if and only if their vertex rotation systems coincide.

notation.meaning: Two embeddings of the same labeled graph.

knowledge_statements.title: Planar Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric duality for a fixed connected plane graph, including cycle–bond correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a finite connected plane graph. Its geometric dual \(G^*\) has one vertex for each face of \(G\) and, for every edge \(e\in E(G)\), one dual edge \(e^*\) crossing \(e\) and joining the faces incident with its two sides. The correspondence \(e\leftrightarrow e^*\) is a bijection. For every \(F\subseteq E(G)\), \(F\) is the edge set of a cycle minimal under inclusion if and only if
\[
F^*=\{e^*:e\in F\}
\]
is a bond of \(G^*\). Moreover, \((G^*)^*\) is naturally isomorphic to \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a connected plane graph exchanges faces with vertices and exchanges inclusion-minimal cycles with inclusion-minimal cuts under the edge correspondence.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite connected graph with a fixed plane embedding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a cycle of \(G\) if and only if \(F^*\) is a bond of \(G^*\), and \((G^*)^*\cong G\).

notation.meaning: Geometric dual of the fixed plane graph G.
Dual edge corresponding to the primal edge e.
Set of dual edges corresponding to F.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual of a Connected Plane Network
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual construction and basic correspondences for a fixed planar embedding; exact cycle-cut statements require distinguishing bonds from arbitrary cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(N,A)\) be a connected plane network. Its dual \(G^*=(N^*,A^*)\) has one node \(f^*\) for each face \(f\) of \(G\) and one dual arc for each primal arc. A primal arc incident to distinct faces \(f_1,f_2\) gives a dual arc joining \(f_1^*\) and \(f_2^*\); an arc incident twice to one face gives a dual loop. Thus \(|N^*|=f(G)\), \(|A^*|=|A|\), \(f(G^*)=|N|\), and \((G^*)^*\cong G\) as embedded networks. Under the standard edge correspondence, dual cycles correspond to primal bonds; a general primal cut may correspond to a union of dual cycles rather than one cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The planar dual places a node in every primal face and assigns one dual arc to every primal arc. Nodes and faces exchange, arc counts agree, and dualizing twice recovers the embedded primal network. Simple cycle correspondence is properly with minimal cuts; arbitrary cuts can yield unions of dual cycles.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is connected and has a fixed planar embedding}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed planar duality and the circuit–cut correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The directed dual depends on a fixed planar embedding. Weak connectivity is required for the stated double-dual isomorphism, but the extracted circuit–cut equivalence is stated independently of that condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D$ be a planar digraph with a fixed planar embedding. For each arc $a=(u,v)$, orient its dual edge $a^*$ from the face lying to the left of $a$ when traversed from $u$ to $v$ toward the face lying to its right; the resulting digraph is $D^*$. If $D$ is weakly connected, then $D^{**}\cong D^{-1}$. Moreover, a set $C$ of arcs is a directed circuit in $D$ if and only if $\{a^*:a\in C\}$ is an inclusionwise minimal directed cut in $D^*$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a fixed planar embedding, each dual edge is directed from the left face of its primal arc to the right face. If the digraph is weakly connected, taking this directed dual twice produces the arc-reversed digraph. Directed circuits correspond exactly to inclusionwise minimal directed cuts in the dual.
assumptions_latex: D\text{ is a planar digraph with a fixed planar embedding}
D\text{ is weakly connected for the assertion }D^{**}\cong D^{-1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ weakly connected}\implies D^{**}\cong D^{-1};\qquad C\text{ is a directed circuit in }D\iff \{a^*:a\in C\}\text{ is an inclusionwise minimal directed cut in }D^*.

Then \(p\) is a nonnegative integer sum of incidence vectors of cuts of \(G\) if and only if \(p(C)\) is even for every circuit \(C\) of \(G\), and \(p(e)\le p(C\setminus\{e\})\) for every circuit \(C\) of \(G\) and every \(e\in C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Planar Dual and Standard Dual Embedding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for directed or undirected embedded planar graphs, allowing loops.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a directed or undirected graph, possibly with loops, and let \(\Phi=(\psi,(J_e)_{e\in E(G)})\) be a planar embedding. The planar dual \(G^*\) has the faces of \(\Phi\) as vertices and an edge \(e^*\) for each \(e\in E(G)\), joining the faces adjacent to \(J_e\); if \(J_e\) is adjacent to only one face, then \(e^*\) is a loop. If \(e=(v,w)\) is directed, orient \(e^*=(F_1,F_2)\) so that \(F_1\) is to the right when \(J_e\) is traversed from \(\psi(v)\) to \(\psi(w)\). Moreover, \(G^*\) has a standard planar embedding in which each dual vertex lies in its corresponding face, \(J_{e^*}\) avoids all primal vertices and every \(J_f\) with \(f\ne e\), and \(|J_{e^*}\cap J_e|=1\); if \(e^*\) is a loop, the face bounded by \(J_{e^*}\) contains exactly one endpoint of \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The planar dual of a fixed embedding has one vertex per face and one dual edge per primal edge, joining its incident faces; an edge incident with only one face produces a dual loop. Directed dual edges are oriented with the right-hand face first. The dual admits a standard planar embedding in which corresponding primal and dual edges cross exactly once, no other primal feature is crossed, and each dual loop bounds a face containing exactly one endpoint of its primal edge.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is directed or undirected and may contain loops}
\Phi=(\psi,(J_e)_{e\in E(G)})\text{ is a planar embedding of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G^*\text{ is defined by facial incidence, with the stated directed orientation when applicable, and admits the stated standard planar embedding.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Abstract Graph Duality and Planarity Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric circuit–minimal-cut definition of abstract duals, its relation to planar duals, and Whitney's existence characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) and \(G'\) be graphs. The graph \(G'\) is an abstract dual of \(G\) if there is a bijection \(\chi:E(G)\to E(G')\) such that, for every \(F\subseteq E(G)\), \(F\) is the edge set of a circuit in \(G\) if and only if \(\chi(F)\) is a minimal cut in \(G'\), and \(F\) is a minimal cut in \(G\) if and only if \(\chi(F)\) is the edge set of a circuit in \(G'\). Every planar dual is an abstract dual, but not every abstract dual is a planar dual. A graph admits an abstract dual if and only if it is planar.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An abstract dual is connected to the original graph by an edge bijection that exchanges circuits and minimal cuts in both directions. Every geometric planar dual is an abstract dual, but the converse need not hold. A graph has an abstract dual exactly when it is planar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G'\text{ is an abstract dual of }G\iff\chi\text{ exchanges circuit edge sets and minimal cuts in both directions};\qquad G\text{ admits an abstract dual}\iff G\text{ is planar}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Planar graph duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual construction, biduality for connected plane graphs, and cycle-cut and spanning-tree correspondences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an embedded planar graph \(G=(V,E)\), its dual \(G^*\) has the faces of \(G\) as vertices and, for each \(e\in E\), an edge \(e^*\) joining the two faces incident with \(e\). The graph \(G^*\) is planar, and if \(G\) is connected then \((G^*)^*\cong G\). For every \(C\subseteq E\), \(C\) is a circuit in \(G\) if and only if \(C^*=\{e^*:e\in C\}\) is an inclusionwise minimal nonempty cut in \(G^*\). Moreover, \(C\) is a spanning tree in \(G\) if and only if \(\{e^*:e\in E\setminus C\}\) is a spanning tree in \(G^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a plane graph has one vertex per face and one dual edge per primal edge. It is planar; for connected graphs, dualizing twice recovers the original graph up to isomorphism. Primal circuits correspond to minimal nonempty dual cuts, and complementary dual edges of a primal spanning tree form a dual spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is an embedded planar graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G^*\text{ is planar},\quad (G^*)^*\cong G\text{ when }G\text{ is connected},\quad C\text{ is a circuit in }G\iff C^*\text{ is an inclusionwise minimal nonempty cut in }G^*,\quad C\text{ is a spanning tree in }G\iff (E\setminus C)^*\text{ is a spanning tree in }G^*

knowledge_statements.title: Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite undirected trees and their standard acyclicity, path, and edge-count characterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite undirected graph \(T=(V,E)\) is a tree if it is connected and contains no cycle. For \(|V|\ge 1\), the following conditions are equivalent: \(T\) is a tree; every pair of distinct vertices is joined by exactly one simple path; \(T\) is connected and \(|E|=|V|-1\); and \(T\) is acyclic and \(|E|=|V|-1\). Consequently, deleting any edge of a tree disconnects it, while adding an edge between two existing vertices creates exactly one cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree is a connected acyclic graph, equivalently a graph with a unique path between each vertex pair or a connected graph with one fewer edge than vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is a tree if and only if it is connected and \(|E|=|V|-1\), equivalently if every vertex pair has a unique simple path.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rooted arborescences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the outward-orientation convention and records the path and minimal-reachability characterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph. An arborescence is a set \(A'\subseteq A\) whose arcs form a spanning tree and enter every vertex at most once. Exactly one vertex \(r\) is not entered; it is the root, and \(A'\) is an \(r\)-arborescence. It has \(|V|-1\) arcs and contains a unique directed \((r,v)\)-path for every \(v\in V\). Equivalently, \(r\)-arborescences are the inclusionwise minimal arc sets containing a directed \((r,v)\)-path for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arborescence is a directed spanning tree with at most one entering arc at each vertex. Its unique vertex with no entering arc is the root. It has one fewer arc than vertices, has a unique directed path from the root to each vertex, and is inclusionwise minimal among arc sets providing all such paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A'\text{ is an }r\text{-arborescence}\iff A'\text{ is inclusionwise minimal among arc sets containing an }(r,v)\text{-dipath for every }v\in V,\quad |A'|=|V|-1.

children.title: Spanning Variants

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected vertex-spanning forests and trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A spanning forest of \(G\) is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) for which \((V,F)\) is acyclic, so isolated vertices remain represented. It is component-spanning if, for every connected component \(W\) of \(G\), the graph \((W,F[W])\) is connected. Equivalently, a component-spanning forest is an inclusion-maximal forest in \(G\). If \(G\) is connected, such an \(F\) is a spanning tree; if \(G\) is not connected, no spanning tree exists, but component-spanning forests do.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning forest includes every vertex; a maximal one spans each original component by a tree and becomes a spanning tree when the graph is connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A component-spanning forest has exactly \(|V|-c(G)\) edges; when \(G\) is connected, it is a spanning tree.

notation.meaning: Number of connected components of G.
Edges of F induced by a vertex set W.

children.title: Matchings
children.top_down_role: Pairing structures with vertex-incidence restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph without loops.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible matching family is \(\mathcal M(G)=\{M\subseteq E: |M\cap\delta(v)|\leq 1\text{ for all }v\in V\}\).

notation.meaning: Set of edges incident with vertex v.
Vertices incident with edges of M.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge matchings in finite undirected graphs.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Bipartite matchings p. 65

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matching in \(G\) is a set \(M\subseteq E\) such that no two distinct edges of \(M\) share an endpoint, equivalently \(|M\cap\delta(v)|\leq 1\) for every \(v\in V\). A vertex in \(V(M)\) is matched, and every other vertex is exposed. The matching is perfect if \(V(M)=V\), and it is maximum if its cardinality is largest among all matchings of \(G\). A maximal matching need only be inclusion-maximal and need not be maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching is a set of pairwise endpoint-disjoint edges. It is perfect when every vertex is matched and maximum when its cardinality is largest.
knowledge_statements.title: Matchings

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4 Bipartite matchings p. 65

children.title: Degree-Constrained Factors
children.top_down_role: Spanning subgraphs governed by prescribed degree regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The \((g,f)\)-factors are exactly the spanning subgraphs whose vertex degrees lie in the prescribed integral intervals.

notation.meaning: Degree of v in the spanning subgraph with edge set F.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected integral degree-constrained spanning factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An edge set \(F\subseteq E\) is a \((g,f)\)-factor of \(G\) if \(g(v)\leq\deg_F(v)\leq f(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). When \(g=f=b\), it is a \(b\)-factor; when \(b(v)=k\) for all vertices, it is a \(k\)-factor. Thus a perfect matching is a \(1\)-factor, while an ordinary matching is a spanning subgraph satisfying only the upper bounds \(\deg_F(v)\leq 1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degree-constrained factor is a spanning subgraph whose degree at each vertex lies between prescribed integral lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Constrained Factors

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A one-to-one assignment is a bijection \(\pi:I\to J\). It corresponds to the perfect matching \(M_\pi=\{(i,\pi(i)):i\in I\}\) of \(K_{I,J}\), and to the binary matrix \(x\) defined by \(x_{ij}=1\) exactly when \(j=\pi(i)\). Conversely, every binary matrix satisfying \(\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\) for all \(i\in I\) and \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\) for all \(j\in J\) determines a unique assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced assignment is equivalently a bijection, a perfect bipartite matching, or a binary matrix with one entry in every row and column.

children.title: Bipartite Versus General Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural differences between bipartite and unrestricted pairing systems.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite loopless undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degree inequalities describe the bipartite matching polytope, but in general graphs odd-set inequalities are additionally necessary.

notation.meaning: Edges having both endpoints in S.
Matching polytope, the convex hull of matching incidence vectors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral distinction between bipartite and general matching.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Bipartite matchings p. 65

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(G\) is bipartite, then \(P_M(G)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{geq 0}^E:\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\leq 1\text{ for every }v\in V\}\). This description fails for general graphs: on a triangle, assigning \(x_e=1/2\) to every edge satisfies all degree inequalities but is not a convex combination of matchings. For general \(G\), validity requires \(\sum_{e\in E(S)}x_e\leq (|S|-1)/2\) for every odd-cardinality \(S\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex-degree inequalities suffice for bipartite matching polytopes. Odd cycles show their failure in general graphs, where odd-set inequalities are also required.
knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Versus General Regimes

children.title: Stable Sets
children.top_down_role: Vertex subsets governed by mutual nonadjacency.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph without loops.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stable-set family is \(\mathcal S(G)=\{S\subseteq V:E(S)=\varnothing\}\).

notation.meaning: Edges with both endpoints in S.
Maximum cardinality of a stable set in G.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex stable sets in finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\subseteq V\) is stable, or independent, if no edge of \(G\) has both endpoints in \(S\); equivalently, \(E(S)=\varnothing\). The family of stable sets is downward closed: if \(T\subseteq S\) and \(S\) is stable, then \(T\) is stable. A maximum stable set has cardinality \(\alpha(G)=\max\{|S|:S\subseteq V,\ E(S)=\varnothing\}\), whereas a maximal stable set is only inclusion-maximal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable set is a vertex subset containing no adjacent pair. Maximum means largest cardinality, while maximal means only that no vertex can be added.
knowledge_statements.title: Stable Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stable-set definition and maximum-versus-maximal distinction are correct, but the record supplies no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Cliques
children.top_down_role: Vertex subsets governed by pairwise adjacency.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph without loops.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The clique family is \(\mathcal K(G)=\{K\subseteq V:\binom{K}{2}\subseteq E\}\).

notation.meaning: Set of all unordered pairs of distinct elements of K.
Maximum cardinality of a clique in G.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex cliques in finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(K\subseteq V\) is a clique if every two distinct vertices in \(K\) are adjacent, equivalently \(\binom{K}{2}\subseteq E\). The clique number is \(\omega(G)=\max\{|K|:K\subseteq V,\ \binom{K}{2}\subseteq E\}\). A maximum clique attains \(\omega(G)\); a maximal clique is merely inclusion-maximal. The empty set and every singleton are cliques under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clique is a vertex subset whose distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. Maximum and maximal cliques need not coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Cliques

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The clique definition and associated terminology are correct under the stated finite simple-graph convention, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Vertex Colorings
children.top_down_role: Partitions of vertices into compatibility classes.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph without loops.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A proper \(k\)-coloring exists exactly when \(V\) can be partitioned into at most \(k\) stable sets.

notation.meaning: A vertex-coloring map using colors 1 through k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper vertex colorings of finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper \(k\)-coloring of \(G\) is a map \(c:V\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\) satisfying \(c(u)\neq c(v)\) for every edge \(uv\in E\). Each color class \(c^{-1}(i)\) is therefore a stable set, and the nonempty color classes partition \(V\). Conversely, any partition of \(V\) into at most \(k\) stable sets defines a proper \(k\)-coloring. The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least \(k\) for which such a coloring exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper coloring assigns different colors to adjacent vertices, equivalently partitioning the vertex set into stable color classes. The chromatic number is the minimum colors needed.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Colorings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equivalence between proper colorings and partitions into stable sets is correct and fits the container, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Complementation Relations
children.top_down_role: Correspondences among stable sets, cliques, and colorings under graph complementation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(G)=\omega(\overline G)\), \(\omega(G)=\alpha(\overline G)\), and \(\chi(G)=\theta(\overline G)\).

notation.meaning: Minimum number of cliques partitioning V in H.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complement dualities for stable sets, cliques, and colorings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\subseteq V\), \(S\) is stable in \(G\) if and only if \(S\) is a clique in \(\overline G\). Hence \(\alpha(G)=\omega(\overline G)\) and \(\omega(G)=\alpha(\overline G)\). Moreover, a proper coloring of \(G\) partitions \(V\) into stable sets of \(G\), equivalently into cliques of \(\overline G\). Therefore \(\chi(G)=\theta(\overline G)\), where \(\theta(H)\) is the minimum number of cliques in a vertex partition of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph complementation exchanges stable sets with cliques and turns proper colorings into clique partitions of the complement.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementation Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complementation identities are correct with \(\theta\) explicitly defined as a clique-partition number, and duality is an appropriate content kind. No supporting source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Set Covers
children.top_down_role: Subfamilies organized by coverage of a ground set.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a finite universe and \(\mathcal A\subseteq 2^U\) is a family of available subsets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The covers are exactly the subfamilies \(\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal A\) satisfying \(\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal C}A=U\).

notation.meaning: Incidence matrix with rows indexed by U and columns by the sets in the family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite uncapacitated set-cover systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set cover of \(U\) by \(\mathcal A\) is a subfamily \(\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal A\) such that \(\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal C}A=U\). With incidence matrix \(M_{uA}=1\) when \(u\in A\) and \(M_{uA}=0\) otherwise, covers correspond exactly to binary vectors \(x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal A}\) satisfying \(Mx\geq\mathbf 1\). Given nonnegative costs \(w_A\), a minimum-weight set cover minimizes \(\sum_{A\in\mathcal A}w_Ax_A\) over these vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set cover selects available subsets whose union is the universe; its incidence-vector formulation has one covering inequality for each universe element.
knowledge_statements.title: Set Covers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-cover definition, incidence formulation, and weighted objective are correct for the stated finite uncapacitated setting, but the record has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Disjoint Packings

knowledge_statements.title: Disjoint Packings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-system packing, with no capacities or multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite set and let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\). A disjoint packing is a subfamily \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal F\) such that \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) for all distinct \(A,B\in\mathcal P\). Its size is \(|\mathcal P|\), and the packing number is \[\nu(\mathcal F)=\max\{\lvert\mathcal P\rvert:\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal F,\ A\cap B=\varnothing\text{ for all distinct }A,B\in\mathcal P\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disjoint packing is a pairwise disjoint subfamily of a finite set system; its maximum possible cardinality is the packing number.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu(\mathcal F)\) is the maximum cardinality of a pairwise disjoint subfamily of \(\mathcal F\).

notation.meaning: finite family of subsets of the ground set

children.title: Covering–Packing Relations
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondences and gaps between covering and packing systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Covering–Packing Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary weak duality between integral set-system packing and transversal numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite, let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\) contain no empty set, and let \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal F\) be pairwise disjoint. Every transversal \(T\subseteq E\) contains at least one distinct element from each member of \(\mathcal P\); hence \(|\mathcal P|\le |T|\). Maximizing over disjoint packings and minimizing over transversals gives \[\nu(\mathcal F)\le\tau(\mathcal F).\] Equality is not guaranteed for an arbitrary set system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every transversal must select distinct representatives from pairwise disjoint members, so the maximum packing size never exceeds the minimum transversal size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu(\mathcal F)\le\tau(\mathcal F)\).
