intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weak packing–transversal inequality is precise, correctly scoped, and appropriately classified as a property, but it lacks an inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Covering and packing integer programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines nonnegative integral covering and packing forms and states the dual relationship between their continuous LP forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb Z_+^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^m\), and \(w\in\mathbb Z_+^n\), a covering integer program has the form \(\min\{w^Tx:Ax\ge b,\ x\in\mathbb Z_+^n\}\), while a packing integer program has the form \(\max\{w^Tx:Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb Z_+^n\}\). After replacing integrality by nonnegativity, the dual of \(\min\{w^Tx:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}\) is the packing LP \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty\le w,\ y\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A covering integer program minimizes a nonnegative weighted sum subject to lower-bound constraints; a packing integer program maximizes one subject to upper-bound constraints. The LP dual of a covering form is a packing form with the transposed constraint matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{w^Tx:Ax\ge b,\ x\in\mathbb Z_+^n\}\text{ is covering, }\max\{w^Tx:Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb Z_+^n\}\text{ is packing, and }\left(\min\{w^Tx:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}\right)^*=\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty\le w,\ y\ge0\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Independence Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite hereditary set systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An independence system is a pair \((E,\mathcal I)\), where \(E\) is finite and \(\mathcal I\subseteq 2^E\), satisfying \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\) and the hereditary axiom \[I\in\mathcal I,\ J\subseteq I\quad\Longrightarrow\quad J\in\mathcal I.\] Members of \(\mathcal I\) are independent sets. A set in \(2^E\setminus\mathcal I\) is dependent, and an inclusion-maximal member of \(\mathcal I\) is a maximal independent set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independence system is a finite family of feasible sets containing the empty set and closed under taking subsets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((E,\mathcal I)\) is an independence system exactly when \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\) and \(\mathcal I\) is hereditary.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank and Closure of an Independence System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines rank and closure for subsets of the ground set of an arbitrary independence system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(E,\mathcal F)$ be an independence system. For $X\subseteq E$, define
\[r(X):=\max\{|Y|:Y\subseteq X,\ Y\in\mathcal F\},\qquad \sigma(X):=\{y\in E:r(X\cup\{y\})=r(X)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rank of X is the maximum cardinality of an independent subset of X. Its closure consists of the ground-set elements whose addition does not increase that rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r(X)=\max\{|Y|:Y\subseteq X,\ Y\in\mathcal F\},\qquad \sigma(X)=\{y\in E:r(X\cup\{y\})=r(X)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower Rank and Rank Quotient of an Independence System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines lower rank and rank quotient for an independence system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(E,\mathcal F)$ be an independence system. For each $X\subseteq E$, define
\[
\rho(X):=\min\bigl\{|Y|:Y\subseteq X,\ Y\in\mathcal F,\text{ and }Y\cup\{x\}\notin\mathcal F\text{ for every }x\in X\setminus Y\bigr\}.
\]
The rank quotient is
\[
q(E,\mathcal F):=\min_{F\subseteq E}\frac{\rho(F)}{r(F)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower rank of X is the minimum cardinality of an independent subset that is maximal within X. The rank quotient is the minimum over subsets F of the ratio of lower rank to rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall X\subseteq E,\ \rho(X)=\min\{|Y|:Y\subseteq X,\ Y\in\mathcal F,\ \forall x\in X\setminus Y,\ Y\cup\{x\}\notin\mathcal F\},\qquad q(E,\mathcal F)=\min_{F\subseteq E}\frac{\rho(F)}{r(F)}

children.title: Matroids

knowledge_statements.title: Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroids in independent-set form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matroid is a pair \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), where \(E\) is finite and \(\mathcal I\subseteq 2^E\), such that \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\), \(J\subseteq I\in\mathcal I\) implies \(J\in\mathcal I\), and the augmentation axiom holds: \[I,J\in\mathcal I,\ |I|<|J|\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{there exists }e\in J\setminus I\text{ with }I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I.\] The members of \(\mathcal I\) are the independent sets of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is a hereditary finite independence system in which every smaller independent set can be augmented toward a larger one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid when heredity and augmentation hold.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Independence Axioms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence-axiom definition of a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matroid is a pair \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), where \(E\) is finite and \(\mathcal I\subseteq 2^E\), such that: (I1) \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\); (I2) if \(X\subseteq Y\in\mathcal I\), then \(X\in\mathcal I\); and (I3) if \(X,Y\in\mathcal I\) and \(|Y|>|X|\), then there exists \(e\in Y\setminus X\) such that \(X\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). The members of \(\mathcal I\) are the independent sets, \(E\) is the ground set, and I3 is the exchange axiom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite matroid consists of a finite ground set and a family of subsets containing the empty set, closed downward under inclusion, and satisfying the exchange axiom: any smaller independent set can be augmented by an element of a larger independent set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M=(E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid if and only if axioms I1--I3 hold.}

children.title: Greedoids
children.top_down_role: Accessible feasible-set families with generalized exchange structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Greedoids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite greedoids in feasible-set form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A greedoid is a pair \((E,\mathcal F)\), where \(E\) is finite and \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\), satisfying \(\varnothing\in\mathcal F\), accessibility, and augmentation. Accessibility requires that every nonempty \(X\in\mathcal F\) contain some \(x\in X\) with \(X\setminus\{x\}\in\mathcal F\). Augmentation requires \[X,Y\in\mathcal F,\ |X|<|Y|\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{there exists }y\in Y\setminus X\text{ with }X\cup\{y\}\in\mathcal F.\] The members of \(\mathcal F\) are feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite greedoid has the empty set as feasible, is accessible by single-element deletion, and satisfies the augmentation axiom; it need not be hereditary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((E,\mathcal F)\) is a greedoid exactly when \(\varnothing\in\mathcal F\), accessibility, and augmentation hold.

children.title: Exchange-Strength Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Structural boundaries among hereditary, exchange, and accessibility regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange-Strength Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical comparison of hereditary, accessible, and augmentation axioms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite set system \((E,\mathcal F)\), heredity implies accessibility. Consequently, every matroid independent-set system is both an independence system and a greedoid. Neither converse holds in general: a greedoid may fail heredity, while an independence system may fail augmentation. Thus the matroid axioms combine the hereditary strength of independence systems with the augmentation property shared by greedoids, but independence systems and greedoids are not nested classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every matroid is both an independence system and a greedoid, while general independence systems and greedoids are incomparable.
assumptions_latex: All classes are interpreted through their standard feasible-set axioms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\text{matroids}\}\subseteq\{\text{independence systems}\}\cap\{\text{greedoids}\}\), with neither ambient class contained in the other.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Cryptomorphic Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of finite matroid independent-set, basis, circuit, and rank descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite ground set \(E\), a matroid may equivalently be specified by any one of its independent sets \(\mathcal I\), bases \(\mathcal B\), circuits \(\mathcal C\), or rank function \(r:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), provided the corresponding standard axioms hold. The translations are \[\mathcal B=\max_{\subseteq}\mathcal I,\qquad \mathcal C=\min_{\subseteq}(2^E\setminus\mathcal I),\qquad r(X)=\max\{|I|:I\subseteq X,\ I\in\mathcal I\},\] and \[\mathcal I=\{I\subseteq E:r(I)=|I|\}.\] Hence each representation determines the others uniquely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent sets, bases, circuits, and rank functions satisfying their matroid axioms determine the same finite matroid and uniquely recover one another.
assumptions_latex: The selected representation satisfies its standard matroid axioms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representations \(\mathcal I\), \(\mathcal B\), \(\mathcal C\), and \(r\) determine one another uniquely.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated independent-set, basis, circuit, and rank cryptomorphisms are standard, but the target role also explicitly includes closure and flats, which are omitted. An authoritative source is needed before choosing a complete formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Construction of a Matroid from Circuit Axioms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit-axiom construction of a matroid through its independent sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a set and let \(\mathcal C\subseteq 2^E\) satisfy (C1) \(\varnothing\notin\mathcal C\), (C2) \(C_1,C_2\in\mathcal C\) and \(C_1\subseteq C_2\) imply \(C_1=C_2\), and (C3) if distinct \(C_1,C_2\in\mathcal C\) and \(e\in C_1\cap C_2\), then some \(C_3\in\mathcal C\) satisfies \(C_3\subseteq (C_1\cup C_2)\setminus\{e\}\). Define \(\mathcal I=\{I\subseteq E:\nexists C\in\mathcal C\text{ with }C\subseteq I\}\). Then \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid whose circuit collection is \(\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family that excludes the empty set, is an inclusion antichain, and satisfies circuit elimination determines a matroid: the subsets containing no member of the family are its independent sets, and the given family is exactly its circuit family.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1\ne C_2,\ e\in C_1\cap C_2\Rightarrow \exists C_3\in\mathcal C:\ C_3\subseteq(C_1\cup C_2)\setminus\{e\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid and }\mathcal C(M)=\mathcal C\), where \(\mathcal I=\{I\subseteq E:\nexists C\in\mathcal C,\ C\subseteq I\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family is the circuit family of a matroid exactly when it excludes the empty set, is an inclusion antichain, and satisfies circuit elimination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C\text{ is the circuit family of a matroid on }E\iff\text{(C1), (C2), and (C3) hold}.\)

children.title: Matroid Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual matroid structure across bases, circuits, cocircuits, and rank viewpoints.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroid duality through complementary bases and rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid with basis family \(\mathcal B(M)\) and rank function \(r_M\). Its dual \(M^*\) is the matroid on \(E\) whose bases are \[\mathcal B(M^*)=\{E\setminus B:B\in\mathcal B(M)\}.\] For every \(X\subseteq E\), its rank is \[r_{M^*}(X)=|X|-r_M(E)+r_M(E\setminus X).\] Duality is involutive: \((M^*)^*=M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual matroid has complements of the original bases as bases; its rank follows the complementary-rank formula, and dualizing twice recovers the matroid.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a matroid on a finite ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B(M^*)=\{E\setminus B:B\in\mathcal B(M)\}\) and \((M^*)^*=M\).

knowledge_statements.title: Deletion Minors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion of an arbitrary subset from a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid and let \(D\subseteq E\). The deletion \(M\setminus D\) is the matroid on \(E\setminus D\) with independent sets \[\mathcal I(M\setminus D)=\{I\in\mathcal I:I\subseteq E\setminus D\}.\] Equivalently, for every \(X\subseteq E\setminus D\), its rank satisfies \[r_{M\setminus D}(X)=r_M(X).\] Any matroid obtained by a sequence of deletions is a deletion minor of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting elements restricts a matroid to the remaining ground set; independence and rank of remaining subsets are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\setminus D\) is the restriction of \(M\) to \(E\setminus D\).

notation.meaning: matroid obtained by deleting the elements of D

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal B(M\setminus T)=\max_{\subseteq}\{B-T:B\in\mathcal B(M)\}

knowledge_statements.title: Contraction Minors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contraction of an arbitrary subset from a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\), and let \(C\subseteq E\). The contraction \(M/C\) is the matroid on \(E\setminus C\) whose rank function is \[r_{M/C}(X)=r_M(X\cup C)-r_M(C)\qquad\text{for every }X\subseteq E\setminus C.\] Equivalently, \(M/C=(M^*\setminus C)^*\). Any matroid obtained by a sequence of contractions is a contraction minor of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contracting a subset removes it after accounting for its rank; contraction is equivalently dual to deletion in the dual matroid.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a matroid on a finite ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{M/C}(X)=r_M(X\cup C)-r_M(C)\) for all \(X\subseteq E\setminus C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank Criterion for Equality of Deletion and Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the necessary and sufficient rank condition for deletion and contraction by the same subset to coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid on ground set \(E\), and let \(T\subseteq E\). Then \[M\setminus T=M/T\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r_M(T)+r_M(E\setminus T)=r(M).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deletion and contraction of T yield the same matroid if and only if the ranks of T and its complement add to the rank of M.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\setminus T=M/T\iff r_M(T)+r_M(E\setminus T)=r(M)

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct sums of finitely many matroids on disjoint ground sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_i=(E_i,\mathcal I_i)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,k\) be finite matroids with pairwise disjoint ground sets. Their direct sum \(M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^k M_i\) is the matroid on \(E=\bigcup_{i=1}^k E_i\) whose independent sets satisfy \[\mathcal I(M)=\{I\subseteq E:I\cap E_i\in\mathcal I_i\text{ for every }i\}.\] Its rank is additive across components: \[r_M(X)=\sum_{i=1}^k r_{M_i}(X\cap E_i)\qquad\text{for every }X\subseteq E.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The direct sum combines matroids on disjoint ground sets; independence is componentwise and rank is the sum of component ranks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\) is independent in \(\bigoplus_i M_i\) exactly when every \(I\cap E_i\) is independent in \(M_i\).

rank function of component matroid i

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between nontrivial matroid sum decompositions and higher connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid on ground set \(E\). A partition \((X,E\setminus X)\), with \(|X|,|E\setminus X|\ge k\), is a \(k\)-separation when \[r_M(X)+r_M(E\setminus X)-r_M(E)\le k-1.\] A nontrivial direct-sum decomposition exists exactly when a \(1\)-separation exists. Consequently, connected matroids are precisely those having no nontrivial direct-sum decomposition. More generally, the absence of \(1\)- and \(2\)-separations marks the boundary beyond which decomposition by \(1\)- and \(2\)-sums is unavailable; such matroids are \(3\)-connected, subject to the usual minimum-size convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separations identify matroid decomposition boundaries: connected matroids admit no nontrivial direct sum, while 3-connected matroids admit neither 1- nor 2-separations.
assumptions_latex: The connectivity convention requires both sides of a \(k\)-separation to have at least \(k\) elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is connected exactly when it has no nontrivial direct-sum decomposition; absence of \(1\)- and \(2\)-separations is the corresponding \(3\)-connectivity boundary.

notation.meaning: A partition of the ground set.

knowledge_statements.title: Graphic Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite undirected multigraph cycle-matroid definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected multigraph \(G=(V,E)\), the graphic matroid, or cycle matroid, \(M(G)\) is the matroid on ground set \(E\) whose independent sets are exactly the edge sets containing no graph cycle. Thus \[\mathcal I(M(G))=\{F\subseteq E:(V,F)\text{ is a forest}\}.\] Its circuits are the edge sets of cycles, its bases are the spanning forests of \(G\), and its rank satisfies \[r_{M(G)}(F)=|V|-c(V,F),\] where isolated vertices are counted among the connected components of \((V,F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graphic matroid has graph edges as elements and forests as independent sets; its circuits are cycles and its bases are spanning forests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(G)=(E,\mathcal I(M(G)))\) is a matroid with rank \(r_{M(G)}(F)=|V|-c(V,F)\).

notation.meaning: Number of connected components of the spanning subgraph \((V,F)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Representable Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroids represented by matrix columns over a fixed field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid and \(\mathbb F\) a field. The matroid \(M\) is representable over \(\mathbb F\) if there exist a matrix \(A\) over \(\mathbb F\) and a bijection from \(E\) to the columns of \(A\) such that, for every \(X\subseteq E\), \[X\in\mathcal I\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{the columns of \(A\) indexed by \(X\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb F\)}.\] Equivalently, its rank function obeys \(r_M(X)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A_X)\) for every \(X\subseteq E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is representable over a field when its independent sets are exactly the linearly independent column subsets of a matrix over that field.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is \(\mathbb F\)-representable exactly when \(r_M(X)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A_X)\) for some matrix \(A\) and every \(X\subseteq E\).

notation.meaning: Submatrix consisting of columns indexed by \(X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extremal Size of a Simple GF(q)-Representable Matroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a sharp size bound and the equality implication for simple finite-field-representable matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(M\) is a simple rank-\(r\) matroid representable over \(GF(q)\), then \(|E(M)|\le\frac{q^r-1}{q-1}\). Moreover, if \(|E(M)|=\frac{q^r-1}{q-1}\), then \(M\cong PG(r-1,q)\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |E(M)|\le\frac{q^r-1}{q-1},\qquad |E(M)|=\frac{q^r-1}{q-1}\Longrightarrow M\cong PG(r-1,q).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hyperplane-function characterization of field representability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient criterion for representability of a matroid over an arbitrary field, expressed through a jointly chosen family of hyperplane-indexed functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid and \(\mathbb F\) a field. Then \(M\) is \(\mathbb F\)-representable if and only if there exists a family \((f_H)_{H\in\mathcal H(M)}\), with \(f_H:E(M)\to\mathbb F\), such that: (i) for every hyperplane \(H\), \(H=\{x\in E(M):f_H(x)=0\}\); and (ii) whenever \(H_1,H_2,H_3\) are distinct hyperplanes with \(r(H_1\cap H_2\cap H_3)=r(M)-2\), there exist \(c_1,c_2,c_3\in\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(c_1f_{H_1}+c_2f_{H_2}+c_3f_{H_3}=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is representable over a field exactly when one can jointly choose a field-valued function for every hyperplane so that each hyperplane is its function's zero set and the functions for any three distinct hyperplanes whose common intersection has rank two below the matroid rank satisfy a linear dependence with all three coefficients nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is }\mathbb F\text{-representable}\iff \exists (f_H)_{H\in\mathcal H(M)}\text{ satisfying conditions (i) and (ii)}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatizations of Representable Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes field representability through maps whose span dimensions recover the matroid rank function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rank-$r$ matroid $M$ is $\mathbb F$-representable if and only if, for some $m\ge r$, there is a map $\psi:E(M)\to V(m,\mathbb F)$ such that $r_M(X)=\dim\langle\psi(X)\rangle$ for every $X\subseteq E(M)$. Such a map is an $\mathbb F$-coordinatization. Every coordinatization satisfies $\dim\langle\psi(E(M))\rangle=r$; consequently, $M$ is $\mathbb F$-representable if and only if it has an $\mathbb F$-coordinatization into $V(r,\mathbb F)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-r matroid is representable over a field exactly when its elements can be mapped to vectors so that the rank of every subset equals the dimension of the span of its images. The full image has span dimension r, so an r-dimensional ambient vector space suffices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is }\mathbb F\text{-representable}\iff\exists m\ge r\;\exists\psi:E(M)\to V(m,\mathbb F)\;\forall X\subseteq E(M),\ r_M(X)=\dim\langle\psi(X)\rangle,\quad\text{and }m\text{ may be chosen as }r.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of graphic and field-representable matroids, together with the field-independent representability of graphic matroids.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Field-independent finite matroid representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite matroid \(M\) is regular if it is representable over every field. Equivalently, there exists a totally unimodular matrix \(A\), meaning every square subdeterminant of \(A\) belongs to \(\{0,1,-1\}\), whose column-dependence matroid is \(M\). Under this representation, reducing \(A\) over any field preserves exactly the same dependent and independent column subsets, so the represented matroid does not depend on the chosen field.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular matroid is representable over every field; equivalently, it has a totally unimodular matrix representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is regular if and only if \(M\) is represented by the columns of a totally unimodular matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Field-Dependence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characteristic-dependent representability illustrated by the Fano and non-Fano matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Matroid representability can depend on the characteristic of the field. The Fano matroid \(F_7\), whose seven elements are the nonzero vectors of \(\mathbb F_2^3\), is representable over a field \(\mathbb F\) if and only if \(\operatorname{char}(\mathbb F)=2\). Its relaxation known as the non-Fano matroid \(F_7^-\) is representable over \(\mathbb F\) if and only if \(\operatorname{char}(\mathbb F)\ne2\). Hence representability over one field neither implies representability over all fields nor depends only on field cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fano matroid is representable exactly in characteristic two, whereas the non-Fano matroid is representable exactly outside characteristic two.
assumptions_latex: \(F_7^-\) denotes the standard relaxation of a circuit-hyperplane of \(F_7\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_7\) is \(\mathbb F\)-representable exactly when \(\operatorname{char}(\mathbb F)=2\), while \(F_7^-\) is representable exactly when \(\operatorname{char}(\mathbb F)\ne2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polymatroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral definition induced by a normalized monotone submodular rank function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and let \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\) be normalized, nondecreasing, and submodular. The polymatroid associated with \(f\) is \[P(f)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}^{E}:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\right\},\] where \(x(S)=\sum_{e\in S}x_e\). More generally, a polyhedron is called a polymatroid when it admits such a representation. If \(f\) is integer-valued, then every vertex of \(P(f)\) is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polymatroid is the nonnegative polyhedron whose subset sums are bounded by a normalized, monotone, submodular rank function.
assumptions_latex: \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\) is normalized, nondecreasing, and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}^{E}:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for all }S\subseteq E\}\) is a polymatroid; it is integral when \(f\) is integer-valued.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recovery of a normalized submodular rank function from its polymatroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-function representation of a normalized monotone submodular function by its associated polymatroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:2^S\to\mathbb R\) is nondecreasing and submodular with \(f(\varnothing)=0\), then for every \(U\subseteq S\), \[f(U)=\max\{x(U):x\in P_f\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a normalized nondecreasing submodular function, the value on every subset equals the maximum coordinate sum over that subset among vectors in its associated polymatroid.
assumptions_latex: f:2^S\to\mathbb R\text{ is nondecreasing and submodular}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(U)=\max\{x(U)\mid x\in P_f\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common rank of maximal vectors in a box-restricted polymatroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equal total value of coordinatewise maximal points in a nonnegative box restriction of a polymatroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polymatroid. For every \(a\in\mathbb R_+^S\), there exists a number \(r(a)\) such that every coordinatewise maximal vector \(x\) in \(P\cap\{y\in\mathbb R^S:y\leq a\}\) satisfies \(x(S)=r(a)\). This number is called the rank of \(a\), and every such maximal vector is called a base of \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every nonnegative upper-bound vector, all coordinatewise maximal points of the box-restricted polymatroid have the same total sum. That common value is the rank of the upper-bound vector, and those maximal points are its bases.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is coordinatewise maximal in }P\cap\{y:y\leq a\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,r(a)\ \forall x\in\operatorname{Max}_{\leq}(P\cap\{y:y\leq a\}):\ x(S)=r(a)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone submodular representation of a polymatroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonization preserves the associated polymatroid and, when it is nonempty, gives an essentially unique monotone defining function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:2^E\to\mathbb{R} be submodular and define
\[
f_{\mathrm{mon}}(S):=\min\{f(T):S\subseteq T\subseteq E\},\qquad S\subseteq E.
\]
Then f_{\mathrm{mon}} is monotone and submodular, and
\[
P_{f_{\mathrm{mon}}}=P_f.
\]
Consequently every polymatroid can be defined by a monotone submodular function. If P_f\ne\varnothing, this function is uniquely determined by P_f on nonempty subsets through
\[
f_{\mathrm{mon}}(S)=\max\{x(S):x\in P_f\},\qquad \varnothing\ne S\subseteq E,
\]
while its value at \varnothing is not determined by P_f.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a submodular function over all supersets produces a monotone submodular function defining the same polymatroid. If the polymatroid is nonempty, this defining function is uniquely recoverable on every nonempty subset by maximizing the corresponding coordinate sum over the polymatroid; its empty-set value remains undetermined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_{\mathrm{mon}}\text{ is monotone and submodular},\quad P_{f_{\mathrm{mon}}}=P_f,\quad P_f\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow\left[\forall\varnothing\ne S\subseteq E,\ f_{\mathrm{mon}}(S)=\max_{x\in P_f}x(S)\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal-gain characterization of polymatroid rank functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes normalized nondecreasing submodular functions through an upper bound formed from marginal gains at an arbitrary reference set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:2^V\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(F(\varnothing)=0\), and define \(\rho_j(A)=F(A\cup\{j\})-F(A)\) for \(A\subseteq V\) and \(j\in V\). Then \(F\) is a polymatroid rank function, meaning that it is submodular and nondecreasing, if and only if, for all \(A,B\subseteq V\), \[F(B)\le F(A)+\sum_{j\in B\setminus A}\rho_j(A).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized set function is a polymatroid rank function exactly when every set value is bounded by a reference-set value plus the marginal gains, evaluated at that reference set, of the newly added elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is submodular and nondecreasing}\iff \forall A,B\subseteq V,\ F(B)\le F(A)+\sum_{j\in B\setminus A}\rho_j(A)

knowledge_statements.title: Submodular Rank Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized monotone submodular set functions used as polymatroid ranks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite ground set \(E\), a function \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) is a submodular rank function when it is normalized, nondecreasing, and submodular: \[f(\varnothing)=0,\qquad S\subseteq T\Longrightarrow f(S)\le f(T),\] and \[f(S)+f(T)\ge f(S\cup T)+f(S\cap T)\qquad(S,T\subseteq E).\] Equivalently, it has diminishing marginal returns: whenever \(S\subseteq T\subseteq E\) and \(e\in E\setminus T\), \[f(S\cup\{e\})-f(S)\ge f(T\cup\{e\})-f(T).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A submodular rank function is normalized and monotone, with diminishing marginal gains as the chosen set grows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is a submodular rank function exactly when it satisfies normalization, monotonicity, and the displayed submodular inequality.

knowledge_statements.title: Base Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Base polyhedron of a normalized submodular set function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and let \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\) be normalized and submodular. Its base polyhedron is \[B(f)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E,\quad x(E)=f(E)\right\}.\] The equality on \(E\) selects the maximal-total-sum face of the associated submodular polyhedron. If \(f\) is also nondecreasing and nonnegative, then every vector in \(B(f)\) is nonnegative, and \(B(f)\) is the base polytope of the polymatroid \(P(f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A base polyhedron imposes all submodular subset inequalities and makes the full-ground-set inequality tight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for all }S\subseteq E,\ x(E)=f(E)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Base-Polyhedron Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the base polyhedron of a matroid rank function as the convex hull of its combinatorial bases.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The base polyhedron of a matroid rank function is exactly the convex hull of the characteristic vectors of all bases of the matroid.
assumptions_latex: \rho\text{ is the rank function of }\mathbf M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm B(\rho)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi_B\mid B\text{ is a base of }\mathbf M\}

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Rank Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matroid independence and base polytopes as integral polymatroid specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid with rank function \(r_M\). Then \(r_M\) is integer-valued, normalized, nondecreasing, and submodular, with \(r_M(\{e\})\le 1\) for every \(e\in E\). Conversely, every integer-valued submodular rank function satisfying these properties is the rank function of a matroid. Moreover, \[P(r_M)=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf1_I:I\in\mathcal I\}\] and \[B(r_M)=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf1_B:B\text{ is a base of }M\}.\] Thus matroid independence and base polytopes are integral polymatroid and base-polyhedron specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid ranks are integer submodular ranks with singleton values at most one; their polymatroid and base-polyhedron vertices encode independent sets and bases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(r_M)=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf1_I:I\in\mathcal I\}\) and \(B(r_M)=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf1_B:B\text{ is a base of }M\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank properties of matroids and independence systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard matroid-rank properties together with the weaker guarantee and failure boundary for arbitrary independence systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a matroid on a finite set $E$, with rank function $r_M$. Then $r_M$ is integer-valued, cardinality-bounded, monotone, and submodular. By comparison, if $N$ is an arbitrary independence system on $E$, then $r_N$ is integer-valued, cardinality-bounded, monotone, and subadditive, but need not be submodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid rank function is integer-valued, bounded by set cardinality, monotone, and submodular. An arbitrary independence-system rank function retains the first three properties and is subadditive, but it may fail to be submodular.
assumptions_latex: N\text{ is, for comparison, an arbitrary independence system on }E
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&\forall X,Y\subseteq E:\quad r_M(X)\in\mathbb Z,\quad 0\le r_M(X)\le |X|,\quad X\subseteq Y\Rightarrow r_M(X)\le r_M(Y),\\&r_M(X\cup Y)+r_M(X\cap Y)\le r_M(X)+r_M(Y);\\&r_N\text{ satisfies the corresponding boundedness, integrality, and monotonicity properties, and }r_N(X\cup Y)\le r_N(X)+r_N(Y),\text{ but need not be submodular.}\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Elementwise rank closure implies collective rank closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records a consequence of the monotonicity and submodularity rank axioms without adding an unsupported codomain assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r\) be a function on \(2^E\) satisfying (R2) monotonicity and (R3) submodularity. If \(X,Y\subseteq E\) and \(r(X\cup\{y\})=r(X)\) for every \(y\in Y\setminus X\), then \(r(X\cup Y)=r(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a set function satisfying the monotonicity and submodularity rank axioms, if every element of Y outside X can be added individually without increasing the value at X, then adding all of Y also leaves the value unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r(X\cup Y)=r(X).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Construction of a matroid from rank axioms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the sufficiency direction of the rank-function characterization of matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a set and let \(r:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfy \(0\le r(X)\le |X|\) for all \(X\subseteq E\), \(X\subseteq Y\Rightarrow r(X)\le r(Y)\), and \(r(X\cup Y)+r(X\cap Y)\le r(X)+r(Y)\) for all \(X,Y\subseteq E\). Define \(\mathcal I=\{X\subseteq E:r(X)=|X|\}\). Then \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid whose rank function is \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative integer-valued set function satisfying the rank bound, monotonicity, and submodularity axioms defines a matroid by declaring precisely the sets whose rank equals their size to be independent. The resulting matroid has the given rank function.
assumptions_latex: r(X\cup Y)+r(X\cap Y)\le r(X)+r(Y)\quad(\forall X,Y\subseteq E)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal I=\{X\subseteq E:r(X)=|X|\}\implies (E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid with rank function }r.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank-axiom characterization of matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes matroid rank functions by cardinality bounds, monotonicity, and submodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a set. A function \(r:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) is the rank function of a matroid on \(E\) if and only if: for every \(X\subseteq E\), \(0\le r(X)\le |X|\); for all \(X\subseteq Y\subseteq E\), \(r(X)\le r(Y)\); and for all \(X,Y\subseteq E\), \[r(X\cup Y)+r(X\cap Y)\le r(X)+r(Y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative integer-valued set function is a matroid rank function exactly when it is bounded above by cardinality, monotone under inclusion, and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r\text{ is a matroid rank function}\iff\left[\begin{array}{l}0\le r(X)\le |X|\quad(\forall X\subseteq E),\\ X\subseteq Y\Rightarrow r(X)\le r(Y),\\ r(X\cup Y)+r(X\cap Y)\le r(X)+r(Y)\quad(\forall X,Y\subseteq E)\end{array}\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Submodularity of matroid rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the submodular inequality for every matroid rank function and notes that equality is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(M\) is a matroid on \(E\) with rank function \(r_M\), then for all \(X,Y\subseteq E\), \[r_M(X\cup Y)+r_M(X\cap Y)\le r_M(X)+r_M(Y).\] The inequality can be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every matroid rank function is submodular: the ranks of a union and intersection sum to at most the sum of the two individual ranks. Strict inequality can occur.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_M(X\cup Y)+r_M(X\cap Y)\le r_M(X)+r_M(Y).

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Incidence Vectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary encoding of a selected vertex subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph and let \(U\subseteq V\). The vertex incidence vector of \(U\) is the vector \(\chi^U\in\{0,1\}^V\) defined coordinatewise by \[\chi^U_v=\begin{cases}1,&v\in U,\\0,&v\notin U.\end{cases}\] The correspondence \(U\mapsto\chi^U\) is a bijection between vertex subsets and binary vectors indexed by \(V\). For every weight vector \(w\in\mathbb R^V\), defining \(w(U)=\sum_{v\in U}w_v\) gives \(w(U)=w^\top\chi^U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex incidence vector places a one at each selected vertex and zero at every unselected vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi^U\in\{0,1\}^V\) uniquely encodes \(U\), and \(w(U)=w^\top\chi^U\) for every \(w\in\mathbb R^V\).

notation.meaning: A real vector of vertex weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge Incidence Vectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary encoding of a selected edge subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(F\subseteq E\). The edge incidence vector of \(F\) is \(\chi^F\in\{0,1\}^E\), defined by \[\chi^F_e=\begin{cases}1,&e\in F,\\0,&e\notin F.\end{cases}\] Thus edge subsets correspond bijectively to binary vectors indexed by \(E\). For any edge-cost vector \(c\in\mathbb R^E\), the total cost of \(F\) is represented linearly as \(c(F)=c^\top\chi^F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge incidence vector places a one at each selected edge and zero at every unselected edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi^F\in\{0,1\}^E\) uniquely encodes \(F\), and \(c(F)=c^\top\chi^F\).

notation.meaning: A real vector of edge costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Arc Incidence Vectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary encoding of a selected directed-arc subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph and let \(F\subseteq A\). The arc incidence vector of \(F\) is \(\chi^F\in\{0,1\}^A\), defined by \[\chi^F_a=\begin{cases}1,&a\in F,\\0,&a\notin F.\end{cases}\] Arc direction is carried by the index \(a=(u,v)\), not by the binary value. Consequently, arc subsets correspond bijectively to binary vectors indexed by \(A\). For every cost vector \(c\in\mathbb R^A\), defining \(c(F)=\sum_{a\in F}c_a\) gives \(c(F)=c^\top\chi^F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc incidence vector places a one at each selected directed arc and zero at every unselected arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi^F\in\{0,1\}^A\) uniquely encodes \(F\), and \(c(F)=c^\top\chi^F\) for every \(c\in\mathbb R^A\).

notation.meaning: A real vector of arc costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Set Characteristic Vectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-ground-set characteristic-vector encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}\) be a finite set. For every subset \(S\subseteq E\), its characteristic vector is \(\chi^S\in\{0,1\}^n\), defined coordinatewise by \[(\chi^S)_i=\begin{cases}1,&e_i\in S,\\0,&e_i\notin S.\end{cases}\] The map \(S\mapsto\chi^S\) is a bijection from \(2^E\) to \(\{0,1\}^n\), with inverse \(x\mapsto\{e_i:x_i=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset of a finite ordered ground set is represented uniquely by a binary vector whose coordinates indicate membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(2^E\leftrightarrow\{0,1\}^n\), via \(S\mapsto\chi^S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incidence vector of a subset
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary encoding of a subset relative to a fixed ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a ground set \(E\) and a subset \(X\subseteq E\), the incidence vector of \(X\) with respect to \(E\) is the vector \(\chi^X\in\{0,1\}^E\) defined by \((\chi^X)_e=1\) for \(e\in X\) and \((\chi^X)_e=0\) for \(e\in E\setminus X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The incidence vector of a subset has coordinate one for elements in the subset and zero for all other elements of the ground set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\chi^X)_e=\begin{cases}1,&e\in X,\\0,&e\in E\setminus X.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.title: Adjacency Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-indexed adjacency representation of finite loopless directed or undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) be a finite loopless directed or undirected graph with \(V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}\). Its adjacency matrix is \(A(H)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{n\times n}\). In the directed case, \(A(H)_{ij}\) is the number of arcs from \(v_i\) to \(v_j\); in the undirected case, it is the number of edges having endpoints \(v_i\) and \(v_j\). If \(H\) is simple, every entry is binary. If \(H\) is undirected, \(A(H)=A(H)^{\mathsf T}\), and looplessness implies \(A(H)_{ii}=0\) for every \(i\in\{1,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adjacency matrix records arc multiplicities between ordered vertex pairs in a directed graph or edge multiplicities between vertex pairs in an undirected graph.
assumptions_latex: \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) is a finite loopless directed or undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(H)_{ij}\) records the appropriate adjacency multiplicity between \(v_i\) and \(v_j\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Block adjacency-matrix characterization of bipartite graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes an undirected graph as bipartite through a vertex ordering that gives its adjacency matrix a block off-diagonal form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An undirected graph \(G\) is bipartite if and only if its vertices can be ordered so that its adjacency matrix has the form \[A=\begin{pmatrix}0&\bar A\\ \bar A^{T}&0\end{pmatrix}.\] For a bipartition \((S,T)\) with \(|S|=p\) and \(|T|=q\), \(\bar A\) is \(p\times q\) and \(\bar A^T\) is \(q\times p\); thus \(G\) may be represented by \(\bar A\) alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected graph is bipartite exactly when its vertices can be ordered so that its adjacency matrix has zero diagonal blocks and transposed off-diagonal blocks. If the two vertex classes have sizes p and q, the upper-right block is p by q and alone encodes the graph.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is an undirected graph with adjacency matrix }A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is bipartite}\iff \exists\text{ a vertex ordering such that }A=\begin{pmatrix}0&\bar A\\ \bar A^T&0\end{pmatrix}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Node–Node Adjacency Matrix Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed-network adjacency encoding, dense-storage cost, and row/column neighborhood access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed network \(G=(V,A)\) with \(|V|=n\), the node–node adjacency matrix \(\mathcal H=(h_{ij})\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) is defined by \(h_{ij}=1\) if \((i,j)\in A\) and \(h_{ij}=0\) otherwise. If \(A\) is an arc set with \(|A|=m\), then \(\mathcal H\) has \(n^2\) entries and \(m\) nonzeros. Additional \(n\times n\) matrices may store arc costs and capacities. Scanning row \(i\) identifies its outgoing arcs, and scanning column \(j\) identifies its incoming arcs, each in time proportional to \(n\); consequently dense adjacency storage is principally suitable for sufficiently dense networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed network's adjacency matrix is an n-by-n binary matrix whose (i,j) entry is one exactly when arc (i,j) exists. It has n² entries and m nonzeros, while parallel matrices may store costs and capacities. Scanning a row lists outgoing arcs and scanning a column lists incoming arcs, each in time proportional to n, so dense adjacency storage is mainly appropriate for dense networks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h_{ij}=\mathbf 1_{\{(i,j)\in A\}},\qquad \operatorname{nnz}(\mathcal H)=m,\qquad T_{\mathrm{row/column\ scan}}=\Theta(n).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjacency matrices of undirected graphs and digraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses binary adjacency and the source convention that a node is not adjacent to itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph, define $a_{ij}=1$ if an arc joins distinct nodes $i$ and $j$, and $a_{ij}=0$ otherwise. Then $a_{ii}=0$ and $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$. For a digraph, define $a_{ij}=1$ if an arc is directed from $i$ to $j$, and $a_{ij}=0$ otherwise; the resulting matrix need not be symmetric, while the no-self-adjacency convention gives $a_{ii}=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected graph's binary adjacency matrix records whether distinct nodes are joined; it has zero diagonal and is symmetric. For a digraph, entry i,j records an arc directed from i to j, so the matrix need not be symmetric; the stated convention still gives a zero diagonal.

knowledge_statements.title: Incidence Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsigned vertex-edge incidence representation for loopless undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite loopless undirected graph, with ordered sets \(V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}\) and \(E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}\). Its unsigned vertex-edge incidence matrix is \(B(G)\in\{0,1\}^{n\times m}\), defined by \[B(G)_{ij}=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v_i\text{ is an endpoint of }e_j.\] Every column contains exactly two ones. Row and column permutations correspond only to relabeling vertices and edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unsigned incidence matrix marks which vertices are endpoints of each edge; every loopless undirected edge produces a column with two ones.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite loopless undirected graph.
The vertex and edge sets are ordered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(G)_{ij}=\mathbf{1}[v_i\text{ is incident with }e_j]\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Signed vertex-arc incidence matrix of a digraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves the tail-minus/head-plus sign convention and assigns a zero column to every loop.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a digraph D=(V,A), its vertex-arc incidence matrix B\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times A} satisfies, for each nonloop arc a, B_{va}=-1 if v is the tail of a, B_{va}=+1 if v is the head of a, and B_{va}=0 otherwise. If a is a loop, then B_{va}=0 for every v\in V. The transpose B^\top is the arc-vertex incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonloop arc contributes -1 at its tail, +1 at its head, and 0 elsewhere in the vertex-arc incidence matrix. Every loop has a zero column, and the transpose is the arc-by-vertex incidence matrix.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)\text{ is a directed graph, possibly with parallel arcs and loops}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B_{va}=\begin{cases}-1&v\text{ is the tail of nonloop }a,\\+1&v\text{ is the head of nonloop }a,\\0&\text{otherwise, including when }a\text{ is a loop.}\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unsigned node–arc incidence matrix of a loopless undirected graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses one row per node, one column per arc, and the extract's unsigned incidence convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(N,A)$ be an undirected graph whose arcs have two distinct endpoints. With rows indexed by nodes $i$ and columns indexed by arcs $k$, the node–arc incidence matrix $B=(b_{ik})$ is defined by $b_{ik}=1$ if node $i$ is incident to arc $k$, and $b_{ik}=0$ otherwise. Every column contains exactly two entries equal to $1$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a loopless undirected graph, the unsigned node–arc incidence matrix has one row per node and one column per arc. An entry is one exactly when the node is an endpoint of the arc, so every column contains exactly two ones.
assumptions_latex: \text{Rows are indexed by nodes and columns by arcs.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b_{ik}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if node }i\text{ is incident to arc }k,\\0,&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}\qquad \sum_{i\in N}b_{ik}=2\quad\forall k.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental-cycle network matrix induced by a directed graph and a spanning tree of its underlying graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph whose underlying undirected graph is connected, and let \(T\subseteq A\) correspond to a spanning tree of that underlying graph. Delete one row from the node-arc incidence matrix and order its columns as \(T,A\setminus T\), obtaining \(M=[B\ N]\). Then \(B\) is square and nonsingular, and \[K=B^{-1}N\] is the network matrix associated with \((D,T)\). For each non-tree arc \(a\in A\setminus T\), let \(e_a\) be its unit vector in \(\mathbb R^{A\setminus T}\). The vector with tree and non-tree components \[\begin{pmatrix}-K e_a\\ e_a\end{pmatrix}\] is the signed arc-incidence vector of the unique fundamental cycle obtained by adding \(a\) to \(T\), normalized so that the coefficient of \(a\) is \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network matrix expresses the tree-arc coefficients needed to form each fundamental cycle with a non-tree arc; under unit normalization of that non-tree arc, the tree component is the negative of the corresponding network-matrix column.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is finite and its underlying undirected graph is connected.
\(T\subseteq A\) corresponds to a spanning tree of the underlying graph.
One row is deleted from the node-arc incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=B^{-1}N\) is the network matrix, and \(\bigl(-K e_a,e_a\bigr)\) represents the normalized fundamental cycle for each \(a\in A\setminus T\).

notation.meaning: reduced node-arc incidence matrix partitioned into tree and non-tree columns
unit vector associated with non-tree arc a

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Representation Correspondences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between adjacency and unsigned incidence matrices of a simple graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite simple undirected graph with adjacency matrix \(A\), unsigned vertex-edge incidence matrix \(B\), and diagonal degree matrix \(D\). Then \[BB^{\mathsf T}=D+A.\] Consequently, \(A_{ij}=(BB^{\mathsf T})_{ij}\) for \(i\ne j\), while \(D_{ii}=(BB^{\mathsf T})_{ii}\). Thus \(B\) determines both adjacency and degrees, up to vertex and edge orderings. The converse loses edge identities: \(A\) determines the incidence structure only up to graph isomorphism and column permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a simple undirected graph, multiplying its unsigned incidence matrix by its transpose yields the degree matrix plus the adjacency matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) use the same vertex ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(BB^{\mathsf T}=D+A\).

children.title: Binary Selection Formulations

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Selection Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-vector representation of feasible subfamilies of a finite ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}\), let \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\), and let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) satisfy \[X=\{\chi^S:S\in\mathcal F\}.\] A binary selection formulation describes \(X\) by constraints on variables \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\), interpreted as \(x_i=1\) exactly when \(e_i\) is selected. For weights \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), the combinatorial objective is preserved: \[\min_{S\in\mathcal F}\sum_{e_i\in S}c_i=\min_{x\in X}c^{\mathsf T}x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary selection formulations encode each feasible subset by membership variables and preserve additive objectives as linear functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\mathcal F\) is represented by \(x=\chi^S\in X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\).

knowledge_statements.title: General Integer Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear integer optimization formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A general integer linear formulation has data \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and takes the form \[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}.\] Equalities and finite bounds may be included as pairs of inequalities. It is a formulation of a discrete feasible set \(\mathcal F\) when a specified decoding map from its feasible integer vectors onto \(\mathcal F\) preserves feasibility and objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general integer formulation optimizes a linear objective over integer vectors satisfying finitely many linear constraints, together with a decoding into discrete solutions.
assumptions_latex: The decoding map and objective correspondence are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\) represents the decoded discrete problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary encoding of bijective assignments between equally sized finite sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) and \(J\) be finite sets with \(|I|=|J|\). Introduce \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\), where \(x_{ij}=1\) means object \(i\) is assigned to position \(j\). The constraints \[\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\quad(i\in I),\qquad \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\quad(j\in J)\] hold exactly for incidence matrices of bijections from \(I\) to \(J\). Hence feasible binary matrices are precisely permutation matrices after orderings of \(I\) and \(J\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bijective assignment is encoded by a binary matrix having exactly one selected entry in every row and every column.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) satisfies the assignment equations exactly when it encodes a bijection \(I\to J\).

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise-precedence encoding of strict total orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite set. For distinct \(i,j\in V\), define \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\), with \(x_{ij}=1\) meaning that \(i\) precedes \(j\). The system \[x_{ij}+x_{ji}=1\quad(i\ne j),\qquad x_{ij}+x_{jk}+x_{ki}\le2\quad(i,j,k\text{ distinct})\] is satisfied exactly by pairwise-precedence vectors of strict total orders on \(V\). The first equations define a tournament, and the triangle inequalities exclude directed three-cycles, thereby enforcing transitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict total order is encoded by binary pairwise-precedence variables satisfying antisymmetry equations and directed-triangle inequalities.
assumptions_latex: A variable is present for every ordered pair of distinct elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) satisfies the displayed system if and only if it encodes a strict total order on \(V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Logical Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear encodings of elementary Boolean connectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary variables \(x,y,z\in\{0,1\}\), elementary Boolean relations have exact linear encodings: \[z=\neg x\iff z=1-x,\] \[z=x\wedge y\iff z\le x,\ z\le y,\ z\ge x+y-1,\] \[z=x\vee y\iff z\ge x,\ z\ge y,\ z\le x+y.\] The implication \(x\Rightarrow y\) is equivalent to \(x\le y\). Introducing one binary output variable for each connective and imposing its corresponding constraints yields an exact encoding of any finite Boolean circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boolean negation, conjunction, disjunction, and implication can be represented exactly by linear constraints on binary variables.
assumptions_latex: A finite circuit uses an auxiliary output variable for each connective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed linear systems have exactly the truth-table assignments of their respective Boolean relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact existential encoding using additional decision variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq X\) be a feasible set. An auxiliary-variable encoding of \(F\) is a set \(Q\subseteq X\times Y\), described using original variables \(x\) and additional variables \(y\), such that \[F=\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y\text{ with }(x,y)\in Q\}.\] Thus an original point is feasible exactly when it admits an auxiliary witness. The auxiliary variables may be continuous, integer, or binary, but their domains and all linking constraints must be included in \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary variables encode a feasible set exactly when projecting all feasible augmented solutions onto the original variables recovers that set.
assumptions_latex: The auxiliary domain \(Y\) and augmented feasible set \(Q\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y,\ (x,y)\in Q\}\).

children.title: Lifted-Space Encodings
children.top_down_role: Higher-dimensional representations of lower-dimensional feasible objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted-Space Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral extended formulation in a higher-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron. A lifted-space encoding, or extended formulation, of \(P\) is a polyhedron \[Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{n+r}:A x+B y\le d\}\] satisfying \[P=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^r,\,A x+B y\le d\}.\] More generally, the projection may be replaced by a specified affine map. The formulation is exact only when its projected image equals \(P\), rather than merely containing or approximating it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted-space encoding represents a polyhedron as the exact projection or affine image of a higher-dimensional polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+r}\) is defined by finitely many linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The extended-formulation definition is mathematically precise and appropriately classified, but no inspectable authoritative citation is supplied.

children.title: Projection Relations
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships between lifted descriptions and their original spaces.

notation.meaning: Lifted feasible set in original and auxiliary variables.
Feasible set represented in the original space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-projection interface for lifted linear or mixed-integer encodings.

source_refs.locator: Encoding p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) be described in variables \((x,y)\), where \(x\) contains the original variables and \(y\) contains auxiliary variables. The projection relation induced by \(Q\) is \[P=\pi_x(Q):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m\text{ such that }(x,y)\in Q\}.\] Thus \(Q\) is an exact lifted encoding of \(P\) precisely when every point of \(P\) has at least one lift in \(Q\), and every point of \(Q\) projects into \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted set exactly encodes an original feasible set when its projection onto the original variables equals that set.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Relations

source_witnesses.locator: Encoding p. 23

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection definition is mathematically coherent and the representation kind fits, but the cited generic encoding page does not establish support for lifted-set projection or exact extended encodings.

children.title: Compactness Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Description-size tradeoffs created by auxiliary dimensions.

assumptions_latex: Encoding size counts variables, constraints, and binary coefficient length under a fixed representation convention.
\(Q\) is an exact lifted encoding of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A smaller lifted description may require auxiliary variables, while projection need not preserve description size.

notation.meaning: Feasible set in the original variable space.
Exact lifted formulation projecting to the original set.
Binary description length under the fixed encoding convention.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation compactness measured by total encoded description, not inequality count alone.

source_refs.locator: Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29
Encoding p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) satisfy \(P=\pi_x(Q)\). A lifted formulation is compact relative to a direct formulation when its complete binary description length \(L(Q)\), including auxiliary variables, constraints, and coefficients, is smaller than the corresponding length \(L(P)\). Compactness is therefore representation-dependent: introducing \(m>0\) auxiliary variables can reduce the number or encoding length of constraints, whereas eliminating those variables can create a substantially larger description. Equality of projected feasible sets alone implies no ordering between \(L(Q)\) and \(L(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary variables can shorten a formulation, but compactness must count all encoded data; exact projection alone gives no description-size guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Tradeoffs

children.title: Encoding Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Alternative descriptions representing the same discrete object family.

assumptions_latex: \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) are sets of valid codewords.
\(d_i:E_i\to\mathcal{O}\) decodes codewords into the same represented object set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) are equivalent when a decode-preserving bijection exists.

notation.meaning: The common set of represented discrete objects.
Valid codeword sets for two encodings.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural equivalence of discrete encodings with a common semantic object space.

source_refs.locator: Encoding p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two encodings \((E_1,d_1)\) and \((E_2,d_2)\) of a discrete object set \(\mathcal{O}\) are encoding-equivalent if there exists a bijection \(\varphi:E_1\to E_2\) satisfying \[d_2(\varphi(e))=d_1(e)\qquad\text{for every }e\in E_1.\] If an optimization model assigns costs through functions \(c_i:E_i\to\mathbb{R}\), objective-preserving equivalence additionally requires \(c_2(\varphi(e))=c_1(e)\) for all \(e\in E_1\). Under these conditions, corresponding codewords represent the same feasible objects and, when applicable, have the same objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two encodings are equivalent when a bijection between their valid codewords preserves decoded objects and, when relevant, objective values.
knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Equivalence

source_witnesses.locator: Encoding p. 23

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Decode-preserving bijection is a coherent possible definition, but encoding equivalence is not uniquely standardized and the cited generic encoding page does not substantiate this particular definition or its objective-preserving extension.

children.title: Redundant Encodings
children.top_down_role: Descriptions containing repeated or implied representational information.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a set of valid codewords.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The encoding is redundant exactly when \(d\) is not injective.

notation.meaning: Decoding map from codewords to objects.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic redundancy arising from multiple valid codewords for one discrete object.

source_refs.locator: Encoding p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An encoding \((E,d)\) of an object set \(\mathcal{O}\) is redundant if its decoding map \(d:E\to\mathcal{O}\) is surjective but not injective. Equivalently, there exist distinct codewords \(e,e'\in E\) such that \[e\ne e'\quad\text{and}\quad d(e)=d(e').\] The fiber \(d^{-1}(o)\) lists all representations of an object \(o\in\mathcal{O}\); redundancy occurs exactly when at least one such fiber has cardinality greater than one. Redundancy concerns representation multiplicity and does not by itself alter the represented object set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An encoding is redundant when distinct valid codewords decode to the same object, so at least one decoding fiber contains multiple representations.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Encodings

source_witnesses.locator: Encoding p. 23

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fiber-based definition is internally correct, but the cited source does not demonstrably support this particular semantic notion of redundant encoding.

children.title: Quotient Encodings
children.top_down_role: Representations identifying objects within common equivalence classes.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a valid codeword set and \(d:E\to\mathcal{O}\) is surjective.
Codewords are equivalent exactly when they decode to the same object.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The induced map \(\bar d:E/{\sim}\to\mathcal{O}\) is bijective.

notation.meaning: Equivalence relation induced by common decoding.
Set of equivalence classes of codewords.
Decoding map induced on equivalence classes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical removal of semantic redundancy by quotienting decoding fibers.

source_refs.locator: Encoding p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a surjective encoding \(d:E\to\mathcal{O}\), define \(e\sim e'\) if and only if \(d(e)=d(e')\). The quotient encoding has codeword set \(E/{\sim}\) and induced decoding map \[\bar d:E/{\sim}\to\mathcal{O},\qquad \bar d([e])=d(e).\] This map is well-defined and bijective: well-definedness follows from the definition of \(\sim\), surjectivity follows from that of \(d\), and injectivity follows because equal decoded objects determine the same equivalence class. Hence each represented object has exactly one quotient codeword.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient encoding identifies precisely those codewords representing the same object; the resulting equivalence classes correspond bijectively to represented objects.
knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Encodings

source_witnesses.locator: Encoding p. 23

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quotient construction is mathematically correct, but the cited page does not support this specialized encoding construction. The statement also contains proof text beginning with the justification of well-definedness, which must be removed once an adequate source is supplied.

children.title: Symmetry-Aware Encodings
children.top_down_role: Descriptions organized around automorphisms and interchangeable states.

assumptions_latex: A group \(G\) acts on the codeword set \(E\) and object set \(\mathcal{O}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Symmetry awareness is expressed by \(d(g\cdot e)=g\cdot d(e)\).

notation.meaning: Group acting on codes and represented objects.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivariant encoding condition for discrete symmetries and orbit-compatible optimization data.

source_refs.locator: Encoding p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An encoding \(d:E\to\mathcal{O}\) is symmetry-aware for actions of a group \(G\) on \(E\) and \(\mathcal{O}\) when it is equivariant: \[d(g\cdot e)=g\cdot d(e)\qquad\text{for all }g\in G\text{ and }e\in E.\] Consequently, codeword orbits map into object orbits. If a feasible subset \(F\subseteq E\) and objective \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\) are part of the model, symmetry compatibility further requires \(g\cdot F=F\) and \(c(g\cdot e)=c(e)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(e\in F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetry-aware encoding commutes with the group action; compatible feasible sets are invariant and objective values are constant along codeword orbits.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Aware Encodings

source_witnesses.locator: Encoding p. 23

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Equivariance is a reasonable symmetry-compatibility condition, but the cited generic encoding page does not support defining all symmetry-aware encodings this way or the additional feasibility and objective conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Hull Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex-combination representation in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its convex hull is \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i s_i:k\in\mathbb{N},\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] It is the intersection of all convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) containing \(S\), and hence the unique smallest convex set containing \(S\). When \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_m\}\) is finite, every point in the hull is generated by a convex combination of those listed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull consists of all finite convex combinations of generating points and is the smallest convex set containing them.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is the smallest convex set containing \(S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex combinations, convex sets, convex hulls, and extreme points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational convex-hull geometry in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k\geq0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\), the point \(x=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x_i\) is a convex combination of \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\). A set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex if \(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in X\) for all \(x,y\in X\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). The convex hull \(\operatorname{conv}(X)\) is the set of all finite convex combinations of points in \(X\). A point \(x\in X\) is an extreme point of \(X\) if \(x\notin\operatorname{conv}(X\setminus\{x\})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex combination uses nonnegative coefficients summing to one. A convex set contains the line segment between every pair of its points. The convex hull consists of all finite convex combinations of points in the set, and an extreme point is not in the convex hull of the remaining points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\text{ is convex}\iff \forall x,y\in X\;\forall\lambda\in[0,1],\ \lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in X;\quad \operatorname{conv}(X)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x_i:k\geq1,\ x_i\in X,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\right\};\quad x\text{ is extreme in }X\iff x\in X\text{ and }x\notin\operatorname{conv}(X\setminus\{x\}).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its affine hull is \[\operatorname{aff}(S)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i s_i:k\in\mathbb{N},\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\in\mathbb{R},\ \sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] Equivalently, for any fixed \(s_0\in S\), \[\operatorname{aff}(S)=s_0+\operatorname{span}\{s-s_0:s\in S\}.\] This set is independent of the chosen base point and is the unique smallest affine subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine hull is the set of affine combinations of points, equivalently a base point plus the span of all relative differences.

children.top_down_role: Dimensional structure relative to an affine hull.

assumptions_latex: A base point \(s_0\in S\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim_{\mathrm{aff}}(S)=\dim\operatorname{span}(S-s_0)\).

Linear span of differences from a base point.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine dimension of a nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is the dimension of its affine hull. For any base point \(s_0\in S\), it is given by \[\dim_{\mathrm{aff}}(S):=\dim\bigl(\operatorname{aff}(S)\bigr)=\dim\operatorname{span}\{s-s_0:s\in S\}.\] The value does not depend on \(s_0\). Equivalently, \(\dim_{\mathrm{aff}}(S)=d\) when the largest affinely independent subset of \(S\) has \(d+1\) points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine dimension is the dimension of the span of point differences, or one less than the largest affinely independent subset size.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a subset $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, its dimension is the minimum dimension among affine subspaces containing $X$; equivalently, $\dim X=\dim(\operatorname{aff}X)$. In particular, any set of $k\le d+1$ points has dimension at most $k-1$.

children.title: Polyhedral Cones
children.top_down_role: Finitely described conic structures in polyhedral geometry.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A polyhedral cone admits both finite inequality and finite generator representations.

notation.meaning: Matrix defining a homogeneous inequality representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional homogeneous halfspace and ray representations.

source_refs.locator: Hulls, Independence, Dimension p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedral cone if there exists a finite matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) such that \[C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le 0\}.\] Equivalently, there exist finitely many vectors \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[C=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_k\}:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i r_i:\lambda_i\ge 0\right\}.\] Thus a polyhedral cone is convex, closed, contains the origin, and is closed under addition and multiplication by nonnegative scalars.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral cone is equivalently the solution set of finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities or the nonnegative span of finitely many rays.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Cones

source_witnesses.locator: Hulls, Independence, Dimension p. 3

children.title: Recession Directions
children.top_down_role: Directional structure governing unbounded polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\) is a recession direction exactly when \(x+td\in P\) for every \(x\in P\) and \(t\ge0\).

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global recession directions of nonempty convex sets and linear inequality systems.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Algorithmic Aspects of Convex Sets: Formulation of the Problems p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), a vector \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a recession direction if \[x+td\in P\qquad\text{for every }x\in P\text{ and every }t\ge 0.\] The set of all recession directions is the recession cone \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\). If \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is a nonempty polyhedron, then \[\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\le0\}.\] In particular, \(P\) is bounded exactly when \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recession direction can be followed indefinitely from every feasible point; for a polyhedron, these directions satisfy the associated homogeneous inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Recession Directions

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H(P)=\{(y,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:Ay\le tb,\ t\ge0\}\), and its slice at \(t=0\) is \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\times\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Homogenization cone of the polyhedron P.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the nonempty polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), define its closed homogenization by \(H(P)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}\{(x,1):x\in P\}\). Then \[H(P)=\{(y,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:Ay\le tb,\ t\ge0\}.\] For every \(t>0\), \((y,t)\in H(P)\) exactly when \(y/t\in P\), while \((y,0)\in H(P)\) exactly when \(y\in\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d:Ad\le0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenization embeds a polyhedron as the positive-height slices of a cone, whose zero-height slice records all recession directions.

children.top_down_role: Conic regimes distinguished by the presence or absence of lines.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is line-free if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\) is pointed, equivalently if and only if \(P\) has a vertex.

notation.meaning: Lineality space of a cone C.
