knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is pointed precisely when \(C\cap(-C)=\{0\}\). For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\), the following conditions are equivalent: \(P\) contains no affine line; its recession cone \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\) is pointed; and \(P\) has at least one vertex. If \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), its lineality directions form \(\{d:Ad=0\}\), so pointedness is equivalent to \(Ad=0\) implying \(d=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is line-free exactly when its recession cone is pointed; for nonempty polyhedra, this is also exactly the regime in which vertices exist.

children.title: Polar Constructions
children.top_down_role: Geometric dual constructions for convex sets and cones.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((C^\circ)^\circ=C\).

notation.meaning: Polar of C with unit upper bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit polar and bipolar identity in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

source_refs.locator: Polyhedra, Inequality Systems p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its polar is \[C^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\le1\text{ for every }x\in C\}.\] If \(C\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains the origin, then the bipolar identity \((C^\circ)^\circ=C\) holds. More generally, for arbitrary \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), one has \((S^\circ)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S\cup\{0\})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar collects vectors whose inner product with every point is at most one; taking the polar twice returns the closed convex hull with the origin.
knowledge_statements.title: Polar Constructions

children.title: Blocking Constructions
children.top_down_role: Dual descriptions associated with upward-closed covering structures.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is a nonempty closed convex set with \(P+\mathbb{R}_+^n=P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{bl}(\operatorname{bl}(P))=P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blocking duality for closed convex upper-comprehensive sets.

source_refs.locator: 5.8 Blocking polyhedra p. 65

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\), define its blocker by \[\operatorname{bl}(P)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:y^Tx\ge1\text{ for every }x\in P\}.\] If \(P\) is nonempty, closed, convex, upper-comprehensive in the sense that \(P+\mathbb{R}_+^n=P\), and excludes the origin, then \(\operatorname{bl}(P)\) has the same properties and \(\operatorname{bl}(\operatorname{bl}(P))=P\). Thus membership in \(P\) is characterized by all blocker inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The blocker of an upper-comprehensive nonnegative convex set consists of nonnegative vectors pairing to at least one with every point, and blocking twice recovers the set.
knowledge_statements.title: Blocking Constructions

children.title: Antiblocking Constructions
children.top_down_role: Dual descriptions associated with downward-closed packing structures.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is nonempty, compact, convex, and downward-comprehensive.
There exists \(\bar x\in P\) with \(\bar x_i>0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{abl}(P)\) is nonempty, compact, convex, and downward-comprehensive, and \(\operatorname{abl}(\operatorname{abl}(P))=P\).

notation.meaning: A point of P with every coordinate strictly positive.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Antiblocking duality for compact downward-comprehensive convex sets containing a strictly positive point.

source_refs.locator: 5.9 Antiblocking polyhedra p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\), define its antiblocker by \[\operatorname{abl}(P)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:y^Tx\le 1\text{ for every }x\in P\}.\] Suppose \(P\) is nonempty, compact, convex, and downward-comprehensive: whenever \(x\in P\) and \(0\le z\le x\), one has \(z\in P\). If there exists \(\bar x\in P\) with \(\bar x_i>0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), then \(\operatorname{abl}(P)\) is also nonempty, compact, convex, and downward-comprehensive, and \(\operatorname{abl}(\operatorname{abl}(P))=P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The antiblocker uses upper inner-product bounds in the nonnegative orthant. For a compact downward-comprehensive convex set containing a strictly positive point, the antiblocker has the same structural properties, and applying the construction twice recovers the original set.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le\mathbf{1},\ x\ge0\}=\min\{\mathbf{1}^Ty:A^Ty\ge c,\ y\ge0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}_+^{m\times n}\) and \(c\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\). The packing program and its covering dual are \[\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le\mathbf{1},\ x\ge0\}\quad\text{and}\quad\min\{\mathbf{1}^Ty:A^Ty\ge c,\ y\ge0\}.\] If the packing optimum is finite, both programs attain optimal solutions and their optimal values are equal. Every feasible pair satisfies \(c^Tx\le\mathbf{1}^Ty\), making covering solutions upper certificates for packings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative linear packing problem has a covering dual; under finite optimality, both attain the same value, and every cover bounds every packing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polytope dimension, full dimensionality, and independent equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic dimension terminology for polytopes and the augmented-vector definition of independence for affine equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polytope \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(\dim(\mathcal P)\) is one less than the maximum number of affinely independent points in \(\mathcal P\), with the convention \(\dim(\varnothing)=-1\). The polytope \(\mathcal P\) is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb R^n\) if \(\dim(\mathcal P)=n\). The equations \(\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_j^i x_j=\beta_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), are linearly independent if their augmented vectors \((\alpha^i,\beta_i)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dimension of a nonempty polytope is one less than the largest number of affinely independent points it contains, while the empty set has dimension −1. A polytope in R^n is full-dimensional when its dimension is n. Affine equations are independent when their augmented coefficient vectors are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow \dim(\mathcal P)=\max\{|S|-1:S\subseteq\mathcal P\text{ is affinely independent}\},\quad \dim(\varnothing)=-1;\qquad \mathcal P\text{ is full-dimensional}\iff\dim(\mathcal P)=n;\qquad \{\text{equations }i\}_{i=1}^m\text{ is independent}\iff\{(\alpha^i,\beta_i)\}_{i=1}^m\text{ is linearly independent}.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An inequality representation of \(P\) is any finite system \(Ax\le b\) whose feasible set equals \(P\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inequality representation of a polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a finite system \(Ax\le b\) satisfying \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:a_i^Tx\le b_i\}.\] An inequality is valid for \(P\) when it holds for every \(x\in P\), and it is redundant in the displayed representation when deleting it leaves the represented set unchanged. Different systems may therefore represent the same polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality representation describes a polyhedron as the feasible set of finitely many linear inequalities; distinct and redundant systems can define the same set.

children.title: Generator Representations
children.top_down_role: Point and ray descriptions of polyhedral sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is a polyhedron if and only if \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)\) for finite sets \(V,R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(V\neq\varnothing\).

source_refs.locator: 5.3 Polyhedra and polytopes p. 60

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty set \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron if and only if finite sets \(V,R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), with \(V\neq\varnothing\), exist such that \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R).\] Equivalently, every \(x\in P\) can be written as \(x=\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_vv+\sum_{r\in R}\mu_rr\), where \(\lambda_v\ge0\), \(\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_v=1\), and \(\mu_r\ge0\). The conical part generates all recession behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty polyhedron is a convex hull of finitely many points plus a cone generated by finitely many rays, and every such set is polyhedral.

children.title: Boundedness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural distinction between polytopes and unbounded polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is bounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d:Ad\le0\}=\{0\}\).

source_refs.locator: 5.3 Polyhedra and polytopes p. 60

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), its recession cone is \[\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+\lambda d\in P\text{ for all }x\in P,\ \lambda\ge0\}=\{d:Ad\le0\}.\] The polyhedron \(P\) is bounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{0\}\). Hence any nonzero solution of \(Ad\le0\) is a directly checkable witness of unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron is bounded exactly when its recession cone contains only zero; any nonzero recession direction certifies unboundedness.

children.title: Faces

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonempty face of \(P\) has the form \(F=\{x\in P:c^Tx=\delta\}\), where \(c^Tx\le\delta\) is valid for \(P\).

notation.meaning: A face exposed by a valid inequality.
Maximum of the exposing linear functional over P.

source_refs.locator: Polyhedra, Inequality Systems p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty subset \(F\subseteq P\) is a face of a nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) when some inequality \(c^Tx\le\delta\), valid for every \(x\in P\), satisfies \[F=\{x\in P:c^Tx=\delta\}.\] Equivalently, \(F\) is the set of maximizers of a linear functional over \(P\), with \(\delta=\max_{x\in P}c^Tx\). By convention, both \(P\) itself and the empty set are also faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is the subset where a valid linear inequality is tight, equivalently the maximizers of a linear functional; the whole polyhedron and empty set are included.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Valid inequalities and faces of a polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines faces exposed by valid inequalities and records their optimization, finite-description, and dimensional properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inequality \(\alpha^Tx\leq\beta\) is valid for a polytope \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) if it holds for every \(x\in\mathcal P\), and it describes the face \(\mathcal F=\mathcal P\cap\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\alpha^Tx=\beta\}\). If \(\mathcal F\neq\varnothing\), then, for \(x^*\in\mathcal P\), \(x^*\) maximizes \(\alpha^Tx\) over \(\mathcal P\) if and only if \(x^*\in\mathcal F\). If \(\mathcal P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_i^Tx\leq b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), every nonempty face is obtained by imposing equality on a subset of the defining inequalities; consequently \(\mathcal P\) has finitely many faces. Faces of polytopes are polytopes; \(\varnothing\) and \(\mathcal P\) are trivial faces, zero-dimensional faces are extreme points, and faces of dimension \(\dim(\mathcal P)-1\) are facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid inequality holds throughout a polytope, and its tight points form a face. For a nonempty such face, the tight points are exactly the maximizers of the inequality's left-hand side. Every nonempty face of a finitely described polytope results from making some defining inequalities tight, so a polytope has finitely many faces. Faces are polytopes; the empty set and the whole polytope are trivial faces, zero-dimensional faces are extreme points, and codimension-one faces are facets.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_i^Tx\leq b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\text{ for the finite-description assertion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F=\mathcal P\cap\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\alpha^Tx=\beta\};\quad \mathcal F\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow\bigl(\forall x^*\in\mathcal P:\ x^*\in\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal P}\alpha^Tx\iff x^*\in\mathcal F\bigr);\quad \forall\text{ nonempty faces }\mathcal G\ \exists I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}:\mathcal G=\mathcal P\cap\{x:a_i^Tx=b_i\ \forall i\in I\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting hyperplanes and faces of a polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the facial-geometry portion of an extract that also introduces broader polyhedron and polytope notions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron. An inequality \(w^Tx\le t\) is valid for \(P\) if \(P\subseteq\{x:w^Tx\le t\}\). For \(w\ne0\), the hyperplane \(\{x:w^Tx=t\}\) is supporting for \(P\) if \(w^Tx\le t\) is valid for \(P\) and \(P\cap\{x:w^Tx=t\}\ne\varnothing\). Such an intersection is a face of \(P\). By convention, \(\varnothing\) and \(P\) are also faces; all other faces are proper faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting hyperplane is the boundary hyperplane of a valid inequality that meets the polyhedron. Its intersection with the polyhedron is a face. The empty set and the whole polyhedron are also faces by convention.
assumptions_latex: w\ne0\text{ when }\{x:w^Tx=t\}\text{ is called a hyperplane}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) contain every face of a nonempty polyhedron \(P\), including \(\varnothing\) and \(P\), ordered by inclusion. Then \((\mathcal{F}(P),\subseteq)\) is a bounded lattice. For faces \(F,G\in\mathcal{F}(P)\), their meet is \(F\wedge G=F\cap G\), and their join is the smallest face containing both, given by \(F\vee G=\bigcap\{H\in\mathcal{F}(P):F\cup G\subseteq H\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its dimension is the dimension of its affine hull: \(\dim(P):=\dim(\operatorname{aff}(P))\). Equivalently, for any \(x_0\in P\), one has \(\dim(P)=\dim\operatorname{span}\{x-x_0:x\in P\}=\dim\operatorname{span}(P-P)\). The polyhedron is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) exactly when \(\dim(P)=n\), equivalently when \(\operatorname{aff}(P)=\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\}\), and fix \(k\in I\). Define \(P_{-k}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\setminus\{k\}\}\). The inequality \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_k\) is redundant in this description exactly when deleting it does not enlarge the feasible set, equivalently when \(P_{-k}=P\), or when every \(x\in P_{-k}\) already satisfies \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite description \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\}\) is irredundant when none of its inequalities is redundant. Equivalently, for every \(k\in I\), there exists a deletion witness \(x^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x^{(k)}\leq b_i\) for every \(i\in I\setminus\{k\}\), while \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x^{(k)}>b_k\). Hence deleting any single inequality strictly enlarges the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality description is irredundant exactly when each inequality has a point satisfying all the others but violating that inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V\neq\varnothing\), let \(d_G(u,v)\) be the minimum number of edges in any path joining \(u\) and \(v\). The graph diameter is \(\operatorname{diam}(G):=\max\{d_G(u,v):u,v\in V\}\). For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the canonical primal linear program is
\[
\sup\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}.
\]
Its feasible region is \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\). The value is \(p^*=\sup_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\), with \(p^*=-\infty\) when \(P=\varnothing\) and \(p^*=+\infty\) when the objective is unbounded above on \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical primal LP maximizes a linear objective over nonnegative variables satisfying componentwise upper-bound constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Associated with the primal program \(\sup\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\) is the dual program
\[
\inf\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c,\ y\ge0\}.
\]
Its feasible region is \(D=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^m:A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c,\ y\ge0\}\), and its value is \(d^*=\inf_{y\in D}b^{\mathsf T}y\), using the corresponding extended-real conventions for infeasibility and unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual minimizes a linear upper bound using nonnegative multipliers whose weighted constraint coefficients dominate the primal objective coefficients.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimum Dual Solutions for Oracle-Described Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of general, basic, oracle-inequality, and standard optimum dual solutions when no fixed explicit constraint system determines the dual variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $P\neq\varnothing$ be a polyhedron given by a strong separation oracle, and suppose $v=\max\{c^Tx:x\in P\}$ exists. An optimum dual solution is a finite collection of valid inequalities $a_i^Tx\leq\alpha_i$ for $P$ and multipliers $\lambda_i>0$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i a_i=c$ and $\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i\alpha_i=v$. It is basic if $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ are linearly independent. It is an optimum dual solution with oracle inequalities if the selected normals are outputs of the strong separation oracle, and an optimum standard dual solution if the selected inequalities belong to a standard representation of $P$, with each equation treated as two inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty oracle-described polyhedron whose objective maximum exists, an optimum dual solution is a finite positive combination of valid inequalities whose combined normal equals the objective and whose combined right-hand side equals the optimum value. It is basic when the selected normals are linearly independent; oracle and standard variants restrict which valid inequalities may be selected.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is a nonempty polyhedron given by a strong separation oracle}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i a_i=c,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i\alpha_i=v;\qquad \text{basic}\iff a_1,\ldots,a_k\text{ are linearly independent, with oracle and standard variants determined by the permitted inequalities.}

knowledge_statements.title: Standard-Form Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-corresponding reductions among equality, inequality, sign-restricted, and free-variable finite-dimensional LP forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A free variable \(x_j\in\mathbb{R}\) may be replaced by \(x_j=x_j^+-x_j^-\), where \(x_j^+,x_j^-\ge0\). An inequality \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\) may be replaced by \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+s_i=b_i\), where \(s_i\ge0\); an inequality in the opposite direction may first be multiplied by \(-1\). An equality may be replaced by the two corresponding opposite inequalities. These transformations preserve feasibility and objective values under the natural correspondence of solutions. A minimization problem with objective \(f(x)\) may be represented as a maximization problem with objective \(-f(x)\); the feasible set is unchanged and the objective values are negated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Free variables, inequalities, and equalities can be converted by variable splitting, slack variables, sign reversal, and paired inequalities while preserving corresponding objective values. Changing minimization to maximization negates, rather than preserves, objective values.
assumptions_latex: All variables and constraints are finite-dimensional and real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint and variable transformations preserve corresponding feasible objective values, while replacing minimization of \(f\) by maximization of \(-f\) negates those values.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative parts replacing a free variable.

assumptions_latex: The primal is \(\sup\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\).
The dual is \(\inf\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c,\ y\ge0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the canonical pair, each primal row \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\) determines a nonnegative dual variable \(y_i\), while each nonnegative primal variable \(x_j\) determines the dual inequality \((A^{\mathsf T}y)_j\ge c_j\). Thus transposition exchanges rows and columns, maximization with upper-bound constraints becomes minimization with lower-bound constraints, and primal and dual slacks are \(b-Ax\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y-c\). Applying the same correspondence to the dual recovers the primal after canonical sign identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualization exchanges constraints and variables, transposes the coefficient matrix, reverses optimization direction and inequalities, and is involutive in canonical form.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Optimal-Basis Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a common primal-feasible and dual-feasible basis for the section's standard-form primal–dual LP pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P'=\max\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), and let \(D'=\min\{b^Ty:A^Ty\ge c\}\). If both \(P'\) and \(D'\) are feasible, then there exists a basis \(\beta\) that is simultaneously primal feasible and dual feasible; consequently, \(\beta\) is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If both members of the standard-form primal–dual pair are feasible, some basis is feasible on both sides and is therefore optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\beta\;\bigl(\beta\text{ is primal feasible and dual feasible}\bigr),\quad\text{hence }\beta\text{ is optimal}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-programming primal–dual correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural correspondence between finite-dimensional primal and dual linear programs under consistent sign conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a linear-programming primal–dual pair, each primal constraint corresponds to a dual variable and each primal variable corresponds to a dual constraint. A primal inequality constraint corresponds to a sign-restricted dual variable, while a primal equality corresponds to an unrestricted dual variable; analogously, the sign restriction on a primal variable determines whether its dual constraint is an inequality or equality. The coefficient matrices are transposes up to the adopted sign convention, the roles of \(b\) and \(c\) are exchanged, and dualization is reflexive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal constraints correspond to dual variables, and primal variables correspond to dual constraints. Equality and sign restrictions determine the corresponding unrestricted variables and equality constraints. The coefficient matrix is transposed, the right-hand-side and objective vectors exchange roles, and the dual of the dual is the primal.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual use mutually consistent objective, inequality, and sign conventions
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dual}(\operatorname{dual}(P))=P

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak duality for the canonical finite-dimensional linear-programming pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \(x\ge0\) and \(Ax\le b\), and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfies \(y\ge0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c\), then \(c^{\mathsf T}x\le b^{\mathsf T}y\). Consequently, when both feasible regions are nonempty, their extended optimal values satisfy \(p^*\le d^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every dual feasible value upper-bounds every primal feasible value, so the primal optimal value cannot exceed the dual optimal value when both feasible regions are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c^{\mathsf T}x\le b^{\mathsf T}y\), and hence \(p^*\le d^*\) whenever both feasible regions are nonempty.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-halfspace interpretation of feasible dual multipliers and supporting-hyperplane interpretation of zero-gap primal-dual pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\). Every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \(y\ge0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c\) defines a valid containing halfspace \(P\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:c^{\mathsf T}x\le b^{\mathsf T}y\}\). If \(x^*\in P\) and a dual-feasible \(y^*\) satisfy \(c^{\mathsf T}x^*=b^{\mathsf T}y^*\), then \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y^*\}\) is a supporting hyperplane of \(P\) at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-feasible multiplier defines a halfspace containing the primal polyhedron. Equality at a primal feasible point makes its boundary a supporting hyperplane there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:c^{\mathsf T}x\le b^{\mathsf T}y\}\); equality at \(x^*\in P\) yields a supporting hyperplane at \(x^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conic characterization of LP boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A geometric duality criterion for boundedness above of a feasible maximization-form linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\). Then \(\max\{cx:Ax\le b\}\) is bounded above if and only if \(c\in\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\), where \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) are the rows of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible maximization LP, the objective is bounded above exactly when its objective vector lies in the cone generated by the constraint-matrix rows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{cx:Ax\le b\}\text{ is bounded above}\iff c\in\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-form Farkas infeasibility certificate for a nonnegative linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the system \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), a Farkas certificate of infeasibility is a vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that
\[
A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\quad\text{and}\quad b^{\mathsf T}y<0.
\]
Indeed, the displayed inequalities are directly checkable from \(A\), \(b\), and \(y\). Farkas' alternative states that such a certificate exists if and only if no vector \(x\ge0\) satisfies \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infeasibility of a nonnegative equality system is certified by a multiplier nonnegative on every column but negative on the right-hand side.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), exactly one of the following systems is feasible:
\[
\text{(I)}\quad Ax=b,\quad x\ge0,

\[
\text{(II)}\quad A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\quad b^{\mathsf T}y<0.
\]
Thus feasibility of the first system excludes every witness for the second, while infeasibility of the first guarantees at least one witness satisfying the second.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(x\ge0\) satisfies \(Ax=b\), and suppose \(y\) satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\). Then
\[
b^{\mathsf T}y=(Ax)^{\mathsf T}y=x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0.
\]
Consequently the additional strict inequality \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) cannot hold. Hence the feasibility system \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\) and its Farkas alternative system are mutually exclusive.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\ge0\), \(Ax\le b\), \(y\ge0\), and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c\). The feasible pair \((x,y)\) is primal-dual optimal if and only if
\[
y_i(b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x)=0\quad\text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m,
\]
and
\[
x_j((A^{\mathsf T}y)_j-c_j)=0\quad\text{for every }j=1,\ldots,n.
\]
Equivalently, every positive variable has a tight corresponding constraint and every positive multiplier has a tight primal constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal-dual pair is optimal exactly when each variable or multiplier is complementary to its corresponding nonnegative slack.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementary Slackness for an Inequality-Form Linear Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for an already feasible primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\) be feasible for \((P)=\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le b\}\), and let \(v\) be feasible for \((D)=\min\{y^Tb:y^TA=c^T,\ y\ge0\}\). Then \(u\) and \(v\) are optimal for their respective programs if and only if \(v_i(b_i-A_i u)=0\) for every \(i\), equivalently \(v_i>0\Rightarrow A_i u=b_i\), or \(A_i u<b_i\Rightarrow v_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal-dual pair is optimal exactly when each positive dual variable corresponds to a tight primal constraint, equivalently each slack primal constraint has zero dual variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u,v\text{ are optimal}\iff \forall i,\ v_i(b_i-A_i u)=0.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise compatibility between primal slack and dual support for the displayed inequality-form primal–dual pair.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-duality-gap certificate for finite-dimensional canonical linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\). A primal-dual optimality certificate is a pair \((x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \(x\ge0\), \(Ax\le b\), \(y\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\). With \(v:=c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\), the certificate establishes that \(x\) and \(y\) are optimal and that \(p^*=d^*=v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and dual feasible points with equal objective values jointly certify their optimality and the common optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(v:=c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\), the pair \((x,y)\) certifies \(p^*=d^*=v\).

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Certificate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pair-specific degeneracy through failure of strict complementarity in standard-form linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible primal-dual pair \((x,y)\), let \(s=c-A^Ty\geq0\). The pair is an optimality certificate when \(c^Tx-b^Ty=x^Ts=0\), equivalently when \(x_i s_i=0\) for every \(i\). Call this certificate pair-degenerate when \(D_0(x,y)=\{i:x_i=s_i=0\}\) is nonempty. Equivalently, it is pair-degenerate when it fails strict complementarity, which requires \(x_i+s_i>0\) for every \(i\). Pair-degeneracy does not by itself imply nonoptimality or nonuniqueness of the primal or dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal primal-dual certificate is pair-degenerate when some primal variable and its complementary dual slack are both zero, equivalently when that pair is not strictly complementary.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(y\) are feasible for \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty\leq c\}\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate is pair-degenerate exactly when \(D_0(x,y)\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Indices simultaneously zero on both complementary sides.

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal basic-solution degeneracy in equality-form linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) contain \(r\) indices such that the columns of \(A_B\) are linearly independent. A basic feasible solution associated with \(B\) has \(x_j=0\) for \(j\notin B\), while \(x_B\) is the unique nonnegative vector satisfying \(A_Bx_B=b\). It is degenerate when at least one component of \(x_B\) is zero. Equivalently, a basic feasible solution \(x\) is degenerate exactly when \(|\{i:x_i>0\}|<r\). Degeneracy does not imply infeasibility or failure of optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic feasible solution is degenerate when at least one basic variable is zero, equivalently when fewer than the rank of the constraint matrix many variables are positive.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a basic feasible solution of \(Ax=b,\ x\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is degenerate}\iff |\{i:x_i>0\}|<r\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \((P)\) and \((D)\) are both feasible, both attain finite optima and their optimal values are equal. If \((P)\) is feasible while \((D)\) is infeasible, then \((P)\) is unbounded below. If \((D)\) is feasible while \((P)\) is infeasible, then \((D)\) is unbounded above. Both programs may be infeasible. Weak duality excludes primal unboundedness when the dual is feasible and excludes dual unboundedness when the primal is feasible. Hence a positive finite duality gap is not a failure regime for this linear-programming model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional primal-dual LP pair, feasible problems have equal attained optima; all remaining failures reduce to the permitted infeasible or unbounded status combinations.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Length of Rational Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One explicit additive binary-size convention for rational scalar, vector, matrix, and linear-program data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a reduced rational number \(p/q\), define \(\lambda(p/q)=1+\lceil\log_2(|p|+1)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(q+1)\rceil\), where the initial bit accommodates the sign. For \(v\in\mathbb{Q}^k\), define \(\lambda(v)=k+\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda(v_i)\). For \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), define \(\lambda(A)=m+n+mn+\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n\lambda(A_{ij})\). For rational linear-program data \((A,b,c)\), define its total encoding length by \(L=\lambda(A)+\lambda(b)+\lambda(c)\). Inequality systems are encoded analogously by including the coefficient arrays, right-hand sides, dimensions, and objective data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under this explicit convention, rational input size is the sum of the binary lengths of reduced numerators, positive denominators, signs, dimensions, and all entries of the matrix, right-hand side, and objective vector.
assumptions_latex: Every rational number is written uniquely as \(p/q\), where \(p\in\mathbb{Z}\), \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), and \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The input size of \((A,b,c)\) is \(L=\lambda(A)+\lambda(b)+\lambda(c)\).

notation.meaning: Binary encoding length of a reduced rational number.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary Encoding Length of Integer and Rational Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-size conventions for integers, reduced rationals, rational arrays, linear inequalities, systems, tuples, and linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define $\langle n\rangle:=1+\left\lceil\log_2(|n|+1)\right\rceil$. If $r=p/q\in\mathbb Q$ is in its unique reduced representation with $q>0$, define $\langle r\rangle:=\langle p\rangle+\langle q\rangle$. The encoding length of a rational vector or matrix is the sum of its entry lengths; the encoding length of $a^Tx\le b$ is $\langle a\rangle+\langle b\rangle$; and the lengths of systems and tuples are obtained by summation. In particular, $\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le b\}$ has encoding length $\langle A,b,c\rangle$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer is encoded in binary with a sign bit, and a rational is encoded through its coprime numerator and positive denominator. The lengths of rational arrays, inequalities, systems, tuples, and linear programs are the sums of the lengths of their numerical data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle n\rangle=1+\left\lceil\log_2(|n|+1)\right\rceil,\qquad \langle r\rangle=\langle p\rangle+\langle q\rangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-time objective compression preserving optimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compression of a rational linear objective to bounded encoding length, uniformly preserving its optimizing vectors over polyhedra with a prescribed vertex-complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\) and \(v\in\mathbb N\), there is a polynomial-time algorithm computing \(a\in\mathbb Q^n\) such that, for every polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) of vertex-complexity at most \(v\), the objective functions \(c^Tx\) and \(a^Tx\) are optimized by the same vectors in \(P\), and \(\langle a\rangle\le 88(n+1)^3(v+1)\). Moreover, the algorithm performs a number of elementary arithmetic operations polynomial in \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational linear objective can be compressed in polynomial time to an objective of explicitly bounded encoding length while preserving all optimizing vectors over every polyhedron whose vertex-complexity is at most v. The arithmetic-operation count is polynomial in v.

children.title: Vertex Encoding Size
children.top_down_role: Bit-length control for rational extreme points.

assumptions_latex: Every coefficient has absolute value less than \(2^\ell\), with \(\ell\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every vertex \(v\) satisfies \(\lambda(v)=O\!\left(n^2(\ell+\log n)\right)\).

notation.meaning: An index set of n linearly independent tight inequalities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cramer-Hadamard bit bound for vertices of an integer inequality description.

source_refs.locator: * 6.2 Complexity of Rational Polyhedra p. 162

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every vertex \(v\) of \(P\), there is an index set \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) of cardinality \(n\) such that \(A_I\) is nonsingular and \(v=A_I^{-1}b_I\). In reduced form, every numerator and denominator of \(v_j\) is bounded in absolute value by \(n^{n/2}2^{n\ell}\). Consequently, each coordinate has encoding length \(O(n(\ell+\log n))\), and \(\lambda(v)=O(n^2(\ell+\log n))\). Clearing denominators first gives a polynomial bound in the total encoding length for rational descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every vertex is determined by independent tight inequalities, and determinant bounds make its rational encoding polynomial in the dimension and coefficient bit size.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Encoding Size

children.title: Face Description Size
children.top_down_role: Representation size associated with faces and supporting descriptions.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\) is a rational polyhedron described by \(m\) indexed inequalities of total encoding length \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\{x\in P:A_Ix=b_I\}\) for some \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), with relative encoding size \(O(m)\) and expanded size at most \(O(L)\).

notation.meaning: Indices of inequalities selected as equalities on the face.
The selected rows and right-hand sides.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Description of a face relative to a fixed rational inequality system.

source_refs.locator: * 6.2 Complexity of Rational Polyhedra p. 162

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a set \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) such that \(F=\{x\in P:A_i x=b_i\text{ for every }i\in I\}\). Relative to the given description of \(P\), the set \(I\) can be encoded by an \(m\)-bit incidence vector. If the defining equalities are written explicitly, they reuse rows of \((A,b)\), so their total coefficient encoding length is at most \(L\), up to dimension and indexing overhead. Thus no coefficients of superpolynomial bit length are required to specify a face of a rationally described polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face is specified by declaring selected original inequalities tight; indices require linear space, and an expanded description reuses at most the original input size.

Certificates are checked using exact binary rational arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a polynomial \(q\) such that each applicable certificate can be chosen with encoding length at most \(q(L,m,n)\).

notation.meaning: Total encoding length of the input data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial bit bounds for exact rational LP status and optimality witnesses.

source_refs.locator: * 6.2 Complexity of Rational Polyhedra p. 162

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Whenever the corresponding status holds, one may choose rational witnesses of polynomial encoding length: a feasible basic solution \(x\); an infeasibility vector \(y\) with \(A^Ty\geq0\) and \(b^Ty<0\); an unboundedness pair \((x^0,d)\) with \(Ax^0=b\), \(x^0\geq0\), \(Ad=0\), \(d\geq0\), and \(c^Td<0\); or an optimal primal-dual pair \((x,y)\) with equal objectives. children.title: Weak Polyhedral Problems
children.top_down_role: Tolerance-based access to rational polyhedral regions.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a bounded closed convex set, \(\varepsilon\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}\), and \(\|c\|_2\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak polyhedral problems permit outer feasibility error and optimize only against the eroded set, with additive objective error \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Points whose closed epsilon-ball lies in K.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean tolerance version of weak feasibility and weak maximization for bounded convex sets.

source_refs.locator: * 6.3 Weak and Strong Problems p. 170

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Weak feasibility at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) asks either for a point \(y\in K^{+\varepsilon}\) or for the correct assertion \(K^{-\varepsilon}=\varnothing\). Weak maximization additionally receives \(c\) with \(\|c\|_2\leq1\) and, unless \(K^{-\varepsilon}=\varnothing\), asks for \(y\in K^{+\varepsilon}\) satisfying \(c^Ty\geq c^Tx-\varepsilon\) for every \(x\in K^{-\varepsilon}\). Thus both geometric feasibility and objective optimality are interpreted with an explicitly encoded tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak problems accept points near the set and compare objective values against an eroded set, allowing a specified additive tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Polyhedral Problems

children.title: Strong Polyhedral Problems
children.top_down_role: Exact access to rational polyhedral data or decisions.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\) is a rational polyhedron and all queries are rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong problems require exact membership, exact separating inequalities, and exact optimal values or status certificates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact separation and optimization versions for rational polyhedra.

source_refs.locator: * 6.3 Weak and Strong Problems p. 170
* 6.4 Equivalence of Strong Optimization and Separation p. 174

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strong separation, given \(y\), must decide exactly whether \(y\in P\); if not, it returns rational \((a,\beta)\) such that \(a^Tx\leq\beta<a^Ty\) for every \(x\in P\). Strong optimization, given \(c\), must return an exact maximizer of \(c^Tx\) over \(P\) and its exact rational value when finite and attained, or correctly report infeasibility or unboundedness with the corresponding exact certificate. No geometric or objective tolerance is part of either specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polyhedral problems demand exact membership and separation, or an exact optimizer and value, with exact certificates for infeasibility or unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Polyhedral Problems

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle-Polynomial Vertex–Ray Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minkowski-type decomposition of a point in a pointed polyhedron, including the stated independence condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every well-described pointed polyhedron $(P;n,\varphi)$ given by a strong optimization oracle and every $y_0\in P\cap\mathbb{Q}^n$, an oracle-polynomial-time algorithm finds vertices $x_0,\ldots,x_t$ of $P$ with $t\geq0$, positive rationals $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_t$ satisfying $\sum_{i=0}^t\lambda_i=1$, and vectors $y_1,\ldots,y_s$ with $s\geq0$ contained in extremal rays of $\operatorname{rec}(P)$, such that $x_1-x_0,\ldots,x_t-x_0,y_1,\ldots,y_s$ are linearly independent and $y_0=\sum_{i=0}^t\lambda_i x_i+\sum_{j=1}^s y_j$.

children.title: Exact–Approximate Complexity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Representation and precision conditions separating the two problem regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact–Approximate Complexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rational-gap boundary separating tolerance answers from recoverable exact polyhedral answers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Distinct reduced rational numbers with denominators at most \(Q\) differ by at least \(1/Q^2\). Therefore, if an approximation \(\widehat z\) to such a rational value \(z\) satisfies \(|\widehat z-z|<1/(2Q^2)\), then \(z\) is the unique rational with reduced denominator at most \(Q\) in that error interval and can be recovered by rational reconstruction. Without a known encoding or denominator bound, no fixed positive tolerance ensures exact recovery: for any \(\varepsilon>0\), choose a rational \(\delta\) with \(0<\delta<\varepsilon\). The intervals \(P_0=[0,1]\) and \(P_\delta=[0,1+\delta]\) admit a common \(\varepsilon\)-accurate maximization answer for objective \(c=1\), although their exact optimal values are \(1\) and \(1+\delta\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximation determines an exact rational answer when its error is strictly below half a known denominator-dependent gap; without such a bound, arbitrarily close polyhedra can have different exact optima.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), and the exact rational value \(z\) has reduced denominator at most \(Q\).
\(\widehat z\) is an approximation to \(z\), and weak answers use a tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact recovery is guaranteed when \(|\widehat z-z|<1/(2Q^2)\); without a known size bound, fixed-tolerance weak information does not determine exact answers.

notation.meaning: Known upper bound on the reduced denominator of the exact rational value.
Approximation to the exact rational value z.

children.title: Precision Requirements
children.top_down_role: Bit precision needed for reliable polyhedral decisions or witnesses.

knowledge_statements.title: Precision Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient absolute accuracy for exact membership decisions on integer inequality systems at rational query points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\). If \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) satisfies \(qy\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), then every slack \(s_i=b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}y\) belongs to \(q^{-1}\mathbb{Z}\). For approximations satisfying \(|\widetilde{s}_i-s_i|<1/(2q)\), one has \(s_i>0\) when \(\widetilde{s}_i>1/(2q)\), \(s_i<0\) when \(\widetilde{s}_i<-1/(2q)\), and \(s_i=0\) when \(|\widetilde{s}_i|<1/(2q)\). These alternatives decide exactly whether \(y\in P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integer inequality system and a rational query with common denominator q, slack approximations with absolute error below 1/(2q) determine every slack sign, including zero, and therefore decide exact membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The approximations determine every slack sign and decide exactly whether \(y\in P\).

notation.meaning: slack of inequality i at the query point
a common denominator of the query coordinates

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Radius Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An explicit outer-radius estimate for bounded polyhedra described by bounded integer data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and \(H\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}\), with \(|A_{ij}|\le H\) and \(|b_i|\le H\) for all indices. If \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is nonempty and bounded, then every \(x\in P\) satisfies \(\|x\|_2\le\sqrt n\,n!H^n\). Equivalently, \(P\subseteq B(0,\sqrt n\,n!H^n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty bounded polyhedron in n dimensions whose integral inequality data have magnitude at most H lies in the Euclidean ball centered at zero with radius √n n! H^n.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}\), \(|A_{ij}|\le H\), and \(|b_i|\le H\) for all indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P\subseteq B\!\left(0,\sqrt n\,n!H^n\right).\]

children.title: Conditioning Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of oracle behavior on geometric conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz sensitivity of linear optimization values to Hausdorff perturbations of compact feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K,L\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty compact sets and let \(d_H(K,L)\le\delta\) under the Euclidean metric, where \(\delta\ge0\). Define \(h_K(c)=\max_{x\in K}c^{\mathsf T}x\) and \(h_L(c)=\max_{x\in L}c^{\mathsf T}x\). For every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(|h_K(c)-h_L(c)|\le\|c\|_2\delta\). In particular, if \(\|c\|_2=1\), then \(|h_K(c)-h_L(c)|\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moving a nonempty compact feasible set by Hausdorff distance at most δ changes any linear optimum by at most the objective norm times δ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[|h_K(c)-h_L(c)|\le \|c\|_2\delta\quad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]

notation.meaning: support functions of K and L

children.title: Tolerance Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where rounding or separation tolerances obscure the intended conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional family showing that tolerance comparable to geometric feature size cannot preserve exact decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(K_\varepsilon=[0,\varepsilon]\subset\mathbb{R}\) and \(y_\varepsilon=2\varepsilon\). Then \(y_\varepsilon\notin K_\varepsilon\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(y_\varepsilon,K_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\). Under a weak-membership convention that permits an IN response whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\), the exterior query \(y_\varepsilon\) may receive IN for every \(\delta\ge\varepsilon\). For the objective \(c=1\), its candidate value \(c y_\varepsilon=2\varepsilon\) exceeds the exact optimum \(h_{K_\varepsilon}(c)=\varepsilon\) by \(\varepsilon\). Thus weak acceptance at this tolerance cannot certify exact membership or exact-feasible optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When tolerance is at least the width of a small interval, weak membership may accept an exterior point whose objective value exceeds the interval's true optimum by that width.
assumptions_latex: The weak-membership convention permits IN when \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak acceptance at tolerance \(\delta\ge\varepsilon\) need not certify exact membership or an exactly feasible optimizer over \(K_\varepsilon\).

children.title: Point Membership

knowledge_statements.title: Point Membership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact membership oracle for a specified convex or polyhedral feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a fixed set represented implicitly. An exact point-membership oracle accepts a query \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and returns YES precisely when \(y\in K\), and NO precisely when \(y\notin K\). When \(K=P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\) is explicitly represented, the predicate is equivalent to \(a_i^{\mathsf T}y\le b_i\) for every row \(i\). The oracle's output is exact: no tolerance band around the boundary is left unspecified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point-membership oracle decides exactly whether a rational query belongs to the fixed feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns YES if and only if \(y\in K\).

children.title: Inequality Validity

knowledge_statements.title: Inequality Validity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validity oracle for linear inequalities over a fixed feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be fixed. An exact inequality-validity oracle receives \((a,\beta)\in\mathbb{Q}^n\times\mathbb{Q}\) and returns YES precisely when \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) holds for every \(x\in K\). If \(K\) is nonempty and compact, this is equivalent to \(h_K(a)=\max_{x\in K}a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\). A NO answer asserts the existence of some \(x\in K\) with \(a^{\mathsf T}x>\beta\), although the interface need not return such a witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality-validity oracle decides whether a queried rational linear inequality holds at every point of the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns YES if and only if \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) for all \(x\in K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Membership–Validity Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact membership–validity conversion through polar duality for convex bodies containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex with \(0\in\operatorname{int}K\), and define \(K^\circ=\{z:z^{\mathsf T}x\le1\text{ for all }x\in K\}\). The bipolar theorem gives \(K=(K^\circ)^\circ\). Hence a membership query \(y\in K\) is equivalent to validity of \(y^{\mathsf T}z\le1\) over \(K^\circ\). Conversely, for \(\beta>0\), validity of \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) over \(K\) is equivalent to membership \(a/\beta\in K^\circ\). Thus exact membership and positive-right-hand-side validity reduce to one another when the polar body is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polar duality converts membership in a convex body into validity over its polar, and positive-threshold validity into polar membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[y\in K\iff y^{\mathsf T}z\le1\ \forall z\in K^\circ,\qquad a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\ \forall x\in K\iff a/\beta\in K^\circ.\]

children.title: Exact Separation
children.top_down_role: Exact identification of containment or a separating inequality.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact strong separation oracle for a nonempty compact convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex. An exact separation oracle receives \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\). If \(y\in K\), it returns IN. If \(y\notin K\), it returns \((a,\beta)\in\mathbb{Q}^n\times\mathbb{Q}\) such that \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y\) for every \(x\in K\). No tolerance band is permitted in either output alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty compact convex set, exact separation either confirms membership or returns a rational valid inequality strictly violated by the rational query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is IN with \(y\in K\), or \((a,\beta)\in\mathbb{Q}^n\times\mathbb{Q}\) with \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y\) for every \(x\in K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact separation oracle for a linear-inequality system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact membership-or-violated-inequality interface, together with its use for ellipsoid cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}$, an exact separation oracle accepts $s\in\mathbb R^n$ and returns YES if $s\in P$. If $s\notin P$, it returns a row $a_i^Tx\le b_i$ such that $a_i^Ts>b_i$; this inequality separates $s$ from $P$. The ellipsoid method queries the oracle at each current center and uses the returned violated inequality to determine its next ellipsoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact separation oracle either certifies that the query point satisfies the system or returns a system inequality violated by that point. The ellipsoid method queries it at the current centers and uses the returned inequalities as cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s\in P\Rightarrow\mathrm{YES};\qquad s\notin P\Rightarrow\exists i:\ a_i^Ts>b_i\text{ and the oracle returns }a_i^Tx\le b_i

children.title: Weak Separation
children.top_down_role: Tolerance-based separation for approximate geometric access.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-based separation with a specified Euclidean near-membership alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(\delta>0\). A \(\delta\)-weak separation oracle queried at \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) may return NEAR only when \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\). Otherwise it returns a vector \(a\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) with \(\|a\|_2=1\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}y\ge h_K(a)+\delta\), where \(h_K(a)=\sup_{x\in K}a^{\mathsf T}x\). Thus queries farther than \(\delta\) receive a valid separating direction with margin at least \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak separation may declare a point near the set within δ; farther points receive a normalized separator with margin at least δ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns NEAR with \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\), or \(a\) with \(\|a\|_2=1\) and \(a^{\mathsf T}y\ge h_K(a)+\delta\).

children.title: Separation Precision Boundary
children.top_down_role: Geometric and encoding conditions controlling transfer between exact and weak access.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Precision Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The rational slack gap separating sufficient precision from an unavoidable weak-oracle ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\). If \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) satisfies \(qy\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), then every violated row satisfies \(a_i^{\mathsf T}y-b_i\ge1/q\), and row-evaluation error strictly below \(1/(2q)\) preserves the sign of every nonzero violation. This scale is sharp up to the factor two: for \(P=(-\infty,0]\subset\mathbb{R}\) and \(y=1/q\), the violation and distance to \(P\) both equal \(1/q\). Under a weak-separation convention permitting NEAR whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(y,P)\le\delta\), \(\delta\ge1/q\) therefore does not require a separating output for this exterior query.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a rational query with common denominator q, nonzero row violations are at least 1/q, so evaluation error below 1/(2q) preserves their signs, while near-set tolerance at least 1/q can hide an exterior point.
assumptions_latex: The weak-separation convention permits NEAR when \(\operatorname{dist}(y,P)\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Evaluation precision strictly below \(1/(2q)\) detects every nonzero row violation, whereas ambiguity tolerance \(\delta\ge1/q\) cannot guarantee a separating output in general.

notation.meaning: common denominator of the query coordinates

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear-optimization oracle over a nonempty compact feasible set, with rational objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and compact. An exact linear-optimization oracle receives \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and returns \(x^*\in K\) satisfying \(c^{\mathsf T}x^*=\max_{x\in K}c^{\mathsf T}x\), together with the exact optimal value if the interface requests it. If \(K\) is a rational polytope, an optimal rational vertex can be returned. The output requires exact feasibility and exact objective optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact optimization returns a feasible point attaining the true maximum of the queried rational linear objective; for a rational polytope, a rational optimal vertex can be selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(x^*\in K\) satisfies \(c^{\mathsf T}x^*=\max_{x\in K}c^{\mathsf T}x\).

children.title: Weak Optimization
children.top_down_role: Approximate objective-based access under explicit tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-error linear optimization with exact feasibility over a compact feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and compact. Given \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), an additive \(\varepsilon\)-weak optimization oracle returns \(x_\varepsilon\in K\) such that \(c^{\mathsf T}x_\varepsilon\ge h_K(c)-\varepsilon\), where \(h_K(c)=\max_{x\in K}c^{\mathsf T}x\). This convention relaxes objective optimality by an absolute amount \(\varepsilon\) but retains exact feasibility. If objectives are normalized by \(\|c\|_2=1\), the tolerance has the same geometric scale as Euclidean perturbations of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak optimization returns an exactly feasible point whose objective is within additive ε of the true linear optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(x_\varepsilon\in K\) satisfies \(c^{\mathsf T}x_\varepsilon\ge h_K(c)-\varepsilon\).

children.title: Optimization Precision Boundary
children.top_down_role: Encoding and scale conditions governing equivalence between exact and weak access.

assumptions_latex: \(L\in\mathbb{N}\) is part of the rational input-size parameter.
Approximate maximization uses the additive guarantee \(c^{\mathsf T}x\geq h_K(c)-\varepsilon\), where \(h_K(c)=\max_{z\in K}c^{\mathsf T}z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon\)-optimization implies exact optimization only when additional data provide a positive lower bound on the gap between distinct attainable objective values, and \(\varepsilon\) is smaller than that bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive weak optimization cannot generally recover an exact rational optimum without a precision bound tied to encoding size.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K_L=\{0,2^{-L}\}\subset\mathbb{R}\) and objective \(c=1\), the exact optimum is \(2^{-L}\). If \(\varepsilon\geq 2^{-L}\), then returning \(x=0\) satisfies \(x\geq \max_{z\in K_L}z-\varepsilon\), although it is not exactly optimal. Hence a weak optimization oracle with tolerance independent of \(L\) does not determine the exact optimum. More generally, conversion from weak to exact optimization requires a known objective-value separation bound derived from rational encoding or comparable discrete structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak optimization yields an exact optimum only when its tolerance is below a known gap between distinct attainable objective values.

children.title: Violation Detection
children.top_down_role: Interfaces reporting whether a candidate inequality or point violates the region.

knowledge_statements.title: Violation Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Boolean detection is distinguished from producing a separating witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact violation-detection oracle for \(K\) maps each query \(y\) to one of two outputs: \(\mathrm{ACCEPT}\) if \(y\in K\), and \(\mathrm{REJECT}\) if \(y\notin K\). Its specification requires only correct evaluation of the membership predicate. A rejection need not include coefficients \((a,\beta)\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y\) for every \(x\in K\); producing such coefficients is the stronger separating-witness task.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Violation detection answers whether a query point belongs to the convex set, without necessarily returning a separating hyperplane.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a specified closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output determines whether \(y\in K\) but supplies no separating inequality when membership fails.

children.title: Separating-Witness Output
children.top_down_role: Interfaces returning an explicit geometric certificate of exclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Separating-Witness Output
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation certificate for a point outside a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A separating-witness output for \(y\) is a pair \((a,\beta)\in(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}\) such that \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta\) for every \(x\in K\), while \(a^{\mathsf T}y>\beta\). Positive rescaling leaves the represented halfspace unchanged, so the witness may be normalized by \(\lVert a\rVert_2=1\). The strict inequality places \(y\) outside a valid halfspace containing all of \(K\), thereby certifying \(y\notin K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separating witness is a valid inequality containing the entire convex set but strictly violated by the query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((a,\beta)\) is a mathematical certificate that \(y\notin K\).

notation.meaning: normal vector of the separating inequality
right-hand side of the separating inequality

children.title: Approximate Violation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Violation interfaces parameterized by numerical or geometric tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Violation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean additive tolerance with an explicit indifference band.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \(\delta\)-approximate violation detector for \(K\), where \(\delta>0\), must return \(\mathrm{ACCEPT}\) whenever \(y\in K\), and must return \(\mathrm{REJECT}\) whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\geq\delta\), where \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)=\inf_{x\in K}\lVert y-x\rVert_2\). For queries satisfying \(0<\operatorname{dist}(y,K)<\delta\), either answer is allowed. Exact violation detection is the separate regime in which every query outside \(K\) must be rejected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate detection must accept members and reject points at least delta away, but may answer arbitrarily within the intervening tolerance band; exact detection rejects every nonmember.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Correct output is mandatory for \(y\in K\) and for \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\geq\delta\), while either output is permitted when \(0<\operatorname{dist}(y,K)<\delta\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance from the query to the set

children.title: Witness-Strength Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Comparative information content of violation and separation outputs.

assumptions_latex: Witness normals are normalized by \(\lVert a\rVert_2=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A larger certified margin is a stronger witness; every positive-margin witness implies violation detection, but a Boolean rejection contains no witness coefficients.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Witnesses are ordered by certified normalized separation margin.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Oracles p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a valid normalized witness \((a,\beta)\), define its margin at \(y\) by \(m(a,\beta;y)=a^{\mathsf T}y-\beta\). If \(m(a,\beta;y)\geq\gamma>0\), the witness is a \(\gamma\)-strong certificate and implies \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\geq\gamma\). Consequently, a \(\gamma_2\)-strong witness also meets every weaker requirement \(0<\gamma_1\leq\gamma_2\). An unquantified strict witness certifies only some positive margin, while a Boolean violation output certifies no explicit halfspace or margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized witnesses are stronger when they certify a larger margin; any such witness detects violation, while a Boolean rejection supplies no hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.title: Witness-Strength Comparisons

children.title: Convex-Body Oracle Equivalences

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a convex body with known rational \(a\), \(0<r\leq R\), and \(B_2(a,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B_2(a,R)\).
All queries and requested tolerances have finite rational encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak separation and weak linear optimization for \(K\) are polynomial-time oracle reducible to one another under these geometric access bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated sandwiching bounds, an oracle solving weak separation over \(K\) can be used to compute, for any rational \(c\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), a point whose objective value is within \(\varepsilon\) of \(\sup_{x\in K}c^{\mathsf T}x\). Conversely, weak optimization can implement weak separation with polynomially related tolerances. The numbers of arithmetic operations and oracle calls are polynomial in \(n\), the input encoding length, \(\log(R/r)\), and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex body with known inner and outer radius bounds, weak separation and weak optimization simulate each other in polynomial time.

knowledge_statements.title: Rational-Polyhedral Oracle Equivalences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong oracle equivalence for bounded, well-described rational polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty bounded rational polyhedron with a known facet-complexity bound \(L\). Strong separation over \(P\) and exact rational linear optimization over \(P\) are polynomial-time oracle reducible to one another. The bit complexity and number of oracle calls are bounded by a polynomial in \(n\), \(L\), and the binary encoding length of the objective vector or query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded rational polyhedron with a known facet-complexity bound, exact linear optimization and strong separation implement one another in oracle-polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty bounded rational polyhedron.
A facet-complexity bound \(L\) for a rational inequality description of \(P\) is known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong separation and exact rational linear optimization over \(P\) are polynomial-time oracle equivalent, with complexity polynomial in \(n\), \(L\), and the query encoding length.

children.title: Oracle-Reduction Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Ellipsoid-mediated and related transformations among polyhedral access problems.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq B_2(a,R)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex and accessed by a valid separation oracle.
The objective \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) are given.

source_refs.locator: * 6.4 Equivalence of Strong Optimization and Separation p. 174

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(E_0=B_2(a,R)\) and an empty incumbent list. At iteration \(k\), query the center \(z_k\). If separation returns \(u^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta<u^{\mathsf T}z_k\), replace \(E_k\) by the minimum-volume standard ellipsoidal update containing \(E_k\cap\{x:u^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta\}\). If \(z_k\) is feasible, retain it and use an objective cut based on \(c^{\mathsf T}x\). Stop when the maintained objective bounds differ by at most \(\varepsilon\), and output the best retained feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ellipsoid method alternates separating and objective cuts until its objective bounds are within tolerance, then returns the best feasible center found.

assumptions_latex: An ellipsoid-based reduction is expected to run in time polynomial in the available input parameters.
No positive inner-radius bound \(r\), or equivalent width parameter, is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The usual ellipsoid oracle bound contains a term proportional to \(\log(R/r)\) when \(B_2(a,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B_2(a,R)\). If only \(R\) is known, convex bodies may have arbitrarily small inradius while all stated parameters remain fixed. The quantity \(\log(R/r)\) is then unbounded and the volume-shrinkage stopping argument supplies no uniform polynomial iteration bound. Lower-dimensional bodies correspond to \(r=0\) in the ambient space and require separate affine-hull or rational-encoding information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without an inner-radius or comparable width bound, standard ellipsoid reductions have no uniform polynomial iteration guarantee, especially for thin or lower-dimensional bodies.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(P_L=[0,2^{-L}]\subset\mathbb{R}\) and maximize \(x\). Its exact optimum has encoding length proportional to \(L\), and distinguishing it from \(0\) by additive optimization requires \(\varepsilon<2^{-L}\). If \(L\) is uncontrolled and omitted from the input-size measure, neither the necessary precision nor the output length is polynomially bounded by dimension alone. Thus exact optimization-separation equivalence requires an explicit rational encoding-complexity bound or an equivalent certificate-size bound.

children.title: Precision-Limited Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Limits on oracle transfer under inadequate numerical accuracy.

assumptions_latex: The available oracle is guaranteed correct only to a fixed tolerance \(\delta>0\).
The requested optimization or separation accuracy is \(\varepsilon<\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fixed-precision oracle does not, without refinement access or discrete gap information, imply an oracle solving the target task to accuracy \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle equivalence transfers accuracies only through an explicit polynomial tolerance relation.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21
1.2 Oracles p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Weak-oracle reductions invoke their source oracle at tolerances determined by the desired target accuracy. If access is restricted to a fixed \(\delta\), admissible answers may conceal geometric or objective differences smaller than \(\delta\). For example, the intervals \(K_0=[-1,0]\) and \(K_1=[-1,\eta]\), with \(0<\eta<\delta\), have support values in direction \(1\) differing by \(\eta\); a \(\delta\)-accurate response need not distinguish them. Hence it cannot guarantee optimization error \(\varepsilon<\eta/2\) without finer queries or gap information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-tolerance oracle cannot generally support reductions demanding finer accuracy because geometries and objective values below its resolution may remain indistinguishable.
knowledge_statements.title: Precision-Limited Equivalence

children.title: Information-Deficient Oracles
children.top_down_role: Non-equivalence regimes caused by oracle outputs too weak for the desired reduction.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) ranges over general closed convex sets.
The oracle returns only a Boolean membership or violation answer and exposes neither a hyperplane nor quantitative distance information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Boolean rejection alone is not a separating certificate, and no unrestricted strong-separation reduction follows without additional geometric, encoding, or refinement assumptions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical output insufficiency of Boolean detection for strong witness production in an unrestricted oracle model.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Oracles p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rejected query \(y\notin K\), a Boolean oracle reveals only the truth value of \(y\in K\). Strong separation instead requires explicit \((a,\beta)\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y\) for all \(x\in K\), with representable coefficients and controlled size. The Boolean answer contains none of these data. Transforming repeated Boolean answers into such a witness therefore requires additional assumptions, such as quantitative radius bounds, finite-precision refinement, rational encoding bounds, or a specified richer oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Boolean rejection does not itself reveal a separating hyperplane; witness recovery requires additional geometric, precision, encoding, or oracle-access assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Information-Deficient Oracles

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Oracles p. 26

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between a Boolean rejection and an explicit separating witness is correct, but the broader nonreducibility assertion depends on the allowed query model, precision, adaptivity, and representation of K. The cited oracle-definition location does not inspectably establish that boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear optimization over a combinatorial convex hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality of linear optimization values over a set family and the convex hull of its incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((E,\mathcal F)\) be a set system, let \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^X:X\in\mathcal F\}\), and let \(c:E\to\mathbb R\). With \(c(X)=\sum_{e\in X}c(e)\), one has \(\max\{c^\top x:x\in P\}=\max\{c(X):X\in\mathcal F\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximizing a linear objective over the convex hull of a family's incidence vectors has the same value as maximizing the corresponding set weight over the family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{x\in P}c^\top x=\max_{X\in\mathcal F}c(X).

knowledge_statements.title: Natural Continuous Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard LP relaxation obtained by dropping integrality while retaining the linear constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\). For the integer feasible set \(S=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n:Ax\le b\}\), its natural continuous relaxation is the rational polyhedron \[R=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}.\] Thus \(S=R\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\) and \(S\subseteq R\). All linear constraints, including any variable bounds, equalities, and sign restrictions in the formulation, remain in \(R\); only the requirement \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) is replaced by \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The natural continuous relaxation retains every linear constraint but permits the integer variables to take real values, producing a rational polyhedron containing every integer-feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=R\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\subseteq R\)

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer hull of a rational polyhedron in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational polyhedron \(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its integer hull is \[R_I=\operatorname{conv}(R\cap\mathbb{Z}^n).\] It is the smallest convex set containing every integral point of \(R\). Moreover, \(R_I\subseteq R\), and the integer hull of a rational polyhedron is itself a rational polyhedron. If \(R\cap\mathbb{Z}^n=\varnothing\), the convention is \(R_I=\varnothing\).
