knowledge_statements.statement_title: Turing-Machine Computation and Running Time
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform step-bounded computation of a total function on binary strings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\{0,1\}^*\to\{0,1\}^*\), let \(T:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\), and let \(M\) be a Turing machine. The machine \(M\) computes \(f\) in \(T(n)\)-time if, for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^*\), when initialized in its start configuration on input \(x\), it halts within at most \(T(|x|)\) steps with \(f(x)\) written on its output tape. The machine \(M\) computes \(f\) if it computes \(f\) in \(T(n)\)-time for some function \(T:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Turing machine computes a binary-string function in time T(n) if, on every input x, it halts within T(|x|) steps and writes f(x) on its output tape. It computes the function without a specified time bound if some such function T exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ computes }f\text{ in }T(n)\text{-time}\iff \forall x\in\{0,1\}^*,\ M\text{ halts within }T(|x|)\text{ steps with }f(x)\text{ on its output tape};\quad M\text{ computes }f\iff\exists T:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\text{ for which this holds}

children.top_down_role: Instance-size measurement for binary-encoded combinatorial and rational data.

assumptions_latex: Integers use signed binary notation without leading zeroes, except that zero is encoded by one bit.
A rational number is represented in reduced numerator-denominator form with positive denominator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell(a)=1+\lceil\log_2(|a|+1)\rceil\) and \(\ell(p/q)=\ell(p)+\ell(q)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed signed-binary convention; alternative conventions differ only by additive constants.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a\in\mathbb Z\), define its signed binary encoding length by \(\ell(a)=1+\lceil\log_2(|a|+1)\rceil\), where the first bit accounts for sign. If \(r=p/q\in\mathbb Q\) is represented uniquely with \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(q\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\), define \(\ell(r)=\ell(p)+\ell(q)\). For a finite vector or matrix of rational entries, its encoding length is the sum of the entry lengths plus a fixed self-delimiting encoding of its dimensions. Polynomial-time bounds are measured as functions of this total length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary encoding length counts the bits for signed integers, reduced rational numerators and denominators, and the dimensions and entries of finite arrays.

assumptions_latex: Each rational is stored as a reduced pair \((p,q)\in\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z_{>0}\).

source_refs.locator: Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent \(p/q\in\mathbb Q\) by coprime integers \((p,q)\) with \(q>0\). For operands \(p/q\) and \(r/s\), compute addition as \((ps+rq)/(qs)\), multiplication as \((pr)/(qs)\), and division, when \(r\ne0\), as \((ps)/(qr)\); subtraction is analogous. children.title: Random-Access Machine Model
children.top_down_role: Memory-access assumptions used in combinatorial runtime analysis.

assumptions_latex: Memory consists of addressable words indexed by nonnegative integers.
The instruction set and word-cost convention are fixed independently of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The running time is \(T_P(x)=\sum_{t=1}^{h(x)}c_t\), where \(c_t\) is the prescribed cost of instruction \(t\).

notation.meaning: number of executed instructions before halting

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General RAM framework encompassing unit-cost and length-sensitive instruction charges.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 The random access machine p. 39

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A random-access machine has finitely many registers and an unbounded array of addressable words. A fixed program \(P\) applies instructions for loading constants, copying, indirect addressing, branching, comparison, and specified arithmetic operations. Any word can be accessed by its address without scanning preceding memory. If the computation on input \(x\) halts after \(h(x)\) instructions and the cost assigned to its \(t\)-th instruction is \(c_t\), then its running time is \(T_P(x)=\sum_{t=1}^{h(x)}c_t\). A complexity claim in this model must state whether \(c_t\) is uniform or depends on operand lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A RAM directly accesses addressed words and executes a fixed instruction set; its running time sums the costs assigned to executed instructions.
knowledge_statements.title: Random-Access Machine Model

children.title: Unit-Cost Arithmetic Model
children.top_down_role: Operation-count analysis treating arithmetic primitives as unit-cost operations.

assumptions_latex: The computation uses a random-access machine.
Every permitted arithmetic, comparison, branch, and memory-access instruction has cost one, regardless of operand magnitude.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_P(x)=h(x)\), the number of executed machine instructions.

notation.meaning: executed instruction count on input x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-cost specialization of the RAM model, including arithmetic on stored words.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 The random access machine p. 39

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the unit-cost arithmetic RAM model, each permitted instruction has cost \(1\), including memory access, comparison, branching, and arithmetic operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and exact division when defined. Consequently, if a program \(P\) executes \(h(x)\) instructions on input \(x\), then \(T_P(x)=h(x)\). The charge is independent of the binary lengths of operands and results. Therefore an operation-count bound in this model is not by itself a bit-complexity bound unless all encountered word lengths are also polynomially bounded in the input encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit-cost model charges one step per permitted RAM operation, even for large operands, so operation counts need not equal bit complexity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unit-Cost Arithmetic Computation Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation counting and input-size conventions in the arithmetic model, contrasted with bit-level Turing cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the arithmetic model, each addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, or comparison counts as one elementary operation. Input size is the number of numerical input entries, without charging for their individual encoding lengths. Bits encoding nonnumerical input are treated as numerical entries, and elementary nonnumeric updates are charged as operations. Thus standard multiplication of two $n\times n$ matrices takes $O(n^3)$ arithmetic operations, whereas its Turing-model running time also depends on the entries' encoding lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The arithmetic model treats basic arithmetic operations and comparisons as unit-cost steps and measures input size by the number of input numbers rather than their bit lengths. Encoded nonnumeric data and elementary nonnumeric actions are counted analogously.

children.title: Arithmetic-Cost Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Complexity changes caused by operand size or arithmetic-cost assumptions.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm performs \(N(x)\) arithmetic or memory operations on input \(x\).
Every operand encountered has binary length at most \(B(x)\).
A corresponding bit implementation charges each operation according to operand length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unit-cost polynomiality transfers to bit polynomiality only when both \(N(x)\) and the relevant length-dependent operation costs are polynomial in \(\ell(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer criterion between arithmetic-operation counts and bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an algorithm executes \(N(x)\) abstract operations and every intermediate operand has length at most \(B(x)\). If each corresponding bit operation on operands of length at most \(B\) costs at most \(C(B)\), then the implemented running time is bounded by \(O(N(x)C(B(x)))\), up to representation-management overhead. Hence a polynomial unit-cost bound yields a polynomial bit bound when \(N(x)\), \(B(x)\), and \(C(B(x))\) are polynomial in \(\ell(x)\). Without a polynomial bound on intermediate lengths, a polynomial arithmetic-operation count may conceal superpolynomial bit cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operation-count complexity transfers to bit complexity only when intermediate numbers and the bit costs of their operations remain polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic-Cost Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transfer principle is appropriately scoped and mathematically plausible, but no inspectable source supports the stated bit-cost transfer bound or its representation-overhead qualification.

children.title: Input Access Representation Classes
children.top_down_role: Representations distinguished by enumeration, compression, or query access.

children.title: Explicit Instance Encodings
children.top_down_role: Representations listing the relevant instance data directly.

assumptions_latex: An instance is a finite combinatorial object whose primitive data can be listed.
A fixed injective, self-delimiting binary serialization convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The explicit input size is \(\ell(I)=|\operatorname{enc}(I)|\), including every listed primitive datum and structural delimiter.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full listing representation for finite combinatorial instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An explicit encoding of a finite instance \(I\) is an injective, self-delimiting binary string \(\operatorname{enc}(I)\) that lists every primitive component needed to reconstruct \(I\), including dimensions, incidences, coefficients, and objective data when present. Its input size is \(\ell(I)=|\operatorname{enc}(I)|\). A standard explicit encoding must admit deterministic decoding in time polynomial in \(\ell(I)\). Complexity measured under this representation may depend polynomially on the number of listed components and on the binary lengths of their numerical values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit encoding lists all primitive instance data in a decodable binary serialization, and input size is the total serialized bit length.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Instance Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches explicit instance encodings and clearly identifies total serialized bit length, but the decoding requirement and representation conventions have no cited authoritative source.

children.title: Succinct Instance Encodings
children.top_down_role: Compressed representations whose described objects may be much larger than their encodings.

assumptions_latex: A finite object \(I\) is generated by a finite binary description \(d\).
A fixed deterministic interpreter maps valid descriptions to represented instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The succinct size is \(|d|\), which can be exponentially smaller than the size of an explicit listing of \(I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator-based representation whose description may be much smaller than its expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a deterministic interpreter \(G\). A succinct encoding of an instance \(I\) is a finite binary description \(d\) satisfying \(G(d)=I\), where \(d\) specifies a circuit, formula, program, or other compact generator rather than listing all components of \(I\). The represented input size is \(|d|\), not the length of an expanded explicit encoding of \(I\). The expansion size may be exponential in \(|d|\); consequently, an algorithm polynomial in the explicit size need not be polynomial in the succinct size. The interpreter \(G\) is part of the representation class and must be fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A succinct encoding uses a fixed compact generator; complexity is measured by the description length, even when the generated explicit instance is exponentially larger.
knowledge_statements.title: Succinct Instance Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly makes the interpreter part of the representation class and says that exponential compression may occur, but no inspectable source supports this representation-sensitive complexity claim.

children.title: Oracle-Access Encodings
children.top_down_role: Representations exposing instance information through permitted queries.

assumptions_latex: The instance contains an implicit object accessible through a specified oracle \(O\).
Each legal query and answer has a finite encoding under a fixed query protocol.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Oracle complexity records the number of calls to \(O\), together with any separately charged local computation and query lengths.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Black-box input representation with an explicit query protocol and cost convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oracle-access encoding specifies an instance through a black box \(O\) and a query domain. On a legal query \(q\), the algorithm receives the exact response \(O(q)\), such as a value, membership answer, separation witness, or optimization result. The oracle protocol fixes the admissible queries, response format, and cost of a call. Query complexity is the number of oracle calls; total complexity additionally charges local computation and, when required, the lengths of queries and responses. Claims made in this representation are relative to the chosen oracle and do not automatically imply complexity bounds for an explicit implementation of \(O\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oracle encoding exposes instance information through specified queries; complexity must distinguish oracle calls from local work and from implementing the oracle.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Access Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits oracle-access encodings and distinguishes query cost from local and implementation cost, but the broad oracle protocol conventions require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Boolean Problem Interface Family

children.title: Feasibility Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Problem presentations centered on the existence of admissible objects.

assumptions_latex: Each encoded instance \(I\) determines a candidate domain \(X_I\) and a feasible subset \(F_I\subseteq X_I\).
The Boolean interface receives the encoded instance \(I\), rather than a supplied candidate solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{feas}}(I)=1\) if and only if \(F_I\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential Boolean interface asking whether an encoded instance has any feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each valid encoded instance \(I\), let \(X_I\) be its candidate domain and let \(F_I\subseteq X_I\) be its feasible set. The feasibility interface is the Boolean map \(D_{\mathrm{feas}}\) defined by \(D_{\mathrm{feas}}(I)=1\) if and only if there exists \(x\in X_I\) such that \(x\in F_I\), equivalently if and only if \(F_I\ne\varnothing\). It asks whether a feasible solution exists and does not require the interface to output such a solution. Running time is measured using the declared encoding of \(I\) and machine model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasibility interface returns yes exactly when the encoded instance has at least one feasible solution; it need not produce that solution.

children.title: Decision Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Binary problem presentations used in classification and reductions.

assumptions_latex: A family of instances is encoded as a language domain \(\mathcal I\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\).
A mathematically specified property \(P(I)\) has a definite truth value for every valid instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decision interface computes \(D_P(I)=1\) if and only if \(P(I)\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General yes-no interface for a property of an encoded instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) be the valid encodings of an instance family and let \(P\) be a property defined on those instances. The associated decision interface is \(D_P:\mathcal I\to\{0,1\}\), with \(D_P(I)=1\) if and only if \(P(I)\) is true. Equivalently, it recognizes the language \(L_P=\{I\in\mathcal I:P(I)\}\). The interface returns only the truth value and need not produce a witness, feasible solution, or optimum. Running time is measured in the length of the complete encoded instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision interface maps each valid encoded instance to yes or no according to a specified property, without requiring a witness or solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision Interfaces

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial equivalence of set optimization and threshold decision
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization-to-decision equivalence for integer-weighted feasible subsets, preserving the possibility of infeasibility and the stated hardness transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) and \(\mathcal F'\) be infinite families of finite sets. Given \(E\in\mathcal F\) and \(c:E\to\mathbb Z\), let \(\mathcal P\) minimize \(c(F)\) over sets \(F\subseteq E\) satisfying \(F\in\mathcal F'\), or decide that no such set exists. Then \(\mathcal P\) is solvable in polynomial time if and only if the problem of deciding, for an instance \((E,c)\) and an integer \(k\), whether \(\operatorname{OPT}((E,c))\le k\) is solvable in polynomial time. If \(\mathcal P\) is NP-hard, then this threshold decision problem is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integer-weighted feasible-subset optimization over families of finite sets, polynomial-time optimization is equivalent to polynomial-time threshold decision, while allowing that no feasible subset may exist. If the optimization problem is NP-hard, its threshold decision problem is also NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal F,\mathcal F'\text{ are infinite families of finite sets}
\{F\subseteq E:F\in\mathcal F'\}\text{ is the feasible-set family, which may be empty}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P\in\mathrm P\iff\bigl[(E,c,k)\mapsto(\operatorname{OPT}((E,c))\le k)\bigr]\in\mathrm P;\qquad \mathcal P\text{ NP-hard}\Rightarrow\text{the threshold decision problem is NP-hard.}

children.title: Witness Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery of explicit certificates from related computational access.

knowledge_statements.title: Witness Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary prefix self-reduction for polynomially bounded witnesses, with explicit witness recognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: First query whether \(R(x)\neq\varnothing\); if not, output \(\bot\). Otherwise initialize \(u:=\epsilon\). Before extending \(u\), test whether \(u\in R(x)\), and output \(u\) if so. For each remaining position up to \(p(|x|)\), query whether a witness in \(R(x)\) has prefix \(u0\). If so, set \(u:=u0\); otherwise query whether a witness has prefix \(u1\) and set \(u:=u1\) when the answer is affirmative. After each extension, test whether \(u\in R(x)\). The initial query and at most two prefix queries per position use at most \(2p(|x|)+1\) oracle calls; witness-membership tests are performed directly by the assumed verifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prefix-feasibility oracle and an efficient witness verifier recover a bounded binary witness by retaining a feasible prefix one bit at a time.
assumptions_latex: Witnesses are binary strings of length at most \(p(|x|)\).
For every prefix \(u\), the oracle decides whether some witness in \(R(x)\) begins with \(u\).
Membership \((x,u)\in R\) is decidable in polynomial time.

children.title: Value-to-Solution Recovery

knowledge_statements.title: Value-to-Solution Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimization with polynomially bounded, self-delimiting binary solution encodings and polynomial-time restriction closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Query \(v^*(x)\); if the answer is \(\bot\), output \(\bot\). Otherwise initialize \(u:=\epsilon\). If \(u\) is a complete feasible encoding with objective value \(v^*(x)\), output it. Otherwise query \(v_{u0}^*(x)\); when it equals \(v^*(x)\), set \(u:=u0\). If it does not, query \(v_{u1}^*(x)\) and set \(u:=u1\), which must preserve the optimum. After each extension, test whether \(u\) is a complete feasible encoding attaining \(v^*(x)\), and stop when it is. The initial query and at most two restricted-value queries per bit use at most \(2p(|x|)+1\) value-oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact value oracle recovers an optimal self-delimiting binary solution by retaining a prefix whose restricted optimum equals the original optimum and stopping when that prefix is a complete optimal encoding.
assumptions_latex: Feasible solutions have self-delimiting binary encodings of length at most \(p(|x|)\).
Whether a string is a complete feasible encoding and its objective value are computable in polynomial time.
Prefix-restricted instances are constructible with encoding length polynomial in \(|x|+|u|\).
An exact value oracle returns the restricted optimum \(v_u^*(x)\), or \(\bot\) when no feasible solution extends \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A solution attaining \(v^*(x)\) is recovered using at most \(2p(|x|)+1\) exact value-oracle calls.

knowledge_statements.title: Output-Sensitive Listing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes total output-polynomial time from the stronger polynomial-delay guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(x)\) be the total encoded length of all witnesses emitted on instance \(x\), and let \(T(x)\) include computation and writing time. A complete duplicate-free listing algorithm is output-polynomial if some polynomial \(q\) satisfies \(T(x)\leq q(|x|+L(x))\). It has polynomial delay if the time before the first output, between consecutive outputs, and after the last output before termination is bounded by a polynomial in \(|x|\). Polynomial delay implies output-polynomial total time when every witness has polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An output-polynomial listing algorithm runs in time polynomial in the combined input and output length. A polynomial-delay algorithm also bounds, polynomially in the input length, the wait before the first output, between consecutive outputs, and between the last output and termination.

Writing one output symbol costs one unit of time.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Class P and examples of polynomial-time recognition problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines P for recognition problems, states its robustness across reasonable computational models, and lists four members of the class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The class \(P\) consists of recognition problems solvable by polynomial-time algorithms. For reasonable models of computation, polynomial-time solvability in one such model implies polynomial-time solvability in the others. The following recognition problems belong to \(P\): deciding whether a graph is connected; deciding whether a digraph \(D=(V,A)\) contains a path from some vertex in \(S\subseteq V\) to some vertex in \(T\subseteq V\); deciding whether a graph has a matching with at least \(k\) edges; and, for a connected graph with edge costs, deciding whether it has a spanning tree of cost at most \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: P is the class of recognition problems solvable in polynomial time, a classification stable across reasonable computational models. Graph connectedness, directed path existence between designated vertex sets, matching-size threshold, and minimum-spanning-tree cost threshold are examples in P.
assumptions_latex: Problems are recognition problems represented by finite inputs.
For directed path existence, \(D=(V,A)\) is a digraph and \(S,T\subseteq V\).
For the matching problem, the input includes a graph \(G\) and an integer \(k\).
For the spanning-tree problem, \(G=(V,E)\) is connected, \(d\) is a cost function on \(E\), and \(L\) is an integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\{A: A\text{ is a recognition problem solvable in polynomial time}\},\quad\text{and the four stated recognition problems are in }P.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nondeterministic-algorithm characterization of NP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Informal guess-and-check characterization, including its positive-instance running-time convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nondeterministic algorithm solves a decision problem \(\Pi\) if, for every \(I\in D_\Pi\), \(I\in Y_\Pi\) if and only if there exists a guessed structure \(S\) for which the deterministic checking stage halts with answer \(\mathrm{yes}\). It operates in polynomial time if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every \(I\in Y_\Pi\), some such guess leads the checking stage to answer \(\mathrm{yes}\) within \(p(\operatorname{Length}(I))\) time. Under reasonable encodings, \(\mathrm{NP}\) is the class of decision problems solvable by polynomial-time nondeterministic algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nondeterministic algorithm solves a decision problem when every yes-instance has at least one accepted guess and no no-instance has an accepted guess. It is polynomial-time when every yes-instance has an accepting guess checked within a polynomial in the input length. Under reasonable encodings, NP consists of the decision problems admitting such algorithms.
assumptions_latex: \Pi\text{ is a decision problem with domain }D_\Pi\text{ and yes-set }Y_\Pi.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi\in\mathrm{NP}\iff \Pi\text{ is solvable, under a reasonable encoding, by a polynomial-time nondeterministic guess-and-check algorithm.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Formal NDTM definition of NP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes existential branch acceptance, positive-instance acceptance time, the no-accepted-input convention, and polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an NDTM program \(M\), \(M\) accepts \(x\) if at least one computation generated by a guessed string in \(\Gamma^*\) enters \(q_Y\), and \(L_M=\{x\in\Sigma^*:M\text{ accepts }x\}\). For \(x\in L_M\), its acceptance time is the minimum number of guessing and checking steps among accepting computations. Let \(T_M(n)\) be the maximum of these acceptance times over accepted strings of length \(n\), with \(T_M(n)=1\) if no string of length \(n\) is accepted. The machine is polynomial-time if \(T_M(n)\le p(n)\) for some polynomial \(p\) and every \(n\ge1\), and \(\mathrm{NP}=\{L:\exists\text{ a polynomial-time NDTM }M\text{ with }L_M=L\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An NDTM accepts an input when at least one computation accepts. Its acceptance time is the shortest accepting-computation time, and its length-n complexity is the largest such time among accepted inputs of that length, set to one if none are accepted. NP is the class of languages recognized by polynomial-time NDTMs.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is an NDTM program over input alphabet }\Sigma\text{ and guessing alphabet }\Gamma.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\in\mathrm{NP}\iff\exists M\,\exists p\text{ polynomial}:L_M=L\ \land\ \forall n\ge1,\ T_M(n)\le p(n).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Class NP via polynomial certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate-verifier definition using certificates of the source's prescribed polynomial length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decision problem \(\mathcal P=(X,Y)\) belongs to \(NP\) if there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a decision problem \(\mathcal P'=(X',Y')\in P\), where \[X'=\{x\#c:x\in X,\ c\in\{0,1\}^{\lfloor p(\operatorname{size}(x))\rfloor}\},\] such that \[Y=\{y\in X:\text{there exists }c\in\{0,1\}^{\lfloor p(\operatorname{size}(y))\rfloor}\text{ with }y\#c\in Y'\}.\] Here \(x\#c\) denotes concatenation of \(x\), the symbol \(\#\), and \(c\). A string \(c\) satisfying \(y\#c\in Y'\) is a certificate for \(y\), and an algorithm for \(\mathcal P'\) is a certificate-checking algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision problem (X,Y) belongs to NP if a polynomial fixes a certificate length and there is a decision problem in P that checks the concatenation of an instance, a separator, and such a certificate. An instance is a yes-instance exactly when at least one certificate of that prescribed length is accepted by the checker.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P\in NP\) if there exist a polynomial \(p\) and \(\mathcal P'=(X',Y')\in P\) with \(X'=\{x\#c:x\in X,\ c\in\{0,1\}^{\lfloor p(\operatorname{size}(x))\rfloor}\}\) and \(Y=\{y\in X:\exists c\in\{0,1\}^{\lfloor p(\operatorname{size}(y))\rfloor},\ y\#c\in Y'\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Class NP via polynomially bounded certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time verification of polynomial-length certificates for affirmative instances, with explicit one-sidedness and no search requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decision problem \(\Pi\) belongs to \(\mathcal{NP}\) if and only if there exist a decision problem \(\Sigma\in\mathcal P\) and a polynomial \(\Phi\) such that, for every \(\sigma\in\{0,1\}^*\), \((\sigma,1)\in\Pi\) if and only if there exists \(\tau\in\{0,1\}^*\) for which \(((\sigma,\tau),1)\in\Sigma\) and \(|\tau|\le\Phi(|\sigma|)\). The string \(\tau\) is a succinct certificate. This condition applies only to affirmative instances and does not require an efficient method for finding \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: NP consists of decision problems whose yes-instances have polynomial-length certificates verifiable in polynomial time. It does not require certificates to be found efficiently or impose an analogous certificate condition on no-instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi\in\mathcal{NP}\iff\exists\Sigma\in\mathcal P\;\exists\Phi\text{ polynomial}\;\forall\sigma:\ (\sigma,1)\in\Pi\iff\exists\tau:\ ((\sigma,\tau),1)\in\Sigma\land |\tau|\le\Phi(|\sigma|).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-certificate definition of NP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines NP through polynomial-length certificates for yes instances that a fixed algorithm verifies in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Sigma\) be a fixed finite alphabet containing a distinguished separator symbol \(\$\). A recognition problem \(A\) is in \(NP\) if there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a certificate-checking algorithm \(a\) such that, for every \(x\in\Sigma^*\), \[x\text{ is a yes instance of }A\iff \exists c\in\Sigma^*:\ |c|\le p(|x|)\ \land\ a(x\$c)\text{ reaches the answer yes within }p(|x|)\text{ steps}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recognition problem belongs to NP exactly when a fixed verifier and polynomial bound exist such that an input is a yes instance if and only if it has a certificate of polynomially bounded length that the verifier accepts within polynomially many steps.
assumptions_latex: \(\Sigma\) is a fixed finite alphabet and \(\$\in\Sigma\) is a distinguished separator symbol.
Inputs \(x\) and certificates \(c\) are strings over \(\Sigma\).
The same polynomial \(p\) bounds the certificate length and the certificate-checking algorithm's number of steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\in NP\iff \exists p\,\exists a\,\forall x\in\Sigma^*:\ x\in A\iff \exists c\in\Sigma^*\text{ such that }|c|\le p(|x|)\text{ and }a(x\$c)\text{ answers yes within }p(|x|)\text{ steps}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complement Problems, coNP, and coNP-Completeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines complementation for decision problems, membership in coNP, and coNP-completeness under polynomial transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a decision problem \(\mathcal P=(X,Y)\), its complement is \(\overline{\mathcal P}=(X,X\setminus Y)\). The class \(\mathrm{coNP}\) consists of the decision problems \(\mathcal P\) for which \(\overline{\mathcal P}\in\mathrm{NP}\). A problem \(\mathcal P\in\mathrm{coNP}\) is coNP-complete when every problem in \(\mathrm{coNP}\) polynomially transforms to \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complement of a decision problem has the same instances and exchanges its yes- and no-instances. A problem belongs to coNP when its complement belongs to NP. A coNP problem is coNP-complete when every coNP problem polynomially transforms to it.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal P=(X,Y)\text{ is a decision problem with }Y\subseteq X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \overline{\mathcal P}=(X,X\setminus Y),\qquad \mathcal P\in\mathrm{coNP}\iff\overline{\mathcal P}\in\mathrm{NP},\qquad \mathcal P\text{ is coNP-complete}\iff\left(\mathcal P\in\mathrm{coNP}\land\forall\mathcal Q\in\mathrm{coNP},\;\mathcal Q\le_p\mathcal P\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every language \(L\), deterministic polynomial-time decidability supplies polynomially verifiable witnesses for both membership and nonmembership, so \(\mathbf{P}\subseteq\mathbf{NP}\cap\mathbf{coNP}\). By set inclusion, \(\mathbf{NP}\cap\mathbf{coNP}\subseteq\mathbf{NP}\cup\mathbf{coNP}\). Polynomial-time nondeterministic computation and its complementary acceptance condition can each be simulated using polynomial space, giving \(\mathbf{NP}\cup\mathbf{coNP}\subseteq\mathbf{PSPACE}\). These containments are unconditional; the equalities \(\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{NP}\), \(\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{coNP}\), and their negations are not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: P lies inside both NP and co-NP, while NP and co-NP lie inside PSPACE. No strictness between these classes is currently asserted.
knowledge_statements.title: Class Containment Landscape

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The containments are mathematically standard and fit the class-containment leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable citation. The statement also includes proof-style justification rather than only the property. An authoritative complexity-theory source with a section or theorem locator is required.

children.title: Polynomially Verifiable Witnesses
children.top_down_role: Certificate-size and verification structures underlying nondeterministic classes.

assumptions_latex: Inputs and witnesses are finite strings over a fixed finite alphabet \(\Sigma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\in\mathbf{NP}\iff \exists V,p\;\forall x\,[x\in L\iff\exists y\,(|y|\le p(|x|)\land V(x,y)=1)]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifier characterization of NP with polynomial certificate length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A language \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) has polynomially verifiable witnesses if there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a deterministic algorithm \(V\), running in time polynomial in \(|x|+|y|\), such that for every \(x\in\Sigma^*\), \[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists y\in\Sigma^*\;\bigl(|y|\le p(|x|)\ \land\ V(x,y)=1\bigr).\] The string \(y\) is a membership certificate. The class of languages admitting such a verifier is exactly \(\mathbf{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An NP membership claim has a certificate of polynomial length that a deterministic algorithm can verify in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomially Verifiable Witnesses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The verifier characterization is mathematically standard, precise, and appropriately classified as a certificate, but no source is cited. Supply an authoritative definition or theorem locator for the polynomial-time verifier characterization of NP.

children.title: Good Characterizations
children.top_down_role: Complementary efficiently checkable evidence for opposite outcomes.

assumptions_latex: Instances are finite strings, and both certificate relations are decidable in polynomial time.
Certificate lengths are bounded by polynomials in the instance length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\in\mathbf{NP}\cap\mathbf{coNP}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity-theoretic form of a good characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decision language \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) has a good characterization when there exist polynomially bounded certificate relations \(R_{+}\) and \(R_{-}\), each decidable in deterministic polynomial time, such that every instance \(x\) satisfies \[x\in L\iff\exists y\,R_{+}(x,y),\qquad x\notin L\iff\exists z\,R_{-}(x,z).\] Consequently, membership and nonmembership both possess succinct, efficiently checkable certificates, and therefore \(L\in\mathbf{NP}\cap\mathbf{coNP}\). This conclusion alone does not provide a polynomial-time algorithm deciding \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A good characterization provides short, efficiently checkable certificates for both yes and no instances, placing the decision problem in NP intersect co-NP.
knowledge_statements.title: Good Characterizations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed NP intersect co-NP consequence matches the intended notion of a good characterization, but its historical and technical sense needs an authoritative source. The statement also uses Sigma without introducing it and leaves the domains and explicit polynomial length bounds for y and z implicit.

children.title: Min–Max Certificate Pairs
children.top_down_role: Primal-side and dual-side witnesses linked through matching objective values.

assumptions_latex: For each encoded instance \(x\), the primal feasible objects form \(P(x)\), and the dual feasible objects form \(D(x)\).
The objectives satisfy weak duality: \(g_x(d)\le f_x(p)\) for every \(p\in P(x)\) and \(d\in D(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\in P(x)\land d\in D(x)\land f_x(p)=g_x(d)\Longrightarrow p\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in P(x)}f_x(q)\land d\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{e\in D(x)}g_x(e)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an encoded instance \(x\), let the primal problem be \(\min_{p\in P(x)}f_x(p)\) and the dual problem be \(\max_{d\in D(x)}g_x(d)\). Suppose weak duality gives \(g_x(d)\le f_x(p)\) for every \(p\in P(x)\) and \(d\in D(x)\). Then any \(p\in P(x)\) and \(d\in D(x)\) satisfying \(f_x(p)=g_x(d)\) constitute a certificate that both objects are optimal and that their common value is the optimum. This certificate is polynomially verifiable when feasibility, both objective values, and equality can be checked in polynomial time from \((x,p,d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under weak duality, a primal-feasible and dual-feasible pair with equal objective values certifies that both objects are optimal and that their common value is the optimum.

children.title: Certificate Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on converting complementary certificates into algorithmic tractability.

assumptions_latex: The integer vertex-cover formulation and its linear relaxation are taken on the three-cycle \(C_3\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{IP}}(C_3)=2>3/2=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(C_3)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality gaps obstruct equivalence between LP certificates and integer optimality certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For vertex cover on \(C_3=(V,E)\), consider \(\min\sum_{v\in V}x_v\) subject to \(x_u+x_v\ge1\) for every \(uv\in E\). With \(x_v\in\{0,1\}\), every cover uses at least two vertices, so the optimum is \(2\). After replacing integrality by \(0\le x_v\le1\), the assignment \(x_v=1/2\) has value \(3/2\) and is LP-optimal. Thus LP primal-dual equality certifies only the relaxed optimum; without integrality or another exact min-max theorem, it cannot certify the integer optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a triangle, vertex cover has integer optimum 2 but LP optimum 3/2, so an exact LP certificate does not certify integer optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Equivalence Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The triangle integrality-gap example is correct and is an appropriate failure boundary, but no source supports the exact formulation or optimum values. The statement also contains a compact derivation that should be removed from a source-backed knowledge statement.

children.title: Optimization Complexity Classes
children.top_down_role: Function and optimization analogues of decision complexity.

assumptions_latex: Instances and feasible solutions use finite binary encodings.
Objective values are integers whose encodings have polynomial length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{opt}_{\Pi}(x)=\min\{m(x,y):R(x,y)\}\) or \(\operatorname{opt}_{\Pi}(x)=\max\{m(x,y):R(x,y)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NPO-style optimization problems and their exact value functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An encoded minimization or maximization problem \(\Pi\) belongs to \(\mathbf{NPO}\) when feasible solutions \(y\) have length polynomially bounded in \(|x|\), feasibility \(R(x,y)\) is decidable in polynomial time, and the integer objective \(m(x,y)\) is computable in polynomial time. Its optimum-value function maps \(x\) to the minimum or maximum of \(m(x,y)\) over feasible \(y\). An exact optimization problem is polynomial-time solvable when an optimal solution, and hence its value, can be produced by a deterministic algorithm in time polynomial in \(|x|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: NPO contains encoded optimization problems with short feasible solutions, efficiently checkable feasibility, and efficiently computable objectives; exact polynomial-time solvability requires producing an optimum efficiently.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization Complexity Classes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The NPO-style definition fits the optimization-complexity topic, but no authoritative source is provided for the exact feasibility, objective, encoding-length, and solution-production conventions. These conventions vary enough across presentations that a precise source is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bit-length size of a minimum-cost network-flow instance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoded input size for the stated adjacency-list representation and binary numerical data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimum-cost network-flow instance with \(n\) nodes, \(m\) arcs, largest arc cost \(C\), and largest arc capacity \(U\), the stated adjacency-list representation requires approximately \(n\log n+m\log m+m\log C+m\log U\) bits. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial, strongly polynomial, and weakly polynomial time
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial time for rational inputs and its classification by dependence on encoded numerical data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm with rational input is polynomial-time if there is an integer \(k\) such that it runs in \(O(n^k)\) time, where \(n\) is the encoded input size, and every number occurring in intermediate computations can be stored with \(O(n^k)\) bits. An algorithm with arbitrary input is strongly polynomial if there is an integer \(k\) such that it runs in \(O(n^k)\) time on every input consisting of \(n\) numbers and is polynomial-time on rational input. The case \(k=1\) is linear time. An algorithm that is polynomial-time but not strongly polynomial is weakly polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial time for rational input requires polynomially many steps in encoded input size and polynomially bounded intermediate encodings. Strong polynomiality instead bounds the step count polynomially in the number of input numbers and also requires polynomial time on rational inputs. Exponent one is linear time; polynomial but not strongly polynomial time is weakly polynomial.

n\text{ is the number of input numbers in the strongly polynomial definition}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial time and transfer from arithmetic to bit complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bit-model polynomial time, gives a sufficient arithmetic-to-bit transfer condition, and preserves the boundary that bit-polynomial solvability does not imply a known arithmetic-model polynomial algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(t\) be the bit length of an encoded input. An algorithm is polynomial-time in the bit model when its bit-operation count is \(O(t^k)\) for some fixed \(k\). If it performs polynomially many elementary arithmetic operations in \(t\), every intermediate number has bit length \(O(t^r)\) for some fixed \(r\), and those arithmetic operations have polynomial bit cost in their operand lengths, then the algorithm is polynomial-time in the bit model. Conversely, the existence of a bit-model polynomial-time algorithm does not establish that an arithmetic-model polynomial-time algorithm is known.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial time means polynomially many bit operations in the encoded input length. A polynomial arithmetic-operation bound transfers to the bit model when intermediate numbers have polynomially bounded bit length and the elementary arithmetic operations can be implemented in polynomial bit time. The reverse inference is not valid as a statement about known algorithms.
assumptions_latex: t\text{ is the bit length of the encoded input.}
\text{For the transfer claim, the number of elementary arithmetic operations is polynomial in }t.
\text{Every intermediate number has bit length polynomial in }t.
\text{Each elementary arithmetic operation has bit cost polynomial in the operand bit lengths.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{time}_{\mathrm{bit}}(t)=O(t^q)\quad\text{for some fixed }q.

children.title: Exponential-Time Regime
children.top_down_role: Runtime growth exponential in a relevant input parameter.

assumptions_latex: Input length \(n\) is the length of a finite binary encoding.
Running time is measured for a deterministic Turing machine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbf{EXP}=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\operatorname{DTIME}(2^{n^k})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity-class convention for deterministic exponential time, including single-exponential algorithms.

source_refs.locator: Time and Space Complexity p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A deterministic decision algorithm is in the exponential-time regime when its worst-case running time is bounded by \(2^{p(n)}\) for some polynomial \(p\), where \(n\) is total input bit length. The associated class is \[\mathbf{EXP}=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\operatorname{DTIME}(2^{n^k}).\] A bound \(O(c^n\operatorname{poly}(n))\) with fixed \(c>1\) is called single exponential and is a special case. This definition is an upper-bound classification and does not assert that exponential time is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: EXP consists of decision problems solvable in deterministic time exponential in a polynomial of the input length; single-exponential time is a narrower regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Time Regime

children.title: Subexponential Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Intermediate growth classifications between polynomial and fully exponential behavior.

assumptions_latex: A natural size parameter \(n\) is fixed for the instance family.
Running times are positive for all sufficiently large \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(n)=2^{o(n)}\iff \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 T(n)}{n}=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subexponential time relative to a specified natural size parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An algorithm has subexponential running time relative to parameter \(n\) if \[T(n)=2^{o(n)},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 T(n)}{n}=0.\] Thus, for every constant \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(n_0\) such that \(T(n)
\le2^{\varepsilon n}\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). The classification depends on the chosen parameter: a time bound subexponential in the number of variables need not be subexponential in total encoding length, and polynomial running times also satisfy this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subexponential time is 2 to a little-o exponent of a declared size parameter; the classification changes when that parameter changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Subexponential Transition Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parameter-relative definition and logarithmic equivalence are mathematically sound, but no source is cited. Because subexponential terminology depends materially on the selected size parameter, an authoritative definition with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Polynomial Numeric-Dependence Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arithmetic-to-Bit Polynomial-Time Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition for transferring polynomial running time from the arithmetic model to the bit model for integer computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm operate on instances of encoded size \(n\). Suppose its running time under the arithmetic model is polynomial in \(n\), and suppose there exists a polynomial \(p\) such that every integer \(z\) produced during the execution on any instance of size \(n\) satisfies \(\operatorname{bitsize}(z)\le p(n)\). Then the algorithm runs in polynomial time under the bit model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an algorithm takes polynomial time in the arithmetic model and every integer it generates has bit length bounded polynomially in the encoded input size, then it also takes polynomial time in the bit model.
assumptions_latex: \exists p\in\mathbb{R}[n]\;\forall I\text{ of size }n\;\forall z\text{ produced while processing }I,\;\operatorname{bitsize}(z)\le p(n).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{bit}}(n)\le r(n)\text{ for some polynomial }r.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a numerically encoded optimization problem, an algorithm has a weakly polynomial running-time guarantee when its number of bit operations is bounded by a polynomial in the complete binary input length \(L\). assumptions_latex: The instance has \(n\) combinatorial components and binary-encoded rational numerical data.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm for a rationally encoded optimization problem is strongly polynomial if the number of elementary arithmetic and comparison operations is bounded by a polynomial in the combinatorial dimension \(n\), independently of the magnitudes and bit lengths of numerical coefficients, and every intermediate number has encoding length bounded by a polynomial in the total input length \(L\). These conditions imply polynomial bit complexity while excluding iteration bounds that grow with coefficient magnitudes or their encoding lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality bounds arithmetic steps by combinatorial dimension alone and also keeps every intermediate number polynomially encoded.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly Polynomial-Time Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong polynomiality defined jointly by arithmetic-operation count and Turing-model space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm runs in strongly polynomial time if it uses polynomial space in the Turing-machine model and performs at most $p(m)$ elementary arithmetic operations—addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and comparison—for some polynomial $p$, where $m$ is the number of numerical input entries. Under these conventions, it is polynomial-space in the Turing model and polynomial-time in the arithmetic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly polynomial algorithm uses polynomial Turing-model space and performs a number of elementary arithmetic operations polynomial in the number of input numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{space}_{\mathrm{Turing}}\le\operatorname{poly}(\text{encoded input length}),\qquad N_{\mathrm{arith}}\le p(m)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly polynomial, linear, and semi-strongly polynomial time
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation-count regimes for inputs divided into numerical parts, including intermediate-number size control and the source's arithmetic-model boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let input part i contain n_i numbers whose maximum encoding size is s_i. An algorithm is strongly polynomial-time if it performs at most p(n_1,\ldots,n_k) operations for some polynomial p independent of s_1,\ldots,s_k, and every number occurring during execution has size O(\max_i s_i). It is linear-time when p may be chosen linear. It is semi-strongly polynomial-time when rounding a rational is counted as one operation. If the problem has no numerical input, strongly polynomial-time and polynomial-time coincide. Under the stated elementary-arithmetic model, computing \lfloor x\rfloor and even deciding whether an integer is odd or even are not strongly polynomial-time operations in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If input part i contains n_i numbers of maximum encoding size s_i, an algorithm is strongly polynomial-time when its operation count is bounded by a polynomial in the array lengths n_i that is independent of the numerical sizes s_i, while every intermediate number has size O(max_i s_i). The corresponding linear-time definition requires a linear operation bound. Semi-strong polynomial time counts rational rounding as one operation. For problems without numerical inputs, strong and ordinary polynomial time coincide. In the stated arithmetic model, rational flooring and integer parity testing are not strongly polynomial-time in general.
assumptions_latex: \text{Input part }i\text{ contains }n_i\text{ numbers of maximum encoding size }s_i.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\le p(n_1,\ldots,n_k)\ \text{with }p\text{ independent of }s_1,\ldots,s_k,\qquad \operatorname{size}(z)=O\!\left(\max_i s_i\right)\ \text{for every intermediate number }z.

children.top_down_role: Operand-growth and encoding effects separating weak from strong guarantees.

assumptions_latex: The target sum \(B\) is a nonnegative integer encoded in binary.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For subset sum with \(n\) nonnegative integers and binary-encoded target \(B\), the standard table over attainable sums \(0,1,\ldots,B\) uses \(O(nB)\) updates. This is polynomial in the numeric magnitude \(B\) but not necessarily in its encoding length \(L=\lceil\log_2(B+1)\rceil\): values with \(B=2^{\Theta(L)}\) make the bound exponential in \(L\). Therefore a magnitude-polynomial bound is pseudopolynomial, not a weakly or strongly polynomial guarantee under binary encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An O(nB) subset-sum algorithm is polynomial in target magnitude B but can be exponential in B's binary encoding length.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Time
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses binary input encoding and integer-valued numerical parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an instance be encoded by a binary string of length \(n\), and let \(M\) be the largest magnitude among its explicitly represented integer parameters. An algorithm runs in pseudo-polynomial time if there exists a polynomial \(p\) such that its running time on every instance is at most \(p(n,M)\). This need not be polynomial in the ordinary input length because representing \(M\) requires only \(O(\!\log(M+1))\) bits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runtime is polynomial in the input length and numerical magnitudes, which may be exponential in their binary encoding lengths.
assumptions_latex: All numerical parameters are integers represented in binary.
Running time is measured in elementary bit or machine operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(I)\le p(|I|,M(I))\) for some polynomial \(p\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pseudo-polynomial-time algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines pseudo-polynomial running time and distinguishes it from ordinary polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm solving a decision problem \(\Pi\) is a pseudo-polynomial-time algorithm if there exists a bivariate polynomial \(r\) such that, for every \(I\in D_\Pi\), its running time satisfies \(T(I)\le r(\operatorname{Length}[I],\operatorname{Max}[I])\). Every polynomial-time algorithm is pseudo-polynomial-time, but NP-completeness alone does not rule out pseudo-polynomial-time solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudo-polynomial-time algorithm runs in time polynomial in both the encoded instance length and the largest numerical magnitude. Every polynomial-time algorithm is pseudo-polynomial-time, while NP-completeness alone does not exclude pseudo-polynomial solvability.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) is a decision problem with associated measures \(\operatorname{Length}\) and \(\operatorname{Max}\).
The algorithm solves every instance \(I\in D_\Pi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists r\text{ polynomial}\;\forall I\in D_\Pi:\ T(I)\le r(\operatorname{Length}[I],\operatorname{Max}[I])\), and polynomial time implies pseudo-polynomial time.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to algorithms that explicitly enumerate or construct variable-size output.

knowledge_statements.title: Many-One Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time many-one reductions between binary decision languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For languages \(L,K\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), a polynomial-time many-one reduction from \(L\) to \(K\) is a total function \(f:\{0,1\}^*\to\{0,1\}^*\), computable in deterministic polynomial time, such that for every string \(x\), \[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)\in K.\] Thus one transformed instance and one answer for \(K\) determine the answer for \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time computable transformation maps each source instance to one target instance while preserving yes and no answers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\le_m^p K\) exactly when such a function \(f\) exists.

notation.meaning: L polynomial-time many-one reduces to K

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-Time Many-One Transformation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a Karp reduction between decision problems, together with the stated implication and transitivity properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P_i=(X_i,Y_i)\) be decision problems. A polynomial transformation from \(\mathcal P_1\) to \(\mathcal P_2\) is a polynomial-time computable function \(f:X_1\to X_2\) such that, for every \(x\in X_1\), \[x\in Y_1\iff f(x)\in Y_2.\] Such a transformation is also called a Karp or polynomial-time many-one reduction and implies a polynomial-time Turing reduction. Polynomial-time many-one reductions and polynomial-time Turing reductions are transitive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time many-one or Karp reduction maps every yes-instance to a yes-instance and every no-instance to a no-instance through one polynomial-time computable function. Every such reduction is also a polynomial-time Turing reduction, and both reduction relations are transitive.
assumptions_latex: f:X_1\to X_2\text{ is computable in polynomial time}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in X_1,\ x\in Y_1\iff f(x)\in Y_2;\qquad \mathcal P_1\leq_m^p\mathcal P_2\Rightarrow\mathcal P_1\leq_T^p\mathcal P_2

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Turing Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic polynomial-time adaptive oracle reductions between decision languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For languages \(L,K\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), an adaptive polynomial-time Turing reduction from \(L\) to \(K\) is a deterministic oracle machine \(M^K\) that decides whether \(x\in L\) in time polynomial in \(|x|\). Each oracle query may depend on \(x\), the machine state, and answers to earlier queries. The polynomial running-time bound includes writing every query, so both the number and lengths of queries are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time machine decides the source problem using target-oracle queries whose contents may depend on earlier oracle answers.
assumptions_latex: Oracle membership queries have unit answer cost, while query construction is charged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The existence of \(M^K\) establishes \(L\le_T^p K\).

notation.meaning: machine M with membership-oracle access to K

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-Time Turing Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines polynomial-time reducibility through oracle access to another problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial-time Turing reduction from \Pi to \Pi' is a polynomial one-oracle Turing machine (T;\Pi') that solves \Pi using \Pi' as its oracle. When such a machine exists, \Pi is polynomial-time Turing reducible to \Pi'. In particular, \Pi'\in\mathcal P implies \Pi\in\mathcal P.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem is polynomial-time Turing reducible to another if a polynomial-time oracle machine solves the first using the second as its oracle. A polynomial-time solver for the oracle problem then gives a polynomial-time solver for the source problem.
assumptions_latex: (T;\Pi')\text{ is a polynomial one-oracle Turing machine solving }\Pi
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi\le_T^p\Pi',\qquad \Pi'\in\mathcal P\Longrightarrow\Pi\in\mathcal P.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-Time Turing Reduction of String Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines oracle Turing reducibility for string relations and records its transitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For string relations \(R,R'\) over \(\Sigma\), a polynomial-time Turing reduction from \(R\) to \(R'\) is an oracle Turing-machine program \(M\) such that, for every function \(g:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*\) realizing \(R'\), the relativized program \(M_g\) runs in polynomial time and computes a function \(f_M^g\) realizing \(R\). This relation, denoted \(R\propto_T R'\), is transitive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time Turing reduction from R to R' is an oracle program that runs in polynomial time and realizes R for every oracle function realizing R'. Polynomial-time Turing reducibility is transitive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R\propto_T R'\text{ via }M,\qquad (R\propto_T R'\land R'\propto_T R'')\Rightarrow R\propto_T R''

children.title: Nonadaptive Truth-Table Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions fixing all target queries before receiving answers.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonadaptive Truth-Table Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time nonadaptive truth-table reductions between decision languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For languages \(L,K\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), a polynomial-time truth-table reduction from \(L\) to \(K\) computes from \(x\) a list of queries \(q_1,\ldots,q_m\) and a Boolean function \(g_x:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}\), all within time polynomial in \(|x|\), such that \[\mathbf 1_L(x)=g_x\bigl(\mathbf 1_K(q_1),\ldots,\mathbf 1_K(q_m)\bigr).\] Every query is fixed before any oracle answer is received.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All target queries are generated in advance, and a polynomially computed Boolean rule combines their answers into the source answer.
assumptions_latex: The query list and an evaluable representation of \(g_x\) have polynomial size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed computation establishes \(L\le_{tt}^p K\).

children.title: Oracle-Access Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reduction frameworks parameterized by access to an abstract target oracle.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Access Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General oracle-machine formulation underlying query-access reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a computational task and let \(O\) be an oracle mapping admissible query strings to answers. An oracle-access reduction of \(F\) to \(O\) is an algorithm \(A^O\) that, on every valid input \(x\), may submit queries to \(O\) and must output \(F(x)\). Its resource bound charges all ordinary computation and query construction while assigning the stipulated oracle cost to each answer. Adaptivity is permitted unless the reduction definition explicitly forbids it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algorithm solves one task by querying an idealized interface for another task under an explicit cost and adaptivity convention.
assumptions_latex: The admissible queries, oracle answers, and oracle cost convention are specified.
\(F(x)\) is defined for every valid input \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every valid \(x\), the oracle algorithm satisfies \(A^O(x)=F(x)\) within the stated resource bound.

notation.meaning: algorithm A with access to oracle O

children.title: Cross-Interface Reduction Family
children.top_down_role: Transformations among problem interfaces with witness and solution recovery.

children.title: Decision-to-Search Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transformations using decision access to recover requested objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-to-Search Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direction means solving the decision interface with access to its associated search interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(x,y)\) be a polynomially decidable relation with polynomially bounded witnesses, let \(D_R(x)=1\) exactly when some \(y\) satisfies \(R(x,y)\), and let \(S_R(x)\) return such a witness or the symbol \(\bot\) when none exists. A decision-to-search reduction is an oracle algorithm that computes \(D_R(x)\) using access to \(S_R\). Canonically, it makes one query and returns \(1\) exactly when the response is not \(\bot\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The existence decision is obtained from a search oracle by checking whether it returns a witness or reports that none exists.
assumptions_latex: Every witness has length polynomially bounded in \(|x|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_R(x)=\mathbf 1[S_R(x)\ne\bot]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The trivial computation is mathematically coherent under the stated total search interface, but no evidence is supplied for calling this direction a decision-to-search reduction or for requiring the search oracle to return a no-witness symbol. A source fixing the directional and interface conventions is required.

children.title: Search-to-Decision Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transformations using construction access to resolve binary questions.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-to-Decision Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time witness recovery using an associated decision oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(x,y)\) be a polynomially decidable relation with witnesses bounded by a polynomial in \(|x|\), and define \(D_R(x)=1\) exactly when \(\exists y\,R(x,y)\). A search-to-decision reduction is a polynomial-time oracle algorithm \(A^{D_R}\) such that, for every \(x\) with \(D_R(x)=1\), it outputs a string \(y\) satisfying \(R(x,y)\); when \(D_R(x)=0\), it outputs \(\bot\). Existence of such a reduction is an additional self-reducibility property, not automatic for every relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time algorithm uses yes-or-no queries to recover a valid witness; this self-reducibility need not hold for every search relation.
assumptions_latex: Witness length is polynomially bounded in \(|x|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_R(x)=1\Rightarrow R(x,A^{D_R}(x))\), and \(D_R(x)=0\Rightarrow A^{D_R}(x)=\bot\).

notation.meaning: existence decision problem for relation R

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional definition correctly notes that witness recovery from a decision oracle is not automatic for every relation. However, no source supports the directional terminology or this exact self-reducibility formulation, so the record cannot be accepted as sourced candidate knowledge.

children.title: Optimization-to-Decision Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transformations resolving optimization tasks through related decision queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-to-Decision Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-valued bounded minimization reduced to threshold decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v^*(x)=\min_{y\in F(x)}c(x,y)\), where feasible objective values are integers in a known interval \([L(x),U(x)]\), and let the decision oracle answer whether \(v^*(x)\le t\). Initialize \(\ell=L(x)\) and \(u=U(x)\). While \(\ell<u\), set \(t=\lfloor(\ell+u)/2\rfloor\); replace \(u\) by \(t\) after a yes answer and replace \(\ell\) by \(t+1\) after a no answer. Stop with output \(\ell=v^*(x)\), using at most \(\lceil\log_2(U(x)-L(x)+1)\rceil\) queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary search over a known integer objective range computes the optimum value using threshold-decision queries.
assumptions_latex: Every feasible objective value is integral and lies in the known interval \([L(x),U(x)]\).
The threshold oracle correctly decides whether \(v^*(x)\le t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs \(v^*(x)\) after at most \(\lceil\log_2(U(x)-L(x)+1)\rceil\) oracle queries.

notation.meaning: known integral range containing the optimum

children.title: Solution-Recovery Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions preserving enough information to reconstruct target solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Recovery Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovers an optimizer from oracle access that initially supplies only objective information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an optimization problem with feasible set \(F(x)\), objective \(c(x,y)\), and optimum value \(v^*(x)\), a polynomial-time solution-recovery reduction is an oracle algorithm \(A^O\) that outputs some \(y^*\in F(x)\) satisfying \(c(x,y^*)=v^*(x)\). The oracle \(O\) exposes only the specified value or restricted-instance interface, and the total number and encoded lengths of queries, together with all non-oracle computation, are polynomial in \(|x|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time oracle procedure reconstructs an actual optimal solution from value information or equivalent queries on restricted instances.
assumptions_latex: The oracle interface and query encoding are fixed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition is plausible, but value-oracle and restricted-instance recovery are materially different interfaces, and no citation establishes a common convention covering both. A source must specify the oracle interface and the exact optimizer-recovery guarantee.

children.title: Objective-Structure Preservation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Optimization transformations preserving objective information or feasible-object structure.

children.title: Value-Preserving Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transformations retaining exact or controlled objective-value information.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Preserving Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimum-value preservation, allowing an explicitly specified decoding map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be optimization problems with optimum-value functions \(v_P\) and \(v_Q\). An exact value-preserving reduction consists of polynomial-time computable maps \(f\) and \(h\) such that \(f(x)\) is a valid instance of \(Q\) for every valid instance \(x\) of \(P\), and \[v_P(x)=h\bigl(x,v_Q(f(x))\bigr).\] In the strict form, \(h(x,z)=z\), so \(v_P(x)=v_Q(f(x))\). The value identity alone does not require recovery of a source optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transformed problem’s optimum determines the original optimum exactly through a polynomial-time decoder; strict preservation makes the two values equal.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) have well-defined attained optimum values on valid instances.
\(f\) and \(h\) are computable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_P(x)=h(x,v_Q(f(x)))\) for every valid source instance \(x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed decoder identity is internally coherent, but value-preserving reduction has multiple non-equivalent conventions across optimization and approximation literature. No source is supplied for this exact decoder-based convention or its strict subtype.

children.title: Structure-Preserving Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transformations retaining relevant feasible-object or incidence structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Preserving Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized definition relative to an explicitly named combinatorial invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P,Q\) be optimization problems and let \(\sigma_P,\sigma_Q\) assign a specified combinatorial structure to their instances or feasible solutions. A \(\sigma\)-structure-preserving reduction consists of a polynomial-time instance map \(f\), a polynomial-time solution map \(g_x\), and a declared correspondence \(\phi_x\) such that \(g_x\) maps relevant solutions of \(f(x)\) to solutions of \(x\) and \[\sigma_P\bigl(x,g_x(z)\bigr)=\phi_x\bigl(\sigma_Q(f(x),z)\bigr)\] for every relevant target solution \(z\). The preserved structure and relevance class must be stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduction preserves a named combinatorial invariant through declared instance, solution, and structure correspondences; preservation is meaningless unless that invariant is specified.
assumptions_latex: The structure assignments \(\sigma_P\) and \(\sigma_Q\) and correspondence \(\phi_x\) are explicitly specified.
The instance and solution maps are polynomial-time computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The declared structural correspondence holds for every target solution in the specified relevance class.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The title does not identify a particular preserved invariant, and the statement quantifies over a 'relevant' solution class without formally defining that class. Because structure-preserving reduction is domain-dependent and no source fixes this parameterized convention, authoritative evidence and a fully specified relevance domain are required.

children.title: Joint Preservation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on simultaneously retaining objective information and solution structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Preservation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary predicate for reductions required to preserve both objective values and a specified combinatorial structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let optimization problems \(A,B\) have objective functions \(v_A,v_B\), and let \(S_A,S_B\) be predicates on feasible solutions. A polynomial-time reduction with instance map \(f\) and solution map \(g\) jointly preserves value and structure when computable functions \(a(x)>0\) and \(b(x)\) satisfy \[v_A(g(x,y))=a(x)v_B(y)+b(x)\] for every feasible \(y\) of \(f(x)\), and simultaneously \[S_A(g(x,y))\Longleftrightarrow S_B(y).\] The joint-preservation boundary is reached when no single pair \((f,g)\) satisfies both conditions, even if separate reductions satisfy them individually.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint preservation requires one reduction to transfer both objective values and the chosen structural predicate; separate value- and structure-preserving reductions do not meet this condition.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are computable in time polynomial in the encoded input and solution lengths.
\(g(x,y)\) is feasible for \(A\) whenever \(y\) is feasible for \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl[v_A(g(x,y))=a(x)v_B(y)+b(x)\bigr]\land\bigl[S_A(g(x,y))\Longleftrightarrow S_B(y)\bigr]\)

notation.meaning: Instance and solution maps of the reduction.

review_flags: The intended preservation formalism is not fixed by the supplied path.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed affine value relation, predicate equivalence, and impossibility boundary are mathematically coherent but are not fixed by the path and have no cited source. A source is needed to determine the intended joint-preservation convention.

children.title: Approximation-Preserving Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reduction interfaces transferring approximation behavior; detailed taxonomies are downstream.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Preserving Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General ratio-transfer interface for positive-objective minimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization problems \(A,B\) with positive optima, an approximation-preserving reduction consists of polynomial-time maps \(fightarrow B\) and \(g\rightarrow A\), together with a nondecreasing transfer function \(h:[1,\infty)\to[1,\infty)\) satisfying \(h(1)=1\). For every instance \(x\) of \(A\) and every feasible solution \(y\) of \(f(x)\), it must satisfy \[\frac{v_A(g(x,y))}{\operatorname{OPT}_A(x)}\le h\!\left(\frac{v_B(y)}{\operatorname{OPT}_B(f(x))}\right).\] Thus any factor \(r\) approximation for \(B\) yields a factor \(h(r)\) approximation for \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reduction maps instances and solutions in polynomial time and converts every approximation ratio for the target problem into a controlled ratio for the source problem.
assumptions_latex: \(g(x,y)\) is feasible for \(x\) whenever \(y\) is feasible for \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_B(y)\le r\Longrightarrow R_A(g(x,y))\le h(r)\)
review_flags: Several inequivalent AP-, L-, PTAS-, and gap-reduction conventions exist.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: AP-, L-, PTAS-, and gap-reductions impose inequivalent requirements. No source identifies this ratio-transfer definition, and the displayed descriptions of f and g do not specify their domains and codomains.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transitivity of Polynomial-Time Many-One Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States transitivity of polynomial-time many-one reductions between decision problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For decision problems \(A,B,C\), if \(A\preccurlyeq B\) and \(B\preccurlyeq C\), then \(A\preccurlyeq C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial-time many-one reductions are transitive: if A reduces to B and B reduces to C, then A reduces to C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\preccurlyeq C.
