knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-Time Many-One Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the direction and Yes/No preservation condition of a polynomial-time many-one reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For decision problems \(A\) and \(B\), a polynomial-time many-one reduction from \(A\) to \(B\) is a polynomial-time computable mapping \(f\) from instances of \(A\) to instances of \(B\) such that, for every instance \(x\) of \(A\), \(x\) is a Yes-instance of \(A\) if and only if \(f(x)\) is a Yes-instance of \(B\). This is denoted \(A\preccurlyeq B\), or \(A\le_m^P B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time many-one reduction from A to B transforms each A-instance into a B-instance in polynomial time and preserves whether the answer is Yes in both directions.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ maps instances of }A\text{ to instances of }B
f\text{ is computable in polynomial time}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\preccurlyeq B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists f\text{ computable in polynomial time such that }\forall x,\ x\in A\iff f(x)\in B.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-Time Reductions, NP-Hardness, and NP-Completeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines polynomial-time many-one reduction between languages in NP, NP-hardness, and NP-completeness, together with their polynomial-time decidability consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $L_1,L_2\in\mathbf{NP}$, write $L_1\preccurlyeq L_2$ if there exists a polynomial-time Turing machine that, on every $x\in\{0,1\}^*$, outputs a string $y$ satisfying $x\in L_1\iff y\in L_2$. If $L_1\preccurlyeq L_2$ and $L_2\in\mathbf P$, then $L_1\in\mathbf P$. A language $L$ is NP-hard if $L'\preccurlyeq L$ for every $L'\in\mathbf{NP}$, and NP-complete if it is NP-hard and $L\in\mathbf{NP}$. Therefore, if an NP-complete language belongs to $\mathbf P$, then $\mathbf P=\mathbf{NP}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time reduction transforms each binary-string instance of one NP language into an instance of another while preserving membership. It transfers polynomial-time decidability from the target language to the source. A language is NP-hard if every NP language reduces to it, and NP-complete if it is also in NP. Thus, a polynomial-time algorithm for an NP-complete language implies P = NP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_1\preccurlyeq L_2\land L_2\in\mathbf P\Rightarrow L_1\in\mathbf P;\qquad L\text{ NP-complete}\land L\in\mathbf P\Rightarrow\mathbf P=\mathbf{NP}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Completeness and Hardness under Polynomial Transformability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General reduction-based definitions used by the classical NP completeness and hardness classifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a class $C$ of languages, $L$ is complete for $C$ with respect to polynomial transformability if $L\in C$ and, for every $L'\in C$, $L'\propto L$. The language $L$ is $C$-hard if, for every $L'\in C$, $L'\propto L$; membership of $L$ in $C$ is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A language is complete for a class when it belongs to that class and every language in the class polynomially transforms to it. It is hard for the class when the transformation condition holds, without requiring membership in the class.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is a class of languages.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\text{ is }C\text{-complete}\iff\left(L\in C\land\forall L'\in C,\ L'\propto L\right),\qquad L\text{ is }C\text{-hard}\iff\forall L'\in C,\ L'\propto L.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Sufficient Criterion for NP–coNP Collapse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A collapse consequence under the source's stated NP-oracle reduction conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_0,L_1,L_2\) be languages. If \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) are NP-complete, \(L_1^c\propto_c^{\mathrm{NP}}L_0\), and \(L_2^c\propto_c^{\mathrm{NP}}L_0^c\), then \[L_0\in\mathrm{NP}\cup\mathrm{coNP}\implies \mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let L0, L1, and L2 be languages satisfying the stated conditions: L1 and L2 are NP-complete, the complement of L1 has the specified NP-oracle reduction to L0, and the complement of L2 has that reduction to the complement of L0. If L0 is in NP or co-NP, then NP equals co-NP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}

children.title: NP-Hardness
children.top_down_role: Classification through reductions from problems in NP.

knowledge_statements.title: NP-Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time many-one hardness for decision problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decision problem \(H\) is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions if, for every language \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\), there exists a polynomial-time computable function \(f\) such that, for every encoded input \(x\), \[x\in L\Longleftrightarrow f(x)\in H.\] Membership of \(H\) in \(\mathrm{NP}\) is not required. For an optimization problem, NP-hardness conventionally means that an associated decision version is NP-hard or that polynomial-time exact optimization would polynomially solve an NP-hard decision problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every problem in NP reduces to an NP-hard problem in polynomial time; the hard problem itself need not belong to NP.
assumptions_latex: Languages use finite encodings, and running time is measured in encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall L\in\mathrm{NP},\;L\le_m^p H\)

notation.meaning: Polynomial-time many-one reducibility from L to H.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementation Preserves NP-Hardness Under Turing Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines decision-problem complementation and states the hardness consequence of mutual Turing reducibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a decision problem \(\Pi\) with domain \(D_\Pi\) and yes-set \(Y_\Pi\), its complement \(\Pi^c\) has domain \(D_\Pi\) and yes-set \(D_\Pi\setminus Y_\Pi\). Since \(\Pi\propto_T\Pi^c\) and \(\Pi^c\propto_T\Pi\), if \(\Pi\) is NP-complete or NP-hard, then \(\Pi^c\) is NP-hard. This conclusion does not require \(\Pi^c\in\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision problem's complement reverses its yes and no instances on the same domain. A problem and its complement Turing-reduce to each other, so the complement of an NP-complete or NP-hard problem is NP-hard, without assuming that the complement belongs to NP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi^c=(D_\Pi,D_\Pi\setminus Y_\Pi),\qquad \Pi^c\text{ is NP-hard}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: NP-hard computational problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction-based definition of NP-hardness, including complement symmetry for decision problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A computational problem \(\mathcal P\) is NP-hard if every problem in \(\mathrm{NP}\) polynomially reduces to \(\mathcal P\). For a decision problem \(D\), NP-hardness is invariant under complementation: \(D\) is NP-hard if and only if \(\overline D\) is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computational problem is NP-hard when every problem in NP polynomially reduces to it. A decision problem is NP-hard exactly when its complement is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P\text{ is NP-hard}\iff (\forall Q\in\mathrm{NP})\,Q\leq_p\mathcal P\), and for decision problems \(D\), \(D\text{ is NP-hard}\iff\overline D\text{ is NP-hard}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: NP-Completeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time many-one completeness for the class NP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decision problem \(C\) is NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions precisely when \(C\in\mathrm{NP}\) and \(C\) is NP-hard: \[C\in\mathrm{NP}\quad\text{and}\quad \forall L\in\mathrm{NP},\;L\le_m^p C.\] The membership condition supplies polynomially verifiable certificates for yes-instances, while the hardness condition ensures that every problem in \(\mathrm{NP}\) can be transformed to \(C\) in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision problem is NP-complete exactly when it belongs to NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: Completeness is measured using polynomial-time many-one reductions on finite encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is NP-complete}\Longleftrightarrow C\in\mathrm{NP}\land C\text{ is NP-hard}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: NP-Completeness and Its Polynomial-Time Consequence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines NP-completeness through NP membership and polynomial-time reductions from every problem in NP, then states the resulting P-versus-NP consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A problem \(\Pi\in\mathcal{NP}\) is \(\mathcal{NP}\)-complete if every problem in \(\mathcal{NP}\) can be reduced to \(\Pi\) in polynomial time. Consequently, if any \(\mathcal{NP}\)-complete problem is solvable in polynomial time, then every problem in \(\mathcal{NP}\) is solvable in polynomial time, and hence \(\mathcal P=\mathcal{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem in NP is NP-complete if every problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time. If any NP-complete problem is solvable in polynomial time, then every NP problem is, and P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: Every problem in \(\mathcal{NP}\) is polynomial-time reducible to \(\Pi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi\text{ is }\mathcal{NP}\text{-complete},\qquad \Pi\in\mathcal P\implies\mathcal P=\mathcal{NP}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: NP-completeness and its polynomial-time characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines NP-completeness by membership in NP and universal polynomial reducibility from NP, and records the resulting P-versus-NP characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A language L is NP-complete if and only if L\in\mathrm{NP} and, for every L'\in\mathrm{NP}, L'\propto L. Analogously, a decision problem \Pi is NP-complete if \Pi\in\mathrm{NP} and every \Pi'\in\mathrm{NP} satisfies \Pi'\propto\Pi. For every NP-complete \Pi, \Pi\in\mathrm P\iff\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}; consequently, if \mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}, then \Pi\in\mathrm{NP}\setminus\mathrm P.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An NP-complete language or decision problem belongs to NP and receives a polynomial reduction from every problem in NP. An NP-complete problem is solvable in polynomial time exactly when P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: L\text{ is a language, or }\Pi\text{ is a decision problem}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\text{ is NP-complete}\iff\left(L\in\mathrm{NP}\land\forall L'\in\mathrm{NP},\ L'\propto L\right),\qquad \Pi\text{ NP-complete}\Rightarrow\left(\Pi\in\mathrm P\iff\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-Time Reduction and NP-Completeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interprets the opening characterization of NP-complete problems as problems in NP. Universal reducibility alone establishes NP-hardness, not NP-completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial-time reduction from a decision problem \Pi' to a decision problem \Pi is a polynomial-time transformation mapping each instance w to an instance v such that w\in\Pi'\iff v\in\Pi. A problem \Pi is \mathcal{NP}\text{-complete} if \Pi\in\mathcal{NP} and, for every \Pi'\in\mathcal{NP}, there exists such a reduction from \Pi' to \Pi.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time reduction transforms instances in polynomial time while preserving yes- and no-answers. A problem is NP-complete when it belongs to NP and every problem in NP polynomial-time reduces to it. The universal-reduction condition without NP membership gives only NP-hardness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi\text{ is }\mathcal{NP}\text{-complete}\iff \Pi\in\mathcal{NP}\ \land\ \forall\Pi'\in\mathcal{NP},\ \Pi'\leq_p\Pi

knowledge_statements.title: Membership Requirement Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The additional membership condition separating NP-hardness from NP-completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) be NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions. The boundary between NP-hardness and NP-completeness is membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\): there must exist a polynomial \(p\) and a polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that \[x\in H\Longleftrightarrow \exists w\in\{0,1\}^*\;\bigl(|w|\le p(|x|)\land V(x,w)=1\bigr).\] Under the NP-hardness assumption, \(H\) is NP-complete exactly when this certificate condition holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an NP-hard decision problem, NP membership—equivalently, polynomial-size certificates verifiable in polynomial time—is exactly the additional condition required for NP-completeness.
assumptions_latex: \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
\(V\) runs in time polynomial in the combined encoded length of \(x\) and \(w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\text{ is NP-complete}\Longleftrightarrow H\in\mathrm{NP}\)

knowledge_statements.title: Weak NP-Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-versus-unary encoding definition for numeric decision problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a numeric decision problem whose instances contain nonnegative integers. Write \(P_{\mathrm{bin}}\) for ordinary binary encoding and \(P_{\mathrm{unary}}\) for the same problem with every numeric datum encoded in unary. In the encoding-based convention, \(P\) is weakly NP-hard when \(P_{\mathrm{bin}}\) is NP-hard but \(P_{\mathrm{unary}}\) is solvable in polynomial time. Thus the hardness depends on the logarithmic compression of potentially large numerical values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numeric problem is weakly NP-hard when binary encoding is NP-hard but replacing all numbers by unary encodings yields a polynomial-time problem.
assumptions_latex: All nondigital combinatorial data retain the same encoding in \(P_{\mathrm{bin}}\) and \(P_{\mathrm{unary}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{bin}}\text{ is NP-hard}\land P_{\mathrm{unary}}\in\mathrm{P}\)

notation.meaning: Problem with numeric values encoded in binary.

children.title: Strong NP-Hardness

knowledge_statements.title: Strong NP-Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness persisting when all numerical magnitudes are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A numeric decision problem \(P\) is strongly NP-hard if there exists a polynomial \(q\) such that the restriction of \(P\) to instances \(x\) whose every numeric datum \(a\) satisfies \(a\le q(|x|)\) remains NP-hard. Equivalently under standard explicit encodings, hardness persists when numerical data are written in unary. Strong hardness therefore cannot be attributed solely to exponentially large binary-encoded numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numeric problem is strongly NP-hard when it remains NP-hard even after all numerical values are restricted to polynomial magnitude, equivalently under standard unary encoding.
assumptions_latex: Instances contain explicitly represented nonnegative integer data.
The bound \(|x|\) measures the nondigital combinatorial encoding together with the bounded numeric encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists q\in\mathbb{Z}[t]\;\text{such that}\;P\!estriction\!\{x:\max a(x)\le q(|x|)\}\text{ is NP-hard}\)

notation.meaning: A numeric datum occurring in instance x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong NP-Hardness and Its One-Way Solvability Consequence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strong NP-hardness using an NP-hard polynomially bounded subproblem and records the limitation of the resulting polynomial-time implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A search problem \(\Pi\) is strongly NP-hard if it contains an NP-hard subproblem satisfying a polynomial bound on \(\operatorname{Max}[1]\). Consequently, if \(\Pi\) is solvable in polynomial time, then \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Unlike NP-completeness, NP-hardness alone does not establish the converse implication that \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) would make \(\Pi\) polynomial-time solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A search problem is strongly NP-hard if it contains an NP-hard subproblem whose Max[1] parameter is polynomially bounded. Polynomial-time solvability would imply P equals NP, but NP-hardness alone does not support the converse implication.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi\text{ is strongly NP-hard};\qquad \Pi\in\mathrm P\Rightarrow\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong NP-hardness and its pseudopolynomial-time obstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strong NP-hardness using reductions with unary-encoded numerical output and records the associated conditional complexity boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A problem \(\Pi\) is strongly NP-hard if every problem in \(\mathbf{NP}\) can be reduced to \(\Pi\) in polynomial time such that all numbers in the resulting instance are encoded in unary. This restriction forces the reduction to produce only polynomially bounded numerical values. Assuming \(\mathbf P\ne\mathbf{NP}\), a strongly NP-hard problem cannot admit a pseudopolynomial-time algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem is strongly NP-hard if every problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time while all numerical values in the resulting instance are unary encoded. This limits those values to polynomial magnitude. Assuming P differs from NP, a strongly NP-hard problem has no pseudopolynomial-time algorithm.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf P\ne\mathbf{NP}\text{ for the pseudopolynomial-time impossibility claim}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi\text{ strongly NP-hard}\Rightarrow\bigl(\mathbf P\ne\mathbf{NP}\Rightarrow\Pi\text{ has no pseudopolynomial-time algorithm}\bigr)

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Tractability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between pseudo-polynomial algorithms, unary encodings, and strong NP-hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an algorithm for a numeric problem runs in time polynomial in the combinatorial encoding length \(n\) and the maximum numeric value \(M\), rather than in \(n+\log M\). It is pseudo-polynomial. On instances satisfying \(M\le q(n)\) for a polynomial \(q\), its running time is polynomial in the ordinary input length. Consequently, if a strongly NP-hard problem had a pseudo-polynomial exact algorithm, its polynomially bounded NP-hard restriction would lie in \(\mathrm{P}\), implying \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudo-polynomial algorithm becomes polynomial when numbers are polynomially bounded; therefore strongly NP-hard problems admit no such exact algorithm unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is exact and runs in time \(\operatorname{poly}(n,M)\).
The problem is strongly NP-hard under polynomial-time reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\Longrightarrow\text{no exact pseudo-polynomial algorithm exists}\)

notation.meaning: Length of the combinatorial portion of the encoding.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Reduction-Source Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transitivity principle justifying the use of standard NP-complete source problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be an established NP-complete decision problem and let \(T\) be a decision problem. If \(S\le_m^p T\), then \(T\) is NP-hard. If additionally \(T\in\mathrm{NP}\), then \(T\) is NP-complete. Established problems such as satisfiability, 3-satisfiability, clique, vertex cover, and Hamiltonian cycle may therefore serve as canonical reduction sources once their NP-completeness under the same reduction convention has been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time many-one reduction from any established NP-complete source problem to a target proves the target NP-hard; target membership in NP additionally proves NP-completeness.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\text{ is NP-hard}\), and \(T\in\mathrm{NP}\Longrightarrow T\text{ is NP-complete}\)

knowledge_statements.title: Inapproximability Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap-reduction interface from decision hardness to approximation hardness for maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be an NP-hard language and \(P\) a maximization problem. Suppose a polynomial-time map \(f\) and constants \(a>b>0\) satisfy \[x\in L\Longrightarrow \operatorname{OPT}_P(f(x))\ge a,\qquad x\notin L\Longrightarrow \operatorname{OPT}_P(f(x))\le b.\] If a polynomial-time algorithm always returns a feasible value at least \(\operatorname{OPT}_P/r\) for some \(r<a/b\), then comparing its value with \(b\) decides \(L\) in polynomial time. Therefore, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), no such factor-\(r\) approximation exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomially created optimum gap from at least a to at most b rules out approximation factors better than a/b unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: All feasible objective values used by the comparison are computable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\Longrightarrow P\text{ has no polynomial-time }r\text{-approximation for }r<a/b\)

notation.meaning: Completeness and soundness thresholds of the gap.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports gap reductions or inapproximability.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximization gap statement and factor threshold are mathematically plausible and the complexity-bound kind fits, but no inspectable citation supports the gap-reduction hypotheses or inapproximability conclusion.

children.title: Tractability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Changes in computational status caused by representation, numerical scale, or structural restrictions.

children.title: Tractable Restrictions of Hard Problems
children.top_down_role: Graph-class, dimension, width, and matrix-structure islands of tractability.

knowledge_statements.title: Tractable Restrictions of Hard Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal criterion for a polynomial-time island inside a globally hard problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a decision problem and \(R\) a polynomial-time recognizable class of its instances. The restriction of \(P\) to \(R\) is \[P|_R=\{x:x\in P\land x\in R\}.\] The class \(R\) is a tractable restriction of \(P\) when \(P|_R\in\mathrm{P}\), even if \(P\) on unrestricted instances is NP-hard. Typical restrictions may bound graph width, dimension, rank, or impose a special matrix or graph class; tractability must be established for the explicitly encoded restricted family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tractable restriction is a polynomial-time recognizable instance class on which a globally hard problem can be solved in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: Instances of \(P|_R\) use the same explicit encoding convention as instances of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P|_R\in\mathrm{P}\)

notation.meaning: Restriction of P to instances in R.

review_flags: The supplied locators do not directly support the formal restriction criterion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restriction criterion is coherent and definition is an appropriate content kind, but the record supplies no source for this formalization or its recognition requirement.

children.title: Hard Extensions of Tractable Problems
children.top_down_role: Hardness introduced by side constraints, multiple commodities, nonlinearities, or succinct inputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard Extensions of Tractable Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal criterion for added modeling features to create an NP-hard extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_0\in\mathrm{P}\) be a base decision problem and \(Q\) an extended problem. The problem \(Q\) is a hard extension of \(P_0\) when there is a polynomial-time embedding \(e\) satisfying \[x\in P_0\Longleftrightarrow e(x)\in Q,\] the image of \(e\) is the subclass where the added features are disabled, and \(Q\) is NP-hard on its full instance class. The added features may be side constraints, multiple commodities, nonlinear objectives, or succinct representations, but hardness is attributed to them only after the base subclass and encoding are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hard extension contains a polynomially solvable base problem as the case with added features disabled, while the full extended problem is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: The embedding \(e\) is computable in polynomial time.
The added features and their disabled values have explicit finite encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\text{ is NP-hard}\land P_0\text{ embeds as the disabled-feature subclass of }Q\)

notation.meaning: Embedding of base instances into extended instances.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly formalizes hard extensions and disabled-feature embeddings.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The disabled-feature embedding gives a coherent formalization and fits a definition container, but no source establishes that this is the intended hard-extension criterion or supports attribution of hardness to the added features.

children.title: Hardness Source Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Distinction between magnitude-driven and structural difficulty.

children.title: Magnitude-Driven Hardness
children.top_down_role: Difficulty arising primarily from large or finely encoded numerical parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Magnitude-Driven Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies weak NP-hardness associated with binary-encoded numerical magnitudes and pseudopolynomial solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s\) be the length of the nonnumerical part of an instance, let \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb Z\) be its numerical parameters, let \(U=\max_i|a_i|\), and let \(\ell=s+O\!\left(m+\sum_{i=1}^m\log(1+|a_i|)\right)\) be its binary encoding length. Call an NP-hard problem family magnitude-driven when it has an exact algorithm whose running time is polynomial in \(s\), \(m\), and \(U\). This running time is pseudopolynomial in the binary model, while it becomes polynomial on restrictions satisfying \(U\leq(s+m)^c\) for a fixed constant \(c\), and under a unary encoding whose length accounts for the magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hardness is magnitude-driven when binary encoding gives an NP-hard family but an exact algorithm is polynomial in the numerical values, making bounded-magnitude or unary-encoded restrictions polynomial-time solvable.
assumptions_latex: \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb Z\) are binary encoded in the unrestricted family.
An exact algorithm has running time polynomial in \(s\), \(m\), and \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated tractability boundary depends on the encoded numerical magnitudes.

notation.meaning: length of the nonnumerical instance data

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

children.title: Structure-Driven Hardness
children.top_down_role: Difficulty arising from combinatorial interactions independent of large magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Driven Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies NP-hardness that persists without unbounded numerical coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A discrete optimization family has structure-driven hardness when its decision version remains NP-hard on a restriction in which all numerical parameters are absent or take values in a fixed finite set \(D\) independent of the instance size. This restricted hardness shows that unbounded coefficient magnitudes are not necessary for the NP-hardness boundary; the remaining obstruction is carried by the admissible combinatorial structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hardness is structure-driven when an NP-hard restriction remains after numerical data are removed or confined to a fixed finite set.
assumptions_latex: The restricted decision problem is defined by the same decision predicate as the unrestricted family.
\(D\) is fixed independently of the instance size, and NP-hardness uses polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: NP-hardness persists without unbounded numerical magnitudes.

notation.meaning: fixed finite set of permitted numerical values

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

children.title: Mixed-Source Hardness
children.top_down_role: Hardness produced by coupled numerical and combinatorial effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Source Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies hardness arising from interaction between numerical magnitudes and combinatorial structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Call the hardness of a discrete optimization family mixed-source when both of the following restrictions yield polynomial-time solvable subfamilies: fixing the relevant structural parameter \(k\) by a constant, and bounding the largest numerical magnitude \(U\) polynomially in the structural input size; yet instances with both \(k\) and binary-encoded \(U\) unbounded form an NP-hard family. Under this operational definition, neither magnitude nor structure alone explains the stated boundary: hardness occurs in their joint unbounded regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hardness is mixed-source when bounding either structural complexity or numerical magnitude restores tractability, but allowing both to grow yields NP-hardness.
assumptions_latex: A structural parameter \(k\) and maximum numerical magnitude \(U\) are specified.
The two restricted subfamilies and the jointly unbounded family use the same decision predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The observed tractability boundary depends jointly on \(k\) and \(U\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is plausible as an operational taxonomy, but no source establishes this exact two-parameter classification. The phrase “fixing k by a constant” also requires uniform quantifiers and a precise structural parameter before the boundary is reliable.

children.title: Representation-Sensitive Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity changes caused by explicit, succinct, lifted, or oracle representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Sensitive Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares complexity only after fixing how feasible objects, constraints, and access operations are encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a fixed abstract optimization problem and let \(R\) be a representation of its instances. Complexity is measured as a function of the representation length \(|R(I)|\) and the permitted access operations. Consequently, polynomial-time solvability is not invariant under arbitrary changes of representation: an explicit list may have exponential length relative to a succinct encoding, while an oracle representation charges for queries and omits the oracle's implementation cost. Complexity claims for \(P\) must therefore name the encoding or oracle model and use reductions that translate representations with polynomial overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same abstract problem can have different complexity under explicit, succinct, lifted, or oracle representations, so every bound must specify its representation model.
assumptions_latex: Each representation has a defined length and access model.
Representation translations are evaluated by their computational and size overhead.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A polynomial bound relative to one representation need not be polynomial relative to another.

children.title: Priority-Order Greedy Methods
children.top_down_role: Incremental methods organized by candidate ordering and feasibility preservation.

knowledge_statements.title: Priority-Order Greedy Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic one-pass greedy construction over a hereditary feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite ground set \(E\), a hereditary family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\), and a priority key \(p:E\to\mathbb R\). Order the elements as \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\) with \(p(e_1)\geq\cdots\geq p(e_m)\), resolving ties by a specified rule. Initialize \(S_0=\varnothing\). For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), set \(S_i=S_{i-1}\cup\{e_i\}\) if this set lies in \(\mathcal F\), and otherwise set \(S_i=S_{i-1}\). Output \(S_m\). Stop after every element has been examined once; optimality requires a separate structural certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scan candidates in priority order, permanently accept each feasible addition, reject infeasible additions, and return the final feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and membership in \(\mathcal F\) is decidable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(S_m\) belongs to \(\mathcal F\) and is maximal relative to the processed priority scan.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and terminal placement are correct, and heredity makes the final set inclusion-maximal after a complete scan. An authoritative algorithm or greedy-systems locator is nevertheless absent.

children.title: Structural Greedy Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Correctness families based on replacements, safe choices, and structural cuts.

children.title: Exchange-Property Certificates
children.top_down_role: Correctness evidence based on replacing selected objects while preserving feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange-Property Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certifies greedy optimality through feasible exchanges that do not decrease total weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite, let \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\), let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), and let \(G=\{g_1,ldots,g_r\}\in\mathcal F\) be a greedy output in its selection order. An exchange certificate consists of a certified optimal set \(O_0\in\mathcal F\) and sets \(O_1,ldots,O_r\in\mathcal F\) such that \(\{g_1,ldots,g_i\}\subseteq O_i\) for every \(i\). For each \(i\), either \(g_i\in O_{i-1}\) and \(O_i=O_{i-1}\), or there is an element \(o_i\in O_{i-1}\) such that \(O_i=(O_{i-1}\setminus\{o_i\})\cup\{g_i\}\) and \(w(g_i)\geq w(o_i)\). If \(O_r=G\), these conditions certify that \(G\) is optimal for maximizing total weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible sequence that transforms a certified optimum into the greedy output using only nondecreasing-weight exchanges certifies greedy optimality.
assumptions_latex: Every listed set, exchange, and weight comparison is explicitly checkable.
\(O_0\) has an independent certificate of optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exchange data certify that \(G\) is a maximum-total-weight member of \(\mathcal F\).

notation.meaning: feasible set after the ith certified exchange
sum of the weights of elements of S

children.title: Cut-Property Certificates
children.top_down_role: Correctness evidence based on choices certified across structural cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Property Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-spanning-tree safe-edge certificate for a cut respected by the current forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph with edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), and let \(A\subseteq E\) be contained in some minimum spanning tree. For a cut \((S,V\setminus S)\) that no edge of \(A\) crosses, let \(e\) be a minimum-weight edge crossing that cut. The tuple \((S,e)\), together with comparisons \(w(e)\leq w(f)\) for every crossing edge \(f\), certifies that \(A\cup\{e\}\) is contained in a minimum spanning tree. Thus \(e\) is a safe greedy choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lightest edge crossing a cut respected by the current forest is certified safe for some minimum spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is contained in a minimum spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a minimum spanning tree containing \(A\cup\{e\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind and MST cut-property statement are mathematically appropriate and sufficiently qualified by the invariant that A lies in an MST. A specific theorem or section locator is required.

children.title: Safe-Choice Certification
children.top_down_role: Connections from structural properties to locally safe greedy selections.

knowledge_statements.title: Safe-Choice Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic certificate that a greedy choice preserves extendibility to an optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem with feasible-solution family \(\mathcal X\) and objective \(c:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), let \(A\) be the current partial choice. A candidate \(e\) has a safe-choice certificate when the certificate identifies a certified optimal solution \(X\in\mathcal X\) extending \(A\) and a locally verifiable transformation producing a feasible solution \(X'\in\mathcal X\) that extends \(A\cup\{e\}\) and satisfies \(c(X')\leq c(X)\). These data certify that \(A\cup\{e\}\) extends to an optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A choice is certified safe when a verified transformation inserts it into a certified optimum without increasing the objective.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem with objective \(c\).
\(X\) has an independent certificate of optimality and extends \(A\).
Feasibility of \(X'\), extension of \(A\cup\{e\}\), and the objective comparison are verifiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The enlarged partial choice \(A\cup\{e\}\) extends to an optimal solution.

children.title: Matroid Greedy Characterization
children.top_down_role: Landmark boundary connecting universal weighted greedy correctness with exchange structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Greedy Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes hereditary set systems on which weighted greedy optimization is universally correct.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\neq\varnothing\) be a collection of subsets of \(S\) that is closed under taking subsets. Then \((S,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid if and only if, for every weight function \(w:S\to\mathbb R_+\), the greedy algorithm produces an \(I\in\mathcal I\) satisfying \(w(I)=\max\{w(J):J\in\mathcal I\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty hereditary set system is a matroid exactly when the greedy algorithm finds a maximum-weight feasible set for every nonnegative element-weight function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (S,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid}\iff \forall w:S\to\mathbb R_+,\;w(I_{\mathrm{greedy}})=\max_{J\in\mathcal I}w(J).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Universal Weighted-Greedy Characterization of Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between matroid structure and hereditary set-system axioms together with universal weighted greedy optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be a collection of subsets of \(E\). Then \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid if and only if \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\), every subset of a member of \(\mathcal I\) also belongs to \(\mathcal I\), and for every weight function \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), the greedy algorithm produces a maximal member of \(\mathcal I\) having maximum weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set system is a matroid exactly when it contains the empty set, is hereditary, and weighted greedy returns a maximum-weight maximal feasible set for every real-valued element-weight function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid}\iff\left[\varnothing\in\mathcal I\ \land\ \forall I\in\mathcal I\,\forall I'\subseteq I,\ I'\in\mathcal I\ \land\ \forall w:E\to\mathbb R,\ B_G\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{B\in\mathcal I\text{ maximal}}\sum_{e\in B}w(e)\right].

children.title: Matroid Feasible-Object Regimes
children.top_down_role: Greedy characterization across maximal and fixed-rank feasible objects.

children.title: Independent-Set Regime
children.top_down_role: Greedy behavior over hereditary feasible families without fixed cardinality.

knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Set Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rado–Edmonds greedy theorem for maximizing nonnegative weight over matroid independent sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid and let \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\). Process elements in nonincreasing order of weight and add an element exactly when independence is preserved. The resulting set \(G\in\mathcal I\) maximizes \(w(I)=\sum_{e\in I}w(e)\) over all \(I\in\mathcal I\). Conversely, if a nonempty hereditary system \((E,\mathcal I)\) has this greedy-optimality property for every nonnegative weight function, then \((E,\mathcal I)\) satisfies the augmentation axiom and is a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedy maximizes every nonnegative additive weight over independent sets exactly for hereditary systems that are matroids.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and \(\mathcal I\) is nonempty and hereditary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Greedy is universally optimal over \(\mathcal I\) if and only if \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid.

notation.meaning: sum of element weights in I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind and independent-set regime are appropriate, and the forward matroid result is standard. The converse must specify whether universal optimality covers every permitted tie-breaking or an equivalent precise greedy convention, and it needs a Rado–Edmonds theorem locator.

children.title: Basis Regime
children.top_down_role: Greedy behavior over maximal feasible objects of common rank.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight basis form of the finite matroid greedy theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid and let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\) be arbitrary. Process all elements in nonincreasing order of weight, accepting an element whenever independence is preserved, until a maximal independent set \(B_G\) is obtained. Every maximal independent set of a matroid is a basis, and \(B_G\) satisfies \(w(B_G)\geq w(B)\) for every basis \(B\) of \(M\). Unlike independent-set maximization, arbitrary negative weights are permitted because every feasible basis has the same cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scanning arbitrary weights from largest to smallest and preserving independence produces a maximum-weight matroid basis.
assumptions_latex: \(w:E\to\mathbb R\) is additive, with ties resolved arbitrarily.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The greedy output \(B_G\) is a maximum-weight basis of \(M\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the basis regime, and the arbitrary-real-weight maximum-basis statement is correct for finite matroids. No authoritative theorem locator is supplied.

children.title: Maximality-to-Rank Transition
children.top_down_role: Structural passage from arbitrary independent objects to fixed-rank bases.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximality-to-Rank Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matroid augmentation turns inclusion maximality into maximum cardinality within every restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid, let \(X\subseteq E\), and let \(I\subseteq X\) be independent and inclusion-maximal among the independent subsets of \(X\). Then \(|I|=r_M(X)\), where \(r_M(X)=\max\{|J|:J\subseteq X,\ J\in\mathcal I\}\). Consequently, every maximal independent subset of \(X\) is a basis of the restriction \(M|X\), and all such subsets have equal cardinality. This property can fail in a hereditary system that does not satisfy matroid augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a matroid restriction, every inclusion-maximal independent set has maximum possible size and therefore realizes the rank.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq E\), and \(I\subseteq X\) is inclusion-maximal independent in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|I|=r_M(X)\), so \(I\) is a basis of \(M|X\).

children.title: Greedy Weight-Order Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dependence of the characterization on weight and priority models.

children.title: Weighted Greedy Regime
children.top_down_role: Greedy characterization under assigned element weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Greedy Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weight-ordered greedy algorithm for a finite matroid, with independent-set and basis output conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), an independence oracle, and weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\). For maximum-weight independent-set optimization, discard elements of negative weight; for maximum-weight basis optimization, retain all elements. Sort the retained elements so that \(w(e_1)\geq\cdots\geq w(e_m)\), initialize \(S_0=\varnothing\), and set \(S_i=S_{i-1}\cup\{e_i\}\) exactly when this union lies in \(\mathcal I\). After the scan, output \(S_m\). The output is respectively a maximum-weight independent set or a maximum-weight basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort matroid elements by decreasing weight and accept every independence-preserving element; discard negative weights only when a basis is not required.
assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid accessed by an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned set is optimal for the selected independent-set or basis regime.

notation.meaning: accepted set after processing i elements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the weighted greedy regime, and the independent-set and basis conventions are explicitly distinguished rather than conflated. The optimality claims require a specific finite-matroid greedy theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Greedy Algorithm for Matroid Independent Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weight-ordered greedy construction of independent sets of successive cardinalities; optimality is stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(S_0:=\varnothing\), \(k:=1\), and \(U:=E\). While \(U\neq\varnothing\), choose a maximum-weight element \(e\in U\), remove it from \(U\), and, if \(S_{k-1}\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I(M)\), set \(S_k:=S_{k-1}\cup\{e\}\) and increment \(k\); otherwise discard \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process elements in nonincreasing weight order, accepting an element exactly when it preserves independence and recording the independent set after each acceptance.
assumptions_latex: M=(E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a finite matroid}
c:E\to\mathbb R\text{ is an element-weight function}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_k=S_{k-1}\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\text{ after each acceptance, with elements processed in nonincreasing weight order}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Weight Greedy Algorithm for a Set Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weight-ordered construction with an explicit positive-weight eligibility rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite set \(S\), a family \(\mathcal I\subseteq 2^S\) with \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\), and weights \(c\in\mathbb R^S\), set \(J=\varnothing\). While there exists \(e\in S\setminus J\) with \(c_e>0\) and \(J\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\), choose an eligible element of maximum weight and replace \(J\) by \(J\cup\{e\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from the empty set, repeatedly add a maximum-weight positive element when the enlarged set belongs to the specified family, and stop when none remains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J\in\mathcal I\quad\text{and}\quad \nexists e\in S\setminus J:\ c_e>0\ \text{and}\ J\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lexicographic ordering of weighted independent sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines comparison by nonincreasing element-weight sequences and records the base and distinct-weight uniqueness consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M=(E,\mathcal I)$ be a matroid with $w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}$. For $I_1=\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}$ and $I_2=\{b_1,\ldots,b_n\}$, list elements in nonincreasing weight order. Then $I_1$ is lexicographically greater than $I_2$ if its weight sequence is larger at the first differing position, or if the sequences agree through the end of $I_2$ and $m>n$. A member of $\mathcal I$ is lexicographically maximum if none is lexicographically greater. Every lexicographically maximum independent set is a base, and it is unique when all element weights are distinct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort each independent set's element weights from largest to smallest. Compare the first unequal weights; if one sequence is a proper prefix of the other, the longer sequence is greater. A lexicographically maximum independent set of a matroid is a base and is unique when all element weights are distinct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\text{ lexicographically maximum}\Rightarrow B\text{ is a base};\qquad \bigl(\forall e\ne f,\ w(e)\ne w(f)\bigr)\Rightarrow B\text{ is unique}.

children.title: Priority-Ordering Regime
children.top_down_role: Greedy behavior governed by externally specified element priorities.

knowledge_statements.title: Priority-Ordering Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy construction on a finite matroid under a fixed total priority order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid and let \(e_1\succ e_2\succ\cdots\succ e_m\) be a total priority order on \(E\). Initialize \(G_0=\varnothing\). For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), set \(G_i=G_{i-1}\cup\{e_i\}\) if this set belongs to \(\mathcal I\), and otherwise set \(G_i=G_{i-1}\). Output \(G_m\). The output is the lexicographically greatest basis with respect to the priority order. If the order is nonincreasing in weights, then the output is a maximum-weight basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scan elements from highest to lowest priority, accepting each feasible element. On a matroid this produces the lexicographically greatest basis and, for weight-ordered priorities, a maximum-weight basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_m\) is the lexicographically greatest basis; a nonincreasing weight order makes \(G_m\) maximum-weight.

notation.meaning: greedy set after processing the first i elements

children.title: Tie-Breaking Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of greedy outcomes or guarantees on equal-priority choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Breaking Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective invariance, but possible solution nonuniqueness, under equal-weight orderings in matroid greedy optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid with weight function \(w:E\to\mathbb R\). Run the greedy basis algorithm using any total order satisfying \(w(e)>w(f)\Rightarrow e\) precedes \(f\). Every permissible ordering of elements tied in weight produces a basis \(B\) satisfying \(w(B)=\max\{w(B'):B'\text{ is a basis of }M\}\). Different tie-breaking orders may produce different bases, but their total weights coincide. Thus tie-breaking affects the selected optimizer, not the optimal objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary ordering within equal-weight classes can change the greedy basis, but every resulting matroid basis has the same optimal total weight.
assumptions_latex: The scan order is nonincreasing in \(w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every tie-breaking rule returns a maximum-weight basis, although the returned basis need not be unique.

notation.meaning: sum of element weights over basis B

children.title: Nonmatroid Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Independence systems lacking the exchange structure needed for universal greedy correctness.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmatroid Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal weight-ordered greedy correctness fails exactly when a finite independence system violates matroid exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite hereditary independence system that is not a matroid. Then there exist \(I,J\in\mathcal I\) with \(|I|<|J|\) and \(I\cup\{e\}\notin\mathcal I\) for every \(e\in J\setminus I\). Assign weight \(1+\varepsilon\) to elements of \(I\), weight \(1\) to elements of \(J\setminus I\), and weight \(0\) otherwise, where \(\varepsilon>0\) is sufficiently small. Weight-ordered greedy can first select all of \(I\), after which it rejects every element of \(J\setminus I\), while \(J\) has greater weight. Hence universal greedy optimality fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exchange violation admits weights for which greedy commits to a smaller independent set and rejects every improving element, while another feasible set has greater total weight.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and \(\mathcal I\) is nonempty and hereditary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a nonnegative weight function for which weight-ordered greedy is not optimal over \(\mathcal I\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary construction is mathematically credible: augmentation failure and sufficiently small positive epsilon make J heavier than I, while a compatible weight order can commit greedy to I. The selected failure_boundary kind fits the topic, but the universal characterization and counterweight construction require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: State-Space Dynamic Programming

knowledge_statements.title: State-Space Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward dynamic programming on a finite acyclic state-transition graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite state set whose feasible transitions form a directed acyclic graph. For each terminal state \(s\), set \(F(s)=g(s)\). Process nonterminal states in reverse topological order and compute \[F(s)=\operatorname{opt}_{a\in A(s)}\bigl(c(s,a)+F(T(s,a))\bigr),\] where \(\operatorname{opt}\) is either minimum or maximum consistently. Store an optimizing action at every processed state. Starting from the initial state \(s_0\), follow stored actions until a terminal state is reached; the resulting policy or path has value \(F(s_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate terminal states, process the acyclic state graph backward, and store an optimal transition at each state. Following stored transitions reconstructs an optimal solution.
assumptions_latex: The state-transition graph is finite and acyclic.
Costs are additively separable across transitions and terminal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The backward recurrence returns the optimal value \(F(s_0)\) and stored actions reconstruct an optimizer.

notation.meaning: optimal continuation value from state s

children.title: Resource-Indexed Dynamic Programming
children.top_down_role: Dynamic programs indexed by bounded budgets, capacities, or numerical resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Indexed Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon dynamic programming indexed by an integral resource budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For stages \(i=1,\ldots,n\) and integral budgets \(b\in\{0,\ldots,B\}\), let action \(a\in A_i\) consume \(r_i(a)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and yield value \(v_i(a)\). Initialize \(F(0,b)=0\). For increasing \(i\), compute \[F(i,b)=\max_{a\in A_i:\,r_i(a)\le b}\bigl(F(i-1,b-r_i(a))+v_i(a)\bigr).\] Record an optimizing action for each reachable entry. Output \(F(n,B)\), and backtrack through recorded actions to recover an optimal resource-feasible selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Index the table by stage and remaining integral budget. Each transition chooses an action, subtracts its resource use, and adds its value.
assumptions_latex: Resource consumptions and budget \(B\) are nonnegative integers.
Stage rewards are additive and feasibility is determined by total resource consumption.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(n,B)\) equals the maximum value attainable with total resource consumption at most \(B\).

notation.meaning: best value through stage i with budget b
resource consumed by action a at stage i
value of action a at stage i

children.title: State-Resource Coupling
children.top_down_role: Dynamic programs whose state dimensions jointly encode structure and resource consumption.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Resource Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bellman states augmented by a discrete resource coordinate when continuation feasibility depends on remaining capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s\in S\) describe the structural state and let \(b\in\{0,\ldots,B\}\) be remaining resource. If action \(a\in A(s)\) has resource consumption \(r(s,a)\), immediate value \(c(s,a)\), and successor \(T(s,a)\), then the coupled value function satisfies \[F(s,b)=\operatorname{opt}_{a\in A(s):\,r(s,a)\le b}\bigl(c(s,a)+F(T(s,a),b-r(s,a))\bigr).\] Terminal values are specified for every terminal pair \((s,b)\). The resource coordinate is necessary whenever two histories reaching the same structural state permit different feasible continuations because they leave different resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augment each structural state with remaining resource. Transitions update both coordinates, preserving exactly the history information needed for future feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The structural state is Markovian once remaining resource is included.
Resource consumption is additive and discretely indexed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The product state \((s,b)\) admits a Bellman recurrence that distinguishes continuation sets with different remaining resources.

notation.meaning: optimal continuation value from the coupled state

knowledge_statements.title: Subset Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic programming whose states are subsets and whose transitions remove or add one admissible element.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a finite ground set and let \(F(S)\) denote the optimal value for the subproblem indexed by \(S\subseteq U\). Set \(F(\varnothing)=\beta\). Process subsets in increasing cardinality and compute \[F(S)=\operatorname{opt}_{x\in A(S)}\bigl(F(S\setminus\{x\})+c(S,x)\bigr),\] where \(A(S)\subseteq S\) contains exactly the elements that may be last in a feasible solution for \(S\). Store an optimizing \(x\), output \(F(U)\), and repeatedly remove stored elements to reconstruct an optimizer. Explicit enumeration uses \(2^{|U|}\) subset states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute each subset state from smaller subsets by choosing an admissible last element. Stored choices reconstruct an optimal ordering or subset-structured solution.
assumptions_latex: Optimal solutions admit decomposition by an admissible last element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recurrence computes the optimum for \(U\) using at most \(2^{|U|}\) subset states.

notation.meaning: optimal value for subset state S
admissible final elements for state S

children.title: Interval Dynamic Programming

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bottom-up optimization over contiguous intervals with split-based composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an ordered input indexed by \(1,\ldots,n\), let \(F(i,j)\) be the optimal value for interval \([i,j]\). Initialize singleton or empty intervals by the problem's base values. For lengths \(\ell=2,\ldots,n\), compute every interval with \(j-i+1=\ell\) using \[F(i,j)=\operatorname{opt}_{i\le k<j}\Phi_{i,k,j}\bigl(F(i,k),F(k+1,j)\bigr),\] where \(\Phi_{i,k,j}\) includes the cost of combining the two subsolutions. Record an optimizing split \(k\). Output \(F(1,n)\) and recursively follow stored splits to reconstruct an optimal decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve short contiguous intervals first, then combine two adjacent subintervals across every possible split. Stored split points reconstruct an optimal decomposition.
assumptions_latex: Every nontrivial feasible interval solution decomposes at a split point.
The objective of a split is determined by its two subproblem values and combination term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bottom-up recurrence computes \(F(1,n)\), the optimal value for the full interval.

notation.meaning: optimal value on interval from i through j

children.title: Sequence Dynamic Programming

knowledge_statements.title: Sequence Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prefix-indexed dynamic programming with a finite summary state for sequence decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the input positions be \(1,\ldots,n\), let \(Q\) be a finite summary-state set, and let \(\delta(q,a)\) be the state reached by action \(a\) from state \(q\). Initialize \(F(0,q_0)=0\) and \(F(0,q)=+\infty\) for \(q\ne q_0\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), compute \[F(i,q)=\min_{q'\in Q,\,a:\,\delta(q',a)=q}\bigl(F(i-1,q')+c_i(q',a)\bigr).\] Store minimizing predecessors, choose a permitted terminal state of minimum value, and backtrack to recover an optimal action sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process prefixes in order while retaining a finite state summarizing all relevant past decisions. Predecessor pointers recover an optimal action sequence.
assumptions_latex: The summary state makes future feasibility and costs independent of earlier history.
The total cost is additive across sequence positions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recurrence yields a minimum-cost feasible action sequence over all \(n\) positions.

notation.meaning: minimum cost for the first i positions ending in state q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Principle of Optimality for Sequential Decisions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence dynamic programming with stagewise decisions and backward recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a combinatorial optimization problem is solved by an optimal sequence of decisions $(D_1,\ldots,D_n)$. For each $k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the suffix $(D_{n-k+1},\ldots,D_n)$ is an optimal completion of the subproblem remaining after decisions $(D_1,\ldots,D_{n-k})$. Dynamic programming applies this principle by decomposing decisions into stages and deriving a recurrence from a later stage to the preceding stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every suffix of an optimal decision sequence is an optimal completion for the remaining subproblem determined by the preceding decisions. Dynamic programming uses this principle through a backward recurrence over decision stages.
assumptions_latex: (D_1,\ldots,D_n)\text{ is an optimal feasible decision sequence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (D_{n-k+1},\ldots,D_n)\text{ is an optimal completion after }(D_1,\ldots,D_{n-k}).

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Decomposition Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Table dynamic programming over a rooted tree decomposition with bounded boundary-state complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\{X_t\}_{t\in V(T)})\) be a rooted tree decomposition of a graph \(G\) of width \(k\). For each node \(t\), construct a table \(D_t\) indexed by realizable boundary summaries \(\sigma\) on bag \(X_t\). Process \(T\) bottom-up: introduce nodes extend compatible child summaries, forget nodes optimize over discarded boundary information, and join nodes combine compatible child entries while correcting duplicated bag contributions. At the root, optimize over accepting summaries and follow stored choices to reconstruct a solution. If each bag has at most \(f(k)\) summaries, a direct implementation uses \(O(|V(T)|f(k)^2)\) combination time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree decomposition localizes graph interactions to bags. Bottom-up tables combine compatible boundary summaries, yielding fixed-parameter running time when the number of summaries depends only on width.
assumptions_latex: A rooted tree decomposition of width \(k\) is supplied.
Feasibility and objective contributions compose through finite bag-boundary summaries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatible table composition returns an optimal solution in \(O(|V(T)|f(k)^2)\) time under direct pairwise joins.

notation.meaning: upper bound on boundary summaries per bag

children.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Dynamic Programming

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numeric dynamic programs polynomial in magnitudes of integer data but not necessarily in their bit lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an integer-valued optimization instance with ordinary combinatorial size \(n\) and a nonnegative numeric parameter \(B\) encoded in binary. A dynamic program with \(O(nB)\) states and polynomial work per state is pseudo-polynomial: its running time is polynomial in \(n\) and the magnitude \(B\), but may be exponential in the input length because \(B\) can be as large as \(2^{\Theta(\log B)}\). It is polynomial-time only when \(B\) is polynomially bounded in the remaining input size or is encoded in unary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A table polynomial in a numeric bound is pseudo-polynomial because the bound's magnitude can be exponential in its binary encoding length.
assumptions_latex: The numeric parameter \(B\) is a nonnegative integer encoded in binary.
The dynamic program has \(O(nB)\) states and polynomial work per state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The running time is polynomial in \(n\) and \(B\), but not necessarily polynomial in the binary input length \(n+\log B\).

notation.meaning: binary encoding length up to constant factors

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value scaling converts a magnitude-dependent exact dynamic program into a polynomial approximation scheme under bounded additive loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a maximization problem selecting at most \(n\) objects with nonnegative values \(v_i\), and suppose an exact dynamic program is polynomial in the sum of integral values. Let \(v_{\max}\) be the value of a feasible singleton, choose \(K=\varepsilon v_{\max}/n\), and define \(v_i'=\lfloor v_i/K\rfloor\). Run the exact dynamic program using \(v_i'\), but return the selected solution evaluated under the original values. If \(v_{\max}\le\mathrm{OPT}\), rounding loses less than \(nK\le\varepsilon\mathrm{OPT}\); hence the returned value is at least \((1-\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\), while the scaled total is at most \(n^2/\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round values to a coarser scale before running an exact numeric dynamic program. The smaller table becomes polynomial in inverse accuracy while losing at most an epsilon fraction.
assumptions_latex: At most \(n\) objects are selected and all values are nonnegative.
The exact dynamic program is polynomial in the total scaled value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scaling yields value at least \((1-\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\) with scaled numeric range at most \(n^2/\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: scaled integral value of object i

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Scheme Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic conversion of pseudo-polynomial dynamic programming into an approximation scheme by geometric value scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a maximization problem with nonnegative integral item values, optimum [1m[0m\(\mathrm{OPT}>0\), and a pseudo-polynomial dynamic program whose running time is polynomial in the input length and the largest scaled total value. Given [1m[0m\(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), choose a computable bound [1m[0m\(L\leq \mathrm{OPT}\leq U\) with [1m[0m\(U/L\) polynomially bounded, set [1m[0m\(K=\varepsilon L/n\), and replace each value [1m[0m\(v_i\) by [1m[0m\(\widehat v_i=\lfloor v_i/K\rfloor\). If the dynamic program optimizes exactly over the scaled instance and its states preserve feasibility, the returned feasible solution has value at least [1m[0m\((1-\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\), with running time polynomial in the input length and [1m[0m\(1/\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling objective values can turn a suitable pseudo-polynomial dynamic program into an FPTAS, provided feasibility survives scaling and rounding loss is bounded by an epsilon fraction of optimum.
assumptions_latex: The scaled dynamic program is exact and polynomial in \(|I|\) and the scaled value bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(S)\geq(1-\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\) in time \(\operatorname{poly}(|I|,1/\varepsilon)\).

The complexity-bound kind fits the approximation-scheme interface, but the generic theorem is not reliable as written.

knowledge_statements.title: State Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential growth of distinguishable dynamic-programming states despite a polynomial number of decomposition stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a decomposition have [1m[0m\(m\) stages and an interface [1m[0m\(B_k\) at stage [1m[0m\(k\). Suppose every subset [1m[0m\(S\subseteq B_k\) can occur as a partial-solution signature and, for any distinct [1m[0m\(S,T\subseteq B_k\), some completion is feasible or has a different optimum after signature [1m[0m\(S\) but not after [1m[0m\(T\). Any exact dynamic program that merges partial solutions only when all completions treat them identically must therefore retain at least [1m[0m\(2^{|B_k|}\) states at stage [1m[0m\(k\). Consequently, polynomially many stages do not imply polynomial running time when interface size is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every interface subset has distinguishable future behavior, an exact dynamic program needs exponentially many states even when it has only polynomially many stages.
assumptions_latex: All \(2^{|B_k|}\) subset signatures are realizable and pairwise completion-distinguishable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact state space at stage \(k\) has cardinality at least \(2^{|B_k|}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the counting conclusion is plausible under pairwise completion distinguishability. However, the condition saying a completion is feasible or has a different optimum after one signature but not the other is not formally defined, and no source supports the chosen state-equivalence model.

children.title: Nonseparable Dependence
children.top_down_role: Failure of useful subproblem composition under long-range interactions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonseparable Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of bounded-state decomposition when future contributions depend on the entire partial solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a decomposition cut, let [1m[0m\(P\) denote a partial solution and [1m[0m\(Q\) a completion. A state map [1m[0m\(\sigma\) is sufficient only if [1m[0m\(\sigma(P_1)=\sigma(P_2)\) implies that, for every admissible [1m[0m\(Q\), feasibility of [1m[0m\(P_1\cup Q\) equals feasibility of [1m[0m\(P_2\cup Q\) and their objective contributions differ by a constant independent of [1m[0m\(Q\). If every pair of distinct partial solutions is separated by some completion, this implication forces [1m[0m\(\sigma\) to be injective. Thus no compression into fewer states than partial solutions is exact; exponential many partial solutions yield exponential state complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic programming cannot compress partial solutions when some future completion distinguishes every pair by feasibility or relative objective value.
assumptions_latex: The decomposition combines partial solutions \(P\) with admissible completions \(Q\).
Every distinct \(P_1,P_2\) is distinguished by at least one completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every exact sufficient state map \(\sigma\) is injective on the partial solutions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the container. A source is needed for the exact sufficient-state equivalence being asserted, including the admissible completion domain and the convention under which objective contributions may differ by a completion-independent constant.

children.title: Interface-Width Barriers
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of decomposition when separators or boundary states become too large.

knowledge_statements.title: Interface-Width Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-space lower bound induced by a decomposition interface carrying independent binary information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an exact dynamic program over a decomposition with an interface of width [1m[0m\(w\). If each interface element carries an independent binary condition and all [1m[0m\(2^w\) assignments are realizable and pairwise distinguishable by completions, then every completion-sufficient state representation contains at least [1m[0m\(2^w\) states. Any implementation explicitly processing every such state requires [1m[0m\(\Omega(2^w)\) time and space at that interface. Hence a running-time form [1m[0m\(f(w)\operatorname{poly}(n)\) is polynomial only when [1m[0m\(f(w)\) is polynomially bounded on the admitted instances; for [1m[0m\(f(w)=2^w\), this includes [1m[0m\(w=O(\log n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interface encoding independent binary choices forces at least two-to-the-width states; exponential-width dependence is polynomial only for logarithmic width.
assumptions_latex: All binary interface assignments are realizable and pairwise completion-distinguishable.
The implementation explicitly stores and processes each sufficient state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Time and space are \(\Omega(2^w)\); if \(w=O(\log n)\), then \(2^w=\operatorname{poly}(n)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary distinguishability argument is plausible but lacks a source and a formal interface model. In this exact terminal container the primary role is a dynamic-programming failure boundary, not merely a complexity bound; a sourced replacement should use content_kind failure_boundary while retaining the quantitative lower bound.

children.title: Augmenting-Path Methods
children.top_down_role: Improvement families based on path-shaped certificates.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with source \(s\in V\), sink \(t\in V\), and integral capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}\).
\(x:E\to\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}\) is a feasible integral \(s\)-\(t\) flow.
Residual capacities are defined relative to the current flow \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure terminates, and the output \(x\) is a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed network \(G=(V,E)\), integral capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}\), a source \(s\in V\), a sink \(t\in V\), and a feasible integral flow \(x\), form the residual network with forward residual capacity \(u_{ij}-x_{ij}\) and reverse residual capacity \(x_{ij}\). While an \(s\)-\(t\) residual path \(P\) exists, set \(\delta=\min_{a\in P}r_a\), increase the flow by \(\delta\) on forward arcs of \(P\), and decrease it by \(\delta\) on reverse arcs. When no such path exists, output \(x\). The procedure terminates, and the final flow is maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly send the bottleneck amount along a source-to-sink residual path. With integral capacities the process terminates, and when no such path remains the feasible flow is maximum.
